reproduction.text: Monster and Dragon egg groups, 20 egg cycles, 87.5% male; the sex ratio is shared with the other starter lines and is probably a game convention.
The young hatch with the tail flame already burning.
Nothing describes courtship, nests or parental care.

defense.text: Its breath inflicts terrible pain on enemies.
Smokescreen (Lv 10) and Scary Face (Lv 21) are wild level-up moves: smoke to blind and a threat face to deter.
Blaze strengthens its fire when it is close to defeat.
Its sheer size, flight and fire leave few animals that could threaten it; no predator is named.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses.
Charmander's tail flame makes a sound as it burns, audible only in quiet places; whether the adult's is louder is not recorded.

life_cycle.text: Charmander (0.6 m, 8.5 kg) becomes Charmeleon at level 16 (1.1 m, 19 kg) and Charizard at level 36 (1.7 m, 90.5 kg). The last step nearly quintuples its mass as it gains wings and the Flying type.
The juvenile's flame shows its strength and emotions: weak when it is weak, bright when healthy, wavering when happy, blazing when enraged; when healthy it keeps burning even if a bit wet.
Charmeleon is the aggressive stage: barbaric in nature, it whips its fiery tail around, slashes with sharp claws and destroys foes without pity; a strong foe makes its tail flare bluish-white.
As Charmeleon, its swinging tail raises the air temperature to unbearable levels, and when agitated it spouts flames that incinerate its surroundings.
Crystal says its fire grows hotter as it gains battle experience; Diamond, Pearl and Platinum give the same idea only as something 'it is said'.
Read as development, the line goes from a fragile juvenile whose flame is its life, through an indiscriminately aggressive adolescent, to a flying adult that chooses its fights.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Fire by level-up: Ember (Lv 7), Fire Fang (Lv 28), Flamethrower (Lv 42), Fire Spin (Lv 49), Heat Wave (Lv 59) and Flare Blitz (Lv 66).
Claws: Slash (Lv 32), with Dragon Claw and Shadow Claw available at Lv 1, matching the sharp claws of the Charmeleon entries.
Flight: Wing Attack comes at Lv 36, as it evolves, and Air Slash at Lv 1. Fly itself is a machine move taught by people.

ecology.text: A fire-maker that changes landscapes: its flames can set forests alight, by accident.
Fires it starts would open the canopy and reset parts of a forest, with knock-on effects for everything living there.
Its trophic position is unknown because its diet is never given.

humans.text: Known to cause forest fires unintentionally, so it is a fire hazard wherever it lives near people.
In the games the line reaches people only as a starter: there are no wild ones.

homestead.text: Air travel and long-range errands: its wings carry it close to 4,600 feet, and Fly (a taught move) lets it carry its trainer.
A heat source in winter, if kept under control: it already features as a candidate for the Hearth hall.
A light after dark: the tail flame of the line shines at night like a star.

Fire safety comes first: keep it away from the hay store, timber and the Glasshouse plantings, and never let it fight near buildings, since its fire melts boulders and can start forest fires by accident.
Its tail flame is a built-in health check: in the juvenile a weak flame means a weak animal, so keepers can read it daily.
Young Charmander need shelter from Blackthorn's rain and snow: their life depends on the tail flame, which only a healthy one keeps burning when a bit wet.

microhabitat: high air up to about 1,400 m
niche.foraging: not described; it flies widely in search of opponents
niche.note: Diet is never stated for any stage, so no guild or trophic level is given.

relationships.note: It sets forest fires by accident.
Charmander prefers them; whether the adult does is not stated.

ecotypes.name: Crag duellist
ecotypes.reading: Dragon Dance raises speed and strength, read here as a display before a fight; Dragon Rush is a full-body charge and Outrage a sustained rampage. A lineage that settles contests with rivals by display and then open combat, the adult's search for strong opponents made central. Fits high crags where flying rivals meet.
ecotypes.behavior: Displays from a high perch, then dives at the challenger.

ecotypes.name: Scree hunter
ecotypes.reading: Rock Slide and Ancient Power bring stone down or hurl it, and Metal Claw is a hard-edged slash. A lineage that works broken rock, loosening scree onto whatever is below and finishing with claws. Fits steep, rocky mountains like those where Charmeleon live.
ecotypes.behavior: Hunts along cliff edges, sending stones down before it follows.

ecotypes.name: Pack raider
ecotypes.reading: Beat Up is an attack the user's companions all join, and Bite and Crunch are jaw attacks. A lineage that hunts or fights in groups and uses its jaws more than its fire. Fits mountain valleys where many Charmeleon live within sight of one another.
ecotypes.behavior: Attacks as a group; the jaws do the work, the fire is held back.

open_questions: What does any stage of the line eat?
Where do wild Charizard live? No Gen I–IV game has a wild one of any stage.
Does the adult's life depend on its tail flame, as Charmander's does?
Does its fire really grow hotter with experience? Crystal says so; Diamond, Pearl and Platinum only report it as hearsay.
Why does it spare weaker opponents? Is it a contest rule, or about energy?
Do Charmeleon live in groups, as 'tails shine at night like stars' suggests?
How does a flame-tailed juvenile survive rain and snow in the mountains?

contradictions.topic: Fire temperature and experience: fact or saying
contradictions.note: Crystal (6.5) states that its fire gets hotter as it gains battle experience; Diamond, Pearl and Platinum (6.10) give the same claim only as 'it is said'. The content agrees; the confidence doesn't.

folklore.text: It is said that Charizard's fire burns hotter if it has experienced harsh battles.
folklore.note: Crystal (6.5) states the same thing as fact.

folklore.text: When it rains, steam is said to spout from the tip of Charmander's tail.
folklore.note: Line folklore, from the juvenile's entries.

Crobat.summary: A four-winged bat whose hind legs have become a second pair of wings, built for fast, nearly silent flight in the dark. Crobat sneaks up on prey on wings that barely make a sound, and on long flights it rests one pair while flying on the other. Its line is the most familiar night animal of Johto's caves: eyeless, echolocating Zubat that roost by day and avoid sunlight, and Golbat, which drink the blood of people and Pokémon and are common in the Ice Path next to Blackthorn. Crobat itself is never wild; it comes only from a Golbat that is close to its trainer.

anatomy.text: A large bat (1.8 m, 75.0 kg) with four wings: its hind legs have turned into a second pair.
Four wings make it faster and quieter in flight, and clumsier on the ground.
anatomy.analogy: Owls achieve near-silent flight differently, with comb-like leading edges and soft fringes on their flight feathers that break up turbulence.

anatomy.text: Golbat has four sharp fangs with small holes for sucking blood, able to puncture even thick, tough hides.
Zubat has no eyes (or eyes grown shut) and finds its way by ultrasonic cries from its mouth.

diet.text: Crobat hunts by stealth: it sneaks up on its intended prey with wings that barely make a sound. The prey is not named.
Golbat drinks blood, from people and Pokémon alike: more than ten ounces (about 300 ml) at a gulp, and it won't stop until it is full, even if it then gets too heavy to fly well.
diet.analogy: The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) also lives on blood alone and can take about half its body weight in a feed, which leaves it heavy enough that it has to shed water quickly before flying.

diet.text: Golbat looks for neck veins and strikes from behind without warning.
Whether Crobat still drinks blood is not stated; its moves suggest it does (Leech Life at Lv 1, Bite, Poison Fang), and its stealthy approach fits the same feeding.

habitat.text: Caves and dark places: Zubat forms colonies in perpetually dark places and roosts by day in caves, old buildings and deep forest. Its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is cave.
Crobat rests by hanging from a tree branch with its rear legs, so it roosts in trees as well as caves.
Crobat is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game.

Golbat is common in the Ice Path (30% on every floor at any hour in HeartGold and SoulSilver; 50-60% in Crystal) and present at the Blackthorn entrance of Dark Cave, so the line lives right around Blackthorn. Zubat and Golbat are in nearly every Johto cave, plus some routes at night.

behavior.text: Nocturnal: Crobat turns active when night comes; Golbat is most active in pitch-black, moonless nights; Zubat sleeps until sundown.
Zubat avoids sunlight, which burns it slightly or makes it unhealthy; it spends daylight hanging upside down, unmoving, in dark places.
Crobat flies long distances by switching wings: flying on one pair means it has come a long way, and by alternately resting front and rear wings it can fly all day without stopping.
It flies so silently through the dark that it may go unnoticed even close by.

social.text: Zubat are colonial: they gather by day and hang from the ceilings of caves and old buildings.
Nothing says whether Golbat or Crobat live in colonies.

reproduction.text: Flying egg group, even sex ratio, 15 egg cycles (shorter than most). Nothing is said about roost nurseries or young.

defense.text: Silence and darkness are its cover; no entry describes predators of the line.
Inner Focus, its only ability, means it can't be made to flinch. Its own moves include Confuse Ray, Supersonic, Screech and Haze.

senses.text: Echolocation: Zubat emits ultrasonic waves from its mouth and reads their reflections to find its way and detect obstacles and targets.
senses.analogy: Most bats echolocate the same way, by reading the echoes of their own calls, though unlike Zubat all real bats have working eyes.

senses.text: Its eyes grew shut over generations of living in pitch-black caverns, by the Emerald account.
senses.analogy: Cave animals often lose their eyes over evolutionary time, as in the blind cave form of the Mexican tetra (Astyanax mexicanus).

senses.text: Whether Crobat keeps echolocating is not said, but its silent approach to prey in the dark implies a sense that works without light.

life_cycle.text: Zubat (0.8 m, 7.5 kg) becomes Golbat at level 22 (1.6 m, 55.0 kg), and Golbat becomes Crobat (1.8 m, 75.0 kg) when it levels up with high friendship.
The new hind wings appear at the last change. Crystal describes them as growing 'as a result of its pursuit of faster, yet more silent flight', a striving-produces-the-trait explanation.
life_cycle.note: Lamarckian phrasing, and Emerald's 'over the course of evolution' blurs individual development with descent. Worth a reviewer's eye.

life_cycle.text: That the final stage needs a close bond with a trainer, not age or size, means wild Crobat may be rare or absent.
life_cycle.note: A friendship trigger read as biology.

moves_in_the_wild.text: The feeding moves are its own: Leech Life (Lv 1), Bite (Lv 13), Poison Fang (Lv 39), and Cross Poison at Lv 1 for Crobat; draining and biting, as the blood-drinking canon would predict.
Supersonic (Lv 5) and Screech are the sound-producing moves of an echolocating animal used offensively.
Mean Look (Lv 33) stops prey escaping, which matches Golbat's refusal to let go once it bites.
Wing Attack, Air Cutter and Air Slash are its own flight moves; Fly is taught.

ecology.text: A blood-feeding micropredator of large animals, people included (trophic level about 3): it takes a meal without killing the host.
Colonial cave roosts concentrate the line, and their droppings (not described) would feed cave communities as bat guano does in real caves.
ecology.note: Guano is not mentioned anywhere in the entries.

ecology.text: Golbat is in the Ice Path with Swinub and Jynx, and on Mt. Silver with Sneasel and Larvitar. Since it drinks the blood of Pokémon, these are its likeliest hosts there.
ecology.note: Co-occurrence plus a general diet; no entry names a host species.

ecology.text: Zubat shares Sinnoh's Wayward Cave with Gible (Zubat 35%).

humans.text: Golbat attacks people at night and drinks their blood, seeking neck veins.
Crobat is the opposite case: it exists only through a strong bond with a person.
Zubat roosts under the eaves of old houses as well as in caves.

homestead.text: A local threat: Golbat are common in the Ice Path and at Dark Cave's Blackthorn entrance, and they drink the blood of people and Pokémon at night. Shut the nursery, pens and Glasshouse at dusk, and expect them in the Ice Path cold vault.
A bonded Crobat as a night scout: fast, silent flight in the dark, unnoticed even close by.
A long-range courier: it can fly all day by resting its wings in turn.
Night travel: the line is built for it, and Zubat's echolocation finds obstacles in total darkness.
Needs: a dark, quiet roost for the day, away from sunlight, which harms the young.
It walks badly; give it perches, not floor space.

niche.foraging: silent nocturnal approach and blood-feeding through punctured skin, guided by echolocation
niche.note: Blood-feeding is Golbat's; Crobat's own prey is not named. 'Parasite' in the sense of a blood-feeding micropredator that leaves its host alive.

relationships.note: Golbat feeds on their blood.
Day roosts.
Ice Path (Golbat).
Mt. Silver (Golbat).
Wayward Cave, Sinnoh (Zubat).

ecotypes.name: Sleeper's bat
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that feeds on hosts it has put to sleep: Hypnosis induces sleep, and Feint Attack is an approach that never misses. A quiet way to take blood from a large animal without a struggle. Fits pasture and farmland near cave roosts, where large animals sleep in the open.
ecotypes.behavior: Lands beside a sleeping animal, keeps it asleep, feeds and leaves before it wakes.
ecotypes.analogy: Common vampire bats mostly feed on sleeping livestock, approaching on the ground.

ecotypes.name: Wind-rider
ecotypes.reading: A lineage for open air: Gust and Whirlwind are blasts of wing-driven air, Brave Bird a reckless full-speed dive. A strong, fast flier that commutes far from its roost to feed. Fits windy highland ridges and sea cliffs.
ecotypes.behavior: Flies further and higher than cave-bound kin; dives on prey in the open.

ecotypes.name: Fleeing-prey hawk
ecotypes.reading: A chaser rather than a sneak: Pursuit hits harder at prey that tries to flee, Quick Attack closes the distance first. A lineage that takes active, flying prey on the wing. Fits forest edges and clearings at night, where flying prey is abundant.
ecotypes.behavior: Hunts moving prey in the air; less dependent on sleeping hosts.

open_questions: Does Crobat still drink blood, or does its stealth serve some other prey?
Does Crobat echolocate, and does it have eyes? Zubat's entries disagree about eyes.
If four wings make it 'tough to stop and rest' (169.2), how does that fit Sapphire's account of resting on a branch (169.5)?
Do Golbat and Crobat form colonies like Zubat?
Which Pokémon does Golbat actually feed on in the Ice Path and on Mt. Silver?
Are wild Crobat possible, given that the trigger is friendship with a trainer?

contradictions.text: Resting: Silver and SoulSilver say four wings make it tough to stop and rest; Sapphire describes it resting by hanging from a branch with its rear legs.
Activity: Diamond says Crobat becomes active at night; Emerald says it can fly all day without stopping.
contradictions.note: 'All day' may mean continuously rather than in daylight.

contradictions.text: Zubat's eyes: Emerald says they grew shut over time; FireRed and Diamond say it has no eyes.

Delibird.summary: A cliff-nesting bird of cold mountains that carries its food bundled in its tail wherever it goes, ferries it to its chicks all day, and throws it at anything that attacks. Several entries add that it shares that food with people lost in the mountains, and tell of an explorer who reached the top of Mt. Everest thanks to one; the tales are kept under folklore here. No entry says what the food actually is. In HeartGold and SoulSilver it lives only in SoulSilver's Ice Path.

anatomy.text: A winged body, 0.9 m and 16.0 kg, typed Ice and Flying.
It carries its food bundled up, or rolled up, in its tail.
anatomy.analogy: Clark's nutcracker (Nucifraga columbiana), a bird of western North American mountains, carries pine seeds in a pouch under its tongue to its caches.

anatomy.text: Whether the tail is a pouch or a wrap is not said; 'bundled' and 'rolled' suggest the tail folds around the load.

diet.text: No entry says what its food is.
It carries food all day long and always has it with it, wherever it goes.
Its only level-up move is Present (Lv 1), the games' version of handing over, or throwing, a parcel.
The Water 1 egg group and the egg move Splash hint at a tie to water, perhaps fishing, but nothing says it eats fish.
diet.note: Egg groups are a breeding mechanic, not a diet record.

habitat.text: It nests at the edge of sharp cliffs, in the mountains.
In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is a SoulSilver exclusive: 20% on all four Ice Path floors (1F, B1F, B2F, B3F) at any time of day, Lv 22-23. In HeartGold the same 20% slot holds Zubat instead.

Silver also had it at all times; Crystal only at night (40%); Gold not at all. Elsewhere: Icefall Cave in FireRed only (5%), and swarms on Route 216 (Diamond, Pearl) and Route 217 (Platinum). The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is mountain.
It is met inside the Ice Path but nests on cliffs, so the cave is probably where it travels or shelters rather than where it breeds.

behavior.text: It spends all day carrying food to its waiting chicks.
It has a habit of sharing food with people lost in the mountains.
behavior.note: Stated as a habit in Diamond, Pearl and Platinum; the older entries tell it as tales.

behavior.text: Vital Spirit (it can't fall asleep) suits an animal said to work all day.
All-day food carrying points to a day-active bird, but Crystal's tables have it only at night and the HGSS tables don't split it.

social.text: Parents provision their chicks at the nest.
Whether it nests alone or in cliff colonies is not said.
Sharing food with lost people is an unusual habit: it gives a resource to another species at a cost to itself.

reproduction.text: It raises chicks in a nest at a cliff edge and feeds them all day.
Water 1 and Field egg groups, 20 egg cycles, even sex ratio.

defense.text: If attacked, it throws its food at the opponent.
Present is the game form of that throw.
Throwing the food spends the provisions it carries for its chicks, so it is presumably a last resort.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. Finding lost people implies it notices them, but how is not described.

life_cycle.text: A single-stage species: no evolution in Generations I-IV.
Chicks are fed at the nest; nothing describes how long they stay or when they fledge.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Present is its only level-up move, the narrowest wild repertoire in the highlands community. Everything else is an egg move, a tutor move or a machine (Fly among them), so its wild behaviour has to be read from the entries, not the moves.

ecology.text: A carrier: it moves food from wherever it forages to cliff nests, so it shifts nutrients across the landscape, with spillage and droppings collecting below the nests.
ecology.note: Follows from the carrying habit; scale unknown.
ecology.analogy: Seabird colonies fertilise the cliffs and slopes below them with droppings, producing nutrient-rich soils.

ecology.text: No predator of Delibird is named. In SoulSilver it shares the Ice Path with Golbat, which drinks the blood of Pokémon.
ecology.note: Co-occurrence plus Golbat's stated diet only.

ecology.text: Its trophic level can't be set until its food is known.

humans.text: Its reputation is as a saviour of people lost in the mountains: it shares its food with them.
A famous explorer is said to have reached the peak of Mt. Everest thanks to a Delibird sharing its food.
humans.note: A single anecdote; filed under folklore as well.

homestead.text: It carries a bundle of food all day; it could carry small loads, such as a parcel between the homestead and Blackthorn, if it can be trained to carry something other than its own food.
homestead.note: Load size and willingness to carry objects are unknown.

homestead.text: A companion for Ice Path crossings: its habit of sharing food with lost people makes it the community's closest thing to a mountain rescuer.
homestead.note: The habit is described for wild birds and lost strangers; untested in a trained one.

homestead.text: Ice-typed, so it would be at home in the highland winter.
It would need a high ledge or cliff shelf to nest on, and something to carry.
The homestead's Delibird as the post: a bird that turns up at the door with a tail-bundle from town.

niche.foraging: unknown food, carried in the tail all day and delivered to chicks

relationships.note: Nest sites.
Graveler gouge horizontal holes in sheer cliff faces; a cliff-nesting bird could use them. Neither entry mentions the other.
Shares the Ice Path in SoulSilver; Golbat drinks Pokémon blood. Untested.

ecotypes.name: Nest guard
ecotypes.reading: Three moves that strike first. A lineage that defends nest and food by hitting before it is hit, instead of throwing its food away. Fits crowded cliff ledges where thieves come close.
ecotypes.behavior: Keeps its bundle; drives intruders off fast.

ecotypes.name: Snow roller
ecotypes.reading: Two rolling moves: a lineage that travels downslope by rolling, bundle and all. Fits long, open snowfields above the Ice Path, where rolling is cheaper than flying.
ecotypes.behavior: Comes down the mountain tumbling; walks or flies back up.

ecotypes.name: Far-seer
ecotypes.reading: A foresight move is odd for a bird. A lineage reading ahead could be the one behind the tales of Delibird appearing for lost travellers; Aurora Beam is a light display that would carry in the dark of the Ice Path. The most speculative of the three.
ecotypes.behavior: Turns up where it is needed before it is called.

open_questions: What food does it carry, and where does it get it?
Is it day-active (all-day carrying, 225.2) or night-active (Crystal's night-only tables)?
Does it nest in the Ice Path, or only on cliffs outside it?
How does it find lost people (225.6), and why share food meant for its chicks?
Should the reconstruction treat Delibird as present in the Ice Path (SoulSilver, where it takes a 20% slot) or absent (HeartGold, where Zubat takes that slot)?
Its egg groups (Water 1, Field) and the egg move Splash hint at water. Does it swim or fish?

folklore.text: There are tales about lost people who were saved by the food it carried.
A famous explorer reached the peak of Mt. Everest thanks to a Delibird sharing its food.

Donphan.summary: Donphan is a heavy, tusked herd animal of rough mountain country: 1.1 m tall but 120 kg, with a hide so tough that ordinary blows don't scratch it. It attacks by curling into a ball and rolling into its foe, and its charge is said to be able to knock down a house. Rank in the herd goes by tusk size, and tusks take a long time to grow. As Phanpy it is a riverbank youngster that nests in pits dug at the water's edge, showers with its trunk in the quiet morning hours and cools itself by fanning its ears. In Johto the line lives on Route 45, the mountain road below Blackthorn, but only in Silver, Crystal and HeartGold.

anatomy.text: A compact, very dense quadruped: 1.1 m and 120 kg, Ground type.
Sharp, hard tusks and a rugged hide toughened to a rock-hard state; an ordinary attack won't leave a scratch on it.
Its tusks take a long time to grow.
anatomy.analogy: Elephant tusks are incisors that keep growing through life, so their size broadly tracks age.

anatomy.text: As Phanpy it has a long, dexterous trunk and big ears that it uses as fans.
Its body can curl into a ball for rolling.

diet.text: No entry for Phanpy or Donphan says what it eats.
Phanpy learns Natural Gift by level-up (Lv 19), a move that needs a held Berry, and has the Pickup ability; both hint that the line handles and collects food items, perhaps fruit.
diet.note: The machine reading's 'lithovore' came from its Ground type alone; nothing supports rock-eating.

habitat.text: Gen 3 Pokédex habitat: rough terrain. The adult entries put it on mountain trails, where it clears rock and mud slides.
The juvenile is tied to rivers: Phanpy digs its nest at a river's edge, comes ashore to shower, and dries itself at the water's edge.
Taken together, the line seems to need both: rugged slopes for the adults and river margins for nesting and young.

In Johto it is a version exclusive: Silver and HeartGold have it, Gold and SoulSilver do not. Phanpy is on Route 45 (and in HeartGold on Mt. Silver); Donphan on Mt. Silver, Route 28 and Victory Road, and in Crystal on Route 45.
Route 45 is the mountain road running south from Blackthorn, so in the games that carry it the line is a near neighbour of the homestead.
habitat.note: The route's position is from the game map, not from the evidence pack.

habitat.text: Outside Johto, Phanpy only: in the Hoenn Safari Zone (the acro-bike area), on two canyons of the Sevii Islands in FireRed and LeafGreen, and on Sinnoh's Route 207 only during a swarm.

behavior.text: Its favourite attack is to curl into a ball and charge, rolling at high speed; once rolling it can't easily stop.
behavior.analogy: Rolling into a ball is a defence in pangolins and three-banded armadillos; using it as an attack has no close real counterpart.

behavior.text: Phanpy comes ashore during the deserted morning hours to shower with its trunk.

Crystal's tables agree: Phanpy appears only in the morning, on Routes 45 and 46, and Donphan on Route 45 only in the morning and day. The line looks diurnal with a morning peak, at least in Crystal; Silver and HeartGold don't split by time for Phanpy.
Phanpy cools off by flapping its ears when hot.
behavior.analogy: African elephants dump heat the same way: blood flowing through the thin, vessel-rich ears is cooled as the ears are flapped.

social.text: Donphan lives in herds ranked by tusk size: the longer and bigger the tusks, the higher the rank.
Because tusks take long to grow, rank probably tracks age, with the oldest animals at the top.
Phanpy are social at the water: when they gather they douse each other thoroughly with water.
social.analogy: Elephants spray water and dust over themselves and each other with the trunk.

social.text: Phanpy shows affection by bumping with its snout, hard enough to send a person flying.

reproduction.text: Phanpy nests in a vertical pit it digs in the ground at the edge of a river, and marks the area around the nest with its trunk to show it is taken.
Nest-site marking implies nest sites are contested, and that others of its kind read the marks.
Field egg group, 20 egg cycles, an even sex ratio.
Even the young are very strong.
Crystal has a Phanpy at level 2 on Route 46 in the morning, the lowest-level wild one in any game, which could be read as a hatchling near its nest.
reproduction.note: Encounter levels are a game-design choice; this is a lead, not evidence of breeding there.

defense.text: Armour: a hide so tough that a normal attack won't scratch it.
Sturdy means it can't be knocked out in one blow, the game form of that hide.
The claim that ordinary attacks don't scratch it is best read as a description of a very tough hide, not an immunity: Normal-type moves damage it normally in every game.
Attack as defence: the rolling charge, and a tackle that can destroy a house.
Scary Face (Lv 39) and Growl (Lv 1) are its threat displays among level-up moves.

senses.text: Phanpy learns Odor Sleuth at level 1, a sniffing move, which suggests the trunk is a nose in function as well as form.
If it smells well, the trunk-marking around the nest (231.4) is most plausibly scent marking.
senses.note: The entry says it marks the area with its trunk, not how.

life_cycle.text: Phanpy (0.5 m, 33.5 kg) becomes Donphan at level 25 (1.1 m, 120 kg), more than tripling its mass.
Development runs from a playful, trunk-swinging juvenile tied to the riverbank to an armoured, tusked adult of the slopes; the tusks keep growing after evolution and set the animal's rank.
The juvenile's playful swinging of its snout is already dangerous because of its strength.
Phanpy is strong enough to pick up and carry an adult human on its back.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Travel and attack: Defense Curl (Lv 1), Rapid Spin (Lv 6) and Rollout (Lv 15) are the rolling charge in move form.
Tusks: Horn Attack (Lv 1) and Fury Attack (Lv 25) are jabbing moves, the natural use of a pair of tusks.
Ground: Magnitude (Lv 19) and Earthquake (Lv 46) shake the ground, which fits a 120 kg animal that rolls and stamps.
Knock Off (Lv 10), which knocks an item from the target's grip, matches a trunk or tusks that can swat.
moves_in_the_wild.note: A reading of the move, not of any entry.

ecology.text: A landscape engineer: it clears rock and mud slides from mountain trails, so it shapes the routes that other animals and people use.
Phanpy's nest pits in riverbanks are excavations that other animals could reuse once abandoned.
ecology.note: Nothing says what happens to old nests.

ecology.text: It shares Route 45 and the slopes of Mt. Silver with Geodude, Graveler and Gligar, all rock or ground animals of broken terrain.
Its trophic role is unclear because its diet is unknown; if it grazes or browses, it is a primary consumer (level 2).
ecology.note: Diet is never stated.

humans.text: It helps people by clearing rock and mud slides that block mountain trails.
It is strong enough to haul a dump truck easily.
Danger: its tackle can knock down a house, and even the juvenile's affectionate bumps can send a person flying.

homestead.text: The homestead's heavy hauler: it can easily haul a dump truck, so carts, sledges and logs are well within reach.
Track and road crew for the mountain approaches: clearing rock and mud slides is something it already does for people.
Phanpy can carry an adult on its back, but only over short distances and for light riders at its 0.5 m size; how far is unrecorded.
Needs: a stream or pond for showering and cooling, especially for the young, and digging ground at the bank if it is to breed.
Keep it away from buildings when it is excited or rolling: once it starts rolling it can't easily stop, and its charge can knock a house down.
Its herd sorts itself by tusk size, so keeping several adults together may mean contests over rank.

niche.foraging: not described
niche.note: Diet is never stated; the guild follows from body plan alone. The diurnal reading rests on Crystal's tables and 231.3.

relationships.note: Nest pits are dug at the river's edge; the young shower and dry off there.
It clears rock and mud slides that block them.
Route 45, Mt. Silver and Victory Road.
Route 45 in Crystal and HeartGold.
Mt. Silver in HeartGold.
Route 45 in Crystal, by day.

ecotypes.name: Rockfall ram
ecotypes.reading: Head Smash is a headlong ram that hurts the user too, Focus Energy is a gathering-up before the strike, and Body Slam is the full weight thrown in. Together they suggest a lineage that charges head-first through obstacles instead of rolling: the trail-clearing habit made into a way of life. Fits steep scree and avalanche-prone slopes.
ecotypes.behavior: Lowers its head and drives straight through fallen rock.

ecotypes.name: Herd shield
ecotypes.reading: Counter returns a physical blow twice as hard, and Endeavor drags an attacker down to the user's own condition. With Sturdy, which lets it survive any single hit, the pair describes an animal that takes the first charge and gives it back. A lineage whose senior animals stand at the front of the herd. Fits open river flats where a herd with young can be caught in the open.
ecotypes.behavior: Takes the blow meant for the calves, then answers it.

ecotypes.name: Crevasse walker
ecotypes.reading: Fissure splits the ground, Ice Shard flings ice fast, and Ancient Power lifts rock. A lineage at home in frozen, broken ground, working with ice and stone rather than mud. Fits glaciated high country like the upper slopes of Mt. Silver or the Ice Path beside Blackthorn.
ecotypes.behavior: Breaks ice and frozen ground to open a way, or a wallow.

open_questions: What does it eat? No entry for either stage says.
Does the adult return to rivers to breed, or does only Phanpy live at the water?
How is the nest area marked: scent, scraping, or something else?
Do tusks grow for life, and does rank simply follow age?
Why is the line found only in Silver and HeartGold among the Johto games?
Who uses the nest pits after Phanpy leaves them?

Dragonair.summary: The middle stage of the Dratini line: a 4-metre serpent with crystal orbs on its neck and tail, said to change the weather around it by releasing stored energy through them. Much of what the Pokédex says about it is hedged with 'they say' and 'it is said', and the one first-hand account is a witness describing a strange aura, so it is the most folkloric animal in the highlands community. In HeartGold and SoulSilver the only wild ones are hooked by Super Rod in Dragon's Den and the Johto Safari Zone. As with Dratini, nothing says what it eats.

anatomy.text: A serpentine body 4.0 m long weighing 16.5 kg: still very slender for its length.
It has crystals on its neck and tail, called crystalline orbs in the Silver entry.
It stores an enormous amount of energy inside its body.
It has no wings but has been seen flying occasionally.

diet.text: No entry says what Dragonair eats.
Its level-up moves are Dratini's at later levels: Wrap, Thunder Wave, Slam, Aqua Tail (Lv 33), Dragon Rush (Lv 39). The same holding-and-stunning kit, on a much larger body.
At 4 m it would need larger prey or more of it than Dratini; Magikarp is the only other species recorded in the den's water.
diet.note: Co-occurrence only.

habitat.text: It is said to live in seas and lakes.
habitat.note: Hedged in both entries ('It is said'); the games put it in cave water.

habitat.text: In HeartGold and SoulSilver: Dragon's Den by Super Rod only, 10% (Lv 40), and the Johto Safari Zone by Super Rod once at least 15 water blocks are placed (Lv 42; Lv 45 with 20). Gold, Silver and Crystal also had it on Route 45 by Super Rod (10%).
Elsewhere it is a rare Super Rod catch in remote water: the Kanto Safari Zone (10% in Yellow, 1% in FireRed and LeafGreen) and Mt. Coronet 4F (5%). The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is waters-edge.

behavior.text: It exudes a gentle aura.
When its whole body brightens slightly or takes on an aura, the weather changes, instantly in some entries.
behavior.note: Stated flatly in Crystal and Diamond/Pearl/Platinum; hedged as 'they say' in Gold and HeartGold.

behavior.text: The aura, the brightening and the strange aura a witness saw read as one visible event described in different words; whatever the weather link is, the glow is the part people observe.
Activity pattern isn't stated, and the Super Rod tables don't split it by time.

social.text: Nothing is said about whether Dragonair live alone or in groups; Dratini were found as a small colony.

reproduction.text: Water 1 and Dragon egg groups, even sex ratio, 40 egg cycles; the line's egg moves sit on Dratini.
Nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding, eggs or care of young.

defense.text: Shed Skin (it may heal its own status problems), the same as Dratini, and Safeguard at Lv 47.
No defensive behaviour is described. The entries call its aura gentle, not threatening.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses; the aura entries describe how it is seen, not how it perceives.

life_cycle.text: It evolves from Dratini at Lv 30 and into Dragonite at Lv 55, which flies and gains the Flying type.
The middle stage is the longest of the line (Dratini 1.8 m, Dragonair 4.0 m, Dragonite 2.2 m); the adult is shorter and about 13 times heavier (210 kg against 16.5 kg).
Its occasional wingless flight foreshadows Dragonite, whose bulky build flies over raging seas.
Read as development, Dragonair is where the line gains a way to hold and release energy (the crystals), where Dratini could only shed it with its skin.

moves_in_the_wild.text: None of its level-up moves sets the weather. Twister (Lv 1 and 11) is the nearest; Rain Dance, Sunny Day and Hail are machine moves taught by people, so the games give the wild animal no weather move to match its lore.
Dragon Dance (Lv 53) and Agility (Lv 25) are display and speed moves; with Safeguard they make a repertoire that leans to avoiding harm rather than inflicting it.

ecology.text: If it eats fish, it shares the top of Dragon's Den's food chain with Dratini.
ecology.note: No diet is recorded.

ecology.text: If the weather claims are literal, Dragonair changes the physical conditions for everything around it, snow, ice and water levels included. No real animal does anything comparable.
ecology.note: Entirely dependent on the weather entries being read literally; most are hedged.

humans.text: Called the divine Pokémon and described as mystical; the Yellow entry rests on a witness who saw it surrounded by a strange aura.
People in Blackthorn want Dragonair: in HeartGold and SoulSilver a trader in Blackthorn City offers a Dodrio for one.

homestead.text: It would need a large body of water, a lake or a deep pond with current, for a 4 m animal.
Weather work at the homestead would come from moves people teach it (Rain Dance, Sunny Day, Hail), not from the hedged weather lore.
Its 'gentle aura' might make it a calming presence around people and stock.
homestead.note: Untested: no entry says what the aura does to others.

homestead.text: At Blackthorn a Dragonair would be treated as the 'divine Pokémon' name implies: kept at a pool by arrangement with the people of the Dragon's Den, not caught and penned.

niche.foraging: unknown; the same constricting kit as Dratini on a 4 m body

relationships.note: Same Dragon's Den Super Rod table.
Only other species in the den's water; untested.

ecotypes.name: Weather-veil
ecotypes.reading: The egg moves closest to the weather lore: a lineage whose 'aura' is mist and screening. Fits still lakes and the den's misty cave water, where concealment matters more than speed.
ecotypes.behavior: Stays hidden in mist; the glow seen through fog is what people report.

ecotypes.name: Sky-leaper
ecotypes.reading: Speed, a full-body ram and a build-up dance: the lineage most likely to produce the occasional wingless flights (148.8). Fits open lakes and coasts, where it is said to live.
ecotypes.behavior: Launches from the water in bursts; seen in the air more than others.

ecotypes.name: Breath-caster
ecotypes.reading: A sound attack to confuse and a breath attack to strike: a hunting lineage for dark or turbid water such as Dragon's Den.
ecotypes.behavior: Hunts close and in the dark.

open_questions: Does it really change the weather, and if so over what area and for how long?
What are the crystals made of, and do they grow with the animal?
What does it eat?
How does a wingless 4 m animal fly (148.8)?
Does it live in seas and lakes, as said (148.8, 148.10), or only in fresh cave water as in the games?
Who are the people of the Dragon's Den, and how do they relate to the wild population? (The pack says nothing; the creative note on the homestead assumes them.)

contradictions.text: Red and Blue state flatly that it 'has the ability to change climate conditions'; Gold ('They say'), Ruby and Sapphire ('It is said') and LeafGreen ('It is said') hedge the same claim.
contradictions.reading: The entries disagree on how certain the weather power is, and Red/Blue says climate where the others say local weather. Neither is resolved here; the weather lore is filed under folklore.

folklore.text: If it emits an aura from its whole body, the weather will begin to change instantly.
It alters the weather around it by discharging energy from the crystals on its neck and tail.
It has the ability to change the weather.
It lives in seas and lakes.
A witness saw its body surrounded by a strange aura that gave it a mystical look.
It is called the divine Pokémon.

Dragonite.summary: A bulky, winged sea dragon that most people never see. The Pokédex describes Dragonite flying over raging seas, circling the globe in sixteen hours, and leading lost ships to shore in storms; much of the rest of its record is rumour, including an island where only Dragonite live and an intelligence said to match ours. Its young are long, slender, skin-shedding Dratini, once thought mythical, which in Johto live in the Dragon's Den behind Blackthorn City. Nothing in any entry says what the line eats.

anatomy.text: A large, upright, winged animal (2.2 m, 210.0 kg) that flies in spite of its big, bulky build.
Its build is described as what lets it fly freely over raging seas.
Dragonair, the stage before, has crystals or crystalline orbs on its neck and tail and stores an enormous amount of energy in its body; whether Dragonite keeps either is not said.

diet.text: No entry for any stage of the line says what it eats.
In the Dragon's Den, the only other Pokémon in the water is Magikarp, which makes it the obvious candidate prey for Dratini and Dragonair there.
diet.note: Co-occurrence only; nothing says the line eats fish.

habitat.text: Called a marine Pokémon, extremely rarely seen; its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is waters-edge.
Where it actually lives is reported, not observed: 'somewhere in the sea', perhaps an island where only Dragonite gather. See folklore.
Dragonite is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game.

Its young live in inland water, not the open sea: in Johto, the Dragon's Den behind Blackthorn (by Surf, Good Rod and Super Rod) and, in Gold, Silver and Crystal, Route 45 by rod; in Sinnoh, water inside Mt. Coronet (4F, Super Rod); in Kanto, the Safari Zone's water. Dragonair is in the same places, rarer.
HeartGold and SoulSilver drop Route 45 from the line's range, leaving the Dragon's Den and the Johto Safari Zone.

behavior.text: A powerful long-distance flier: it can circle the globe in sixteen hours.
behavior.note: That is about 2,500 km/h at the equator, roughly twice the speed of sound.

behavior.text: Kindhearted toward people at sea: it leads lost and foundering ships to land in storms, and guides crews of shipwrecks to shore.
Rarely seen: only a very few people ever see one.
No entry gives an activity pattern.

social.text: Dratini were found as a small colony living underwater, so the young live in groups.
Whether adults live together is only rumoured: an island somewhere in the ocean where only Dragonite gather.

reproduction.text: Water 1 and Dragon egg groups, an even sex ratio, slow growth, and 40 egg cycles (twice the usual).
Dratini is born large to start with.
A long incubation and a large hatchling fit a species that puts a lot into each young and produces few.

defense.text: Nothing describes predators of Dragonite or how it defends itself; size, flight and rarity are its obvious protection.
Dratini molt in the shelter of a rapid waterfall, which protects them while they are vulnerable.
Its ability, Inner Focus, stops it flinching. Safeguard (Lv 47), which it learns on its own, protects against status problems; Dratini and Dragonair have Shed Skin, which can cure them.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. Finding lost ships in storms implies a good sense of direction and the ability to locate people in poor visibility.

life_cycle.text: Dratini (1.8 m, 3.3 kg) becomes Dragonair at level 30 (4.0 m, 16.5 kg) and Dragonite at level 55 (2.2 m, 210.0 kg). The serpentine young shorten and gain more than twelve times their mass in the last change, and grow wings.
Dratini grows by repeatedly shedding its skin, many layers of it, because the life energy in its body builds up to uncontrollable levels.
life_cycle.analogy: Snakes also shed their whole skin (ecdysis), most often when young and growing fast.

life_cycle.text: Its shed skins are found where living Dratini are not, which is how the species is known: it is called the Mirage Pokémon because so few have seen it.
Dragonair flies occasionally without wings; Dragonite flies with them. Flight appears before wings do.
life_cycle.note: The Dragonair entry hedges where it lives but states the flying as seen.

life_cycle.text: Dragonite learns Wing Attack at level 55, the moment it evolves, which matches wings appearing with the final form.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Thunder Wave (Lv 5) and Twister (Lv 11) are among the line's first moves; with Dragonair's energy-discharging crystals and weather lore, they read as electrical and atmospheric powers the line is born with.
Wrap and Slam (Lv 1 and 21) use the serpentine body; Aqua Tail (Lv 31-33) is a water attack from the tail.
Dragonite starts with Roost, Fire Punch and Thunder Punch at Lv 1; the punches are also tutor moves, so a trained Dragonite with them may have been taught.
Fly, Surf, Waterfall and Rain Dance are machine moves: taught by people, not part of the wild repertoire.

ecology.text: Its role in a food web is unknown because its diet is.
If Dragonair can change the weather around it, the line would affect its surroundings on a scale few animals do; the entries are split between stating and hedging this.
ecology.note: See folklore and contradictions.

ecology.text: The Dragon's Den holds a very simple community: Dratini, Dragonair and Magikarp, nothing else.

humans.text: Dratini was thought mythical until a small underwater colony was found, and its existence was confirmed by a fisherman who caught one.
Its relationship with people is protective: it guides shipwrecked crews to shore.
In HeartGold and SoulSilver a Dratini is given in the Dragon's Den once Clair has handed over her TM; it is also a Game Corner prize in Goldenrod.
Base friendship is low (35) across the line: it does not warm to people quickly.

homestead.text: The line is local: Dratini and Dragonair live in the Dragon's Den behind Blackthorn, the one place in Johto (with the Safari Zone) where they are wild in HeartGold and SoulSilver.
Work with the Den's Dratini goes through the dragon clan, whose shrine the Den is; the Dragon's Den research site should study them in place rather than remove them.
Rescue on water: guiding people in trouble to shore is canon, which suits the lakes and rivers around Blackthorn.
Long-distance air travel: a strong flier with a build made for storms. No entry says it carries riders; Fly is a taught move.
Its size suits a saddle, but its low base friendship means a long bond before anyone rides it.
Dratini need fast, clean water to molt safely: a pool below a rapid waterfall is the habitat feature to build or protect.
Collected shed skins could be studied at the Research Institute without disturbing the animals; finding sheds is how the species is usually known.
Weather work is unproven: Dragonair's weather-changing is half stated and half hearsay, and Rain Dance is a machine move.
homestead.note: Don't plan around it until someone has seen it.

microhabitat: freshwater cave pools and lakes, near waterfalls (young)
niche.foraging: unknown; no entry says what any stage eats
niche.note: Guild left empty: the machine reading's predator comes from the Dragon type alone, and there is no diet evidence to replace it.

relationships.note: Shelter for molting Dratini.
People benefit; nothing says what Dragonite gets from it, so it is recorded as one-sided.
The only other Pokémon in the Dragon's Den water (Dratini and Dragonair).

ecotypes.name: Fog-bank dragon
ecotypes.reading: Dragonair's weather lore in heritable form: Mist shrouds it and blocks stat-lowering, Haze wipes out every stat change on the field, and Light Screen softens special attacks. A defensive lineage that hides in weather rather than making it. Fits fog-bound lakes and sea cliffs where the air is usually thick.
ecotypes.behavior: Stays in mist and low cloud; seldom seen in clear weather.

ecotypes.name: Long-haul flier
ecotypes.reading: A speed lineage: Extreme Speed always strikes first, Dragon Dance builds speed and power together, Dragon Rush is a full-body charge. It is the circle-the-globe canon as an inheritance. Fits open ocean, where distances are huge and storms must be outrun.
ecotypes.behavior: Ranges further than most; arrives fast and leaves fast.

ecotypes.name: Den-pool caller
ecotypes.reading: A lineage built for murky, enclosed water: Supersonic disorients with sound, which carries where light doesn't, and Dragon Breath can paralyse at close range. Fits cave pools like the Dragon's Den, where a confused animal is easy to take.
ecotypes.behavior: Calls in the dark; the young of the cave pools.

open_questions: What does any stage eat? Magikarp is the only other animal in the Dragon's Den, but nothing connects them.
Do Dragonite really live at sea, when every wild Dratini and Dragonair in the games lives in fresh water?
Is there an island where Dragonite gather (149.5)? Where do adults breed?
Can Dragonair change the weather, and if so how far around it?
How does Dragonair fly without wings (148.8), and do wings change how Dragonite flies?
Is Dragonite's intelligence really comparable to a human's (149.1, 149.9)?
What happens to the 'uncontrollable' life energy that drives Dratini's molting once it stops growing?

contradictions.text: Whether it flies: Yellow says the idea that it lives in the sea and flies is only a rumour; Silver, Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald and FireRed state its flight as fact.

Rescuing people: Gold and HeartGold report that it rescues drowning people as hearsay; Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald, Diamond, Pearl and Platinum state that it leads ships and guides shipwrecked crews to shore.
Dratini's length: FireRed says even the young can exceed 6.5 feet (about 2 m), but the game data gives Dratini as 1.8 m.
contradictions.note: Entry versus game data. A large young Dratini could exceed the listed average.

contradictions.text: Dragonair's weather powers: stated as fact in Red, Blue, Crystal and Diamond-Platinum ('the weather changes instantly'), but hedged in Gold, HeartGold, Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald and LeafGreen ('they say', 'it is said').
Habitat: the adults are called marine, but the only wild young in the games live in inland water: cave pools, a mountain route and Safari Zone ponds.
contradictions.note: Entries versus encounter data.

folklore.text: Its intelligence is said to match that of humans.
It is said to live somewhere in the sea and to fly, though Yellow calls this only a rumour.
It is said to fly constantly over the immense seas and rescue drowning people.
It is said that somewhere in the ocean lies an island where Dragonite gather, and only they live there.
It is said to make its home somewhere in the sea.
Dratini was long considered mythical, until a small colony was found living underwater.
folklore.note: The discovery is stated as fact; the myth is the history.

folklore.text: Dragonair is called the divine Pokémon, and is said to change the weather by releasing energy from the crystals on its neck and tail; a witness reported a strange aura around its body.
Dragonair is said to live in seas and lakes.

Dratini.summary: A long, very light water serpent that lives in Dragon's Den and a few other remote waters. Dratini is born large and grows by shedding its skin again and again; the entries put the constant moulting down to 'life energy' building up inside it. It was long thought to be mythical and is still called the Mirage Pokémon because so few people have seen one, though its shed skins turn up. No entry says what it eats, so its place in the den's food web is a gap, not a fact.

anatomy.text: A serpentine body (squiggle shape) 1.8 m long that weighs only 3.3 kg.
That is very little mass for the length, so the body must be narrow and light-built along its whole length.
It is born large and grows by repeatedly shedding its skin; even the young can exceed 6.5 feet (about 2 m).
The moult is continual and comes away in many layers.
anatomy.analogy: Snakes shed the outer layer of the skin in one piece (ecdysis), and growing young snakes shed more often than adults.

diet.text: No entry says what Dratini eats.
Its first moves are Wrap and Leer (Lv 1) and Thunder Wave (Lv 5): a coiling grip and a paralysing jolt, the kit of an animal that holds and stuns prey rather than biting it.
diet.analogy: Boas and pythons subdue prey by coiling around it and squeezing.

diet.text: Magikarp is the only other species on Dragon's Den's fishing and surfing tables, and Magikarp are named elsewhere as easy prey that collect in pooled water. If Dratini hunts fish in the den, Magikarp is the obvious candidate.
diet.note: Co-occurrence plus Magikarp's general reputation as prey; no entry links the two species.

habitat.text: An aquatic animal: a small colony was found living underwater, and Crystal places it under a rapid waterfall while it moults.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver the only wild ones are in Dragon's Den: Good Rod 10% (Lv 20), Super Rod 30% (Lv 40) and surfing 10% (Lv 5-15), with no time-of-day split. There is also a gift Dratini in the den (Lv 15, tied to story progress, the condition naming a TM from Clair), a Goldenrod Game Corner prize (2,100 coins), and Johto Safari Zone fishing, part of which depends on how many water blocks are placed.
Gold, Silver and Crystal also had it on Route 45 by Good and Super Rod; the remakes dropped Route 45, so in HeartGold and SoulSilver the den is the only highland water with Dratini.
Outside Johto it is always in remote water: the Kanto Safari Zone (Red, Blue, Yellow, FireRed, LeafGreen) and Mt. Coronet 4F in Sinnoh, both by Super Rod. The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is waters-edge.

behavior.text: Rarely seen: it is called the Mirage Pokémon because so few have seen it, and its existence was only recently confirmed by a fisherman who caught one.
Its shed skin has been found where the animal itself is not seen, the usual sign of a secretive animal that keeps to deep or fast water.
Activity pattern isn't stated, and HeartGold's Dragon's Den tables don't split it by time of day.

social.text: It was found as 'a small colony', so at least some Dratini live in groups.
social.note: The sentence also carries the 'long considered mythical' framing, which is legend; the colony itself is reported as a finding.

social.text: Nothing is said about how members of a colony interact.

reproduction.text: Water 1 and Dragon egg groups, an even sex ratio, and 40 egg cycles, twice the 20 of most species in the highlands community.
A long incubation and a hatchling that is 'born large' fit a species that puts a lot into each egg.

defense.text: While it moults it is protected by a rapid waterfall, which implies the moult leaves it vulnerable and that fast water keeps attackers off.
Its ability, Shed Skin, lets it heal its own status problems: the games tie moulting to recovery.
Agility (Lv 25) and Safeguard (Lv 41) are its defensive level-up moves; speed and avoidance, not armour.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. Leer at Lv 1 is a stare, which suggests sight matters to it, but that is a reading of a move, not a description.

life_cycle.text: It becomes Dragonair at Lv 30 and Dragonite at Lv 55; the type stays Dragon until Dragonite adds Flying.
The entries give a reason for the moulting: Dratini is full of life energy, which builds to uncontrollable levels, and it sloughs its skin because of it.

Read as development, the moult works as a release for an energy that keeps accumulating; Dragonair, the next stage, 'stores an enormous amount of energy' and discharges it through crystals, as if the adult grows an organ for what the juvenile has to shed.
life_cycle.note: No entry links the Dratini moult to the Dragonair crystals.

life_cycle.text: Size through the line: 1.8 m and 3.3 kg, then 4.0 m and 16.5 kg, then 2.2 m and 210 kg. The line lengthens and then shortens into a heavy flier, so the last change is a remodelling, not just growth.

moves_in_the_wild.text: It fights with its body: Wrap (Lv 1), Slam (Lv 21), Aqua Tail (Lv 31) and Dragon Rush (Lv 35) are all coils, lashes and rams, as a serpent would use. Twister (Lv 11) and Dragon Rage (Lv 15) are its ranged attacks.
Thunder Wave at Lv 5 gives a water animal an electrical way to stop prey or attackers.
moves_in_the_wild.analogy: Electric eels (Electrophorus) use high-voltage discharges that make prey's muscles seize.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Surf, Waterfall and Whirlpool are machine moves, taught by people; its own repertoire has Aqua Tail but no swimming field move.

ecology.text: If it eats fish, Dratini and Dragonair are the top predators of Dragon's Den's water, where the only other recorded species is Magikarp.
ecology.note: Rests on the constricting move set and co-occurrence; no diet is recorded.

ecology.text: Its shed skins stay behind in its habitat and are presumably used by something (scavengers, decomposers); nothing says what.
ecology.note: A regular input of skin into a cave pool is real material; who uses it is not recorded.

ecology.text: What feeds the den's water in the first place (the base under Magikarp) is not recorded.

humans.text: Long considered mythical until a small colony was found; its existence was confirmed by a fisherman.
People hand Dratini on: it is a gift in Dragon's Den and a Game Corner prize in Goldenrod (HeartGold, SoulSilver) and Celadon (Red, Blue, FireRed, LeafGreen).

homestead.text: It would need clean water deep or fast enough to hide in, ideally with a fall or strong current to shelter under while it moults. A still stock pond is a poor fit.
Taught Surf or Waterfall it can travel water with a trainer in the games, but at 3.3 kg it could not plausibly carry a person; treat that as a game convention.
Breeding them would be slow: each egg takes 40 egg cycles, twice the usual 20.
Its shed skins, collected from the pool edge, as a light, tough craft material at the homestead.

microhabitat: deep or fast water under falls
niche.foraging: unknown; the level-up moves suggest a constrictor that grips with Wrap and stuns with Thunder Wave

relationships.note: Dragon's Den fishing and surfing tables in HeartGold and SoulSilver.
The only other species in the den's water; Magikarp is named as easy prey elsewhere (129.4). Untested.
Dragonair is on the same Dragon's Den Super Rod table.
Shelter during the moult (Crystal).

ecotypes.name: Torrent striker
ecotypes.reading: A burst-speed lunge and a full-body ram: a lineage built for the fast water the Crystal entry puts it in. Fits plunge pools under falls, where prey is swept past and has to be taken quickly.
ecotypes.behavior: Holds station in the current and strikes out of it.

ecotypes.name: Fog-veiled
ecotypes.reading: Three moves that blunt or screen an opponent's efforts rather than attack. A concealment lineage that fits the Mirage Pokémon's reputation and the weather lore of Dragonair; its place is still, misty water where not being seen is the defence.
ecotypes.behavior: Rarely surfaces; avoids contests rather than winning them.

ecotypes.name: Sonar hunter
ecotypes.reading: A sound attack that confuses and a breath attack to follow it up: a lineage for dark or murky water, such as the cave water of Dragon's Den, where prey must be found without good light.
ecotypes.behavior: Hunts at close range in darkness.

open_questions: What does Dratini eat? No entry says, and the den's only recorded fish is Magikarp.
What is the 'life energy' that builds up (147.4, 147.6), and where does it come from if not from food?
How often does it moult, and does the Dragon's Den population shelter under falls as the Crystal entry describes (147.5)?
How big is the den colony, and is it isolated from the Mt. Coronet and Safari Zone populations?
What uses the shed skins left in the den (147.9)?
Gold, Silver and Crystal had Dratini on Route 45; HeartGold and SoulSilver do not. For the reconstruction, is Route 45's water connected to the den?

contradictions.text: 147.8 says even the young can exceed 6.5 feet (about 2 m), but the game height is 1.8 m.
contradictions.reading: Entry against game data rather than entry against entry. Either the listed height is a typical young animal and adults run larger, or the entry exaggerates. Not resolved here.

folklore.text: Long considered a mythical Pokémon until a small colony was found living underwater.
Its existence was only recently confirmed by a fisherman who caught one.
Called the Mirage Pokémon because so few have seen it; its shed skin has been found.

Dunsparce.summary: A 1.5-metre 'land snake' with a drill-tipped tail and small wings. The moment it is spotted it bores backwards into the ground with its tail; the wings let it float or fly just a little. It hides deep in caves where no light reaches, stays almost motionless, and digs complex, maze-like nests deep underground. Nothing says what it eats. In HeartGold and SoulSilver it lives at the Violet City end of Dark Cave, nearly always found by smashing rocks, and not at the Blackthorn end.

anatomy.text: A long body (squiggle shape), 1.5 m and 14.0 kg, typed Normal.
Its tail ends in a drill.
It has wings that let it float, hover or fly just a little.

diet.text: No entry says what Dunsparce eats.
Its early level-up moves immobilise rather than wound, Yawn (Lv 9) and Glare (Lv 13), and Pursuit (Lv 25) hits a fleeing target. If it eats animals, the kit fits taking slow or fleeing small prey.
diet.note: A reading of moves only.

diet.text: An animal that burrows deep and stays still in the dark may live on soil animals or on detritus, as most deep-cave animals do.
diet.note: Nothing in the pack names any food.

habitat.text: It hides deep inside caves where no light ever reaches.
It makes its nest in complex, maze-like shapes deep underground.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is only at the Violet City end of Dark Cave: Rock Smash 90% (Lv 4-8), walking 1% (Lv 4), and walking 40% (Lv 2-3) on swarm days. Gold, Silver and Crystal had the 1% and the swarm. Elsewhere: Three Isle Port (FireRed, LeafGreen, 100%) and Route 208 swarms in Sinnoh. The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is cave.
Found nine times in ten by smashing rocks, it shelters in or under breakable boulders.
It is recorded at the Violet City end of Dark Cave but not the Blackthorn end, so in the highland reconstruction it belongs to the cave system as a whole rather than to the Blackthorn side.

behavior.text: When spotted, it escapes backward by furiously boring into the ground with its tail.
It remains virtually motionless in the dark.
Swarm days, when it suddenly makes up 40% of walking encounters, could be read as emergence events, when many come up at once.
behavior.note: Swarms are a game mechanic that picks a species for the day; the biological reading is speculative.

behavior.text: Activity pattern isn't stated, and the tables don't split it by time.

social.text: Nothing is said about groups or interactions.

reproduction.text: Its nest is a complex maze deep underground; nothing says what happens in it.
Field egg group, 20 egg cycles, even sex ratio.

defense.text: Escape by burrowing is its defence; Run Away (a sure getaway from wild Pokémon) is the game form of it. Its other ability is Serene Grace.
Staying motionless in total darkness keeps it from being noticed at all.
Defense Curl (Lv 5), Glare (Lv 13), Yawn (Lv 9), Screech (Lv 29) and Roost (Lv 33) are its wild defensive moves.

senses.text: Living where no light ever reaches, it can't rely on sight there; how it senses its surroundings is not described.

life_cycle.text: A single-stage species: no evolution in Generations I-IV.
Young are not described.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Dig is a natural move for it (Lv 45), matching the burrowing in every entry. Roost (Lv 33) is resting to heal, in keeping with the motionless habit, and Rollout (Lv 17) with Defense Curl is the curled roll.
Ancient Power (Lv 41) and Take Down (Lv 37) are its heavier attacks.

ecology.text: A burrower whose maze nests make underground galleries other animals could use, and which open up soil to air and water.
ecology.note: No other species is recorded using them.
ecology.analogy: Gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) burrows shelter hundreds of other species.

ecology.text: Its diet, and so its trophic level, is unknown.
No predator is named. Zubat and Geodude share its end of Dark Cave.

humans.text: It flees the moment it is spotted, so people rarely get a look at it.
Trainers find it by smashing the rocks it shelters under; the usual way of meeting it destroys its cover.

homestead.text: A tunneller: a drill tail that bores into the ground backwards could open narrow channels for drainage or pipes, if it can be got to dig on purpose rather than in flight.
homestead.note: It digs to escape; digging on request is untested.

homestead.text: Its burrows might aerate garden soil.
homestead.note: Untested; it may simply undermine beds.

homestead.text: It needs dark, undisturbed ground and will vanish into the ground whenever it is watched.
A Dunsparce maze under the potato beds, discovered only when a spade goes through the ceiling.

niche.foraging: unknown; nothing records what it eats

relationships.note: Burrows and nests.
Found by Rock Smash 90% of the time.
Maze burrows as shared shelter; nothing recorded.
Violet City end of Dark Cave; both turn up under smashed rocks.
The cave's water.

ecotypes.name: Still sleeper
ecotypes.reading: Bide waits and returns damage, Curse (for a non-Ghost) trades speed for strength and toughness, and Snore works while asleep. A low-energy lineage built around not moving; fits the deepest, food-poorest reaches of a cave.
ecotypes.behavior: Barely stirs; tough to dislodge when it does.

ecotypes.name: Ambush biter
ecotypes.reading: A bite and a startle: a predatory lineage that strikes from a burrow mouth at whatever passes. Fits soft-floored passages where burrows are easy to dig.
ecotypes.behavior: Waits at the mouth of its maze.

ecotypes.name: Rock-borer
ecotypes.reading: Three moves that work rock: a lineage that tunnels through rubble rather than soil. Fits boulder-choked passages like the Violet City end of Dark Cave, where Dunsparce turn up under smashed rocks.
ecotypes.behavior: Lives in the rubble, not the earth.

open_questions: What does Dunsparce eat?
How does it sense its surroundings in total darkness?
What are the 'complex shapes' of its nest for: ventilation, defence, rearing young?
Why is it absent from the Blackthorn end of Dark Cave?
Can it really fly, or only hover? The entries say float, hover and 'fly just a little' (206.2, 206.6, 206.7).
Is a swarm day a real emergence, or only a game device?

Empoleon.summary: A large, proud diving bird of cold northern seas, with wing edges sharp enough to cut drifting ice. Empoleon swims as fast as a jet boat and carries three horns on its beak; the leader of a group has the biggest. Its line is defined by pride at every stage: Piplup won't take food from people and won't listen to its trainer, and Prinplup are so convinced of their own importance that they never form groups. The adult avoids needless fights but will destroy anything that threatens its pride.

anatomy.text: A large, upright bird (1.7 m, 84.5 kg) with three horns extending from its beak; their size shows its power.
The edges of its wings are sharp enough to slice apart drifting ice and cleave an ice floe.
Piplup is insulated by thick down against the cold.
Its Steel typing, gained only at the last stage, fits blade-edged wings and a hardened body; nothing in the Pokédex explains it.

diet.text: A diving predator: Piplup dives for more than ten minutes to hunt, and Prinplup searches for prey in icy seas.
diet.analogy: Emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) are the deepest-diving birds, with dives recorded at over 20 minutes.

diet.text: The prey is never named; fish or other marine animals are the natural guess for a diving seabird.
diet.note: Nothing in the entries names a prey type.

diet.text: It feeds itself: Piplup hates accepting food from people.

habitat.text: Shores in northern countries, hunting in icy seas.
It is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game. Piplup is a starter gift at Lake Verity in Diamond and Pearl and on Route 201 in Platinum; no Johto game offers the line.

behavior.text: A very fast swimmer: Empoleon swims as fast as a jet boat.
A poor walker on land: Piplup often falls down, but puffs up its chest regardless.
behavior.analogy: Penguins are likewise clumsy on land and agile in water, a trade-off of a body built for swimming.

behavior.text: Proud at every stage, and it governs how the animal behaves: it slashes anyone who hurts its pride, though it avoids unnecessary disputes.
No activity pattern is given.

social.text: Prinplup are solitary: each believes it is the most important, so they never form groups.
Empoleon live in groups with a leader, and the leader has the biggest horns, so horn size signals rank.
Its restraint (avoiding unnecessary disputes) is what a group of proud, dangerous animals would need to live together.

reproduction.text: Water 1 and Field egg groups, 20 egg cycles, 87.5% male (the usual starter ratio). Nothing is said about nesting, eggs or care of chicks.

defense.text: Sharp-edged wings, used against anyone who wounds its pride; Prinplup's wing blows snap even the thickest trees.
Torrent, its ability, strengthens its Water moves when it is badly hurt.
Mist (Lv 46), which blocks stat-lowering, and Swords Dance (Lv 11) are among its own moves.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. A predator diving for ten minutes in icy water must find prey in dim light, but how is not described.

life_cycle.text: Piplup (0.4 m, 5.2 kg) becomes Prinplup at level 16 (0.8 m, 23.0 kg) and Empoleon at level 36 (1.7 m, 84.5 kg), adding Steel to Water at the last stage.
The social life reverses with age: solitary Prinplup become Empoleon that live under a leader.
The wings change role: Piplup is a clumsy walker, Prinplup's wings are clubs that snap trees, Empoleon's are blades that cut ice.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Water and beak moves make up its level-up list: Bubble, Peck (Lv 15), Bubble Beam, Fury Attack, Brine, Whirlpool, Drill Peck (Lv 52) and Hydro Pump (Lv 59).
Aqua Jet, learned on evolving (Lv 36), is a fast first strike from the water, the move form of 'as fast as a jet boat'.
Swagger (Lv 24) is pride in move form: it enrages and confuses the opponent.
Surf, Waterfall and Steel Wing are machine moves, taught rather than its own.

ecology.text: A cold-water diving predator, probably near the top of a coastal food web (trophic level about 3.5-4).
Its behaviour toward other species, beyond defending its pride, is not described.

humans.text: Difficult to keep: Piplup doesn't like to be taken care of, won't listen to its trainer, and hates taking food from people.
Its line reaches people as a Sinnoh starter.

homestead.text: Winter ice-breaking: its wings cut drifting ice and ice floes, which could keep a water intake or pond open through a Blackthorn winter.
Cold work suits it: thick down and a life hunting in icy seas.
Fast water transport on lakes; Surf is a taught move, but the swimming speed is its own.
Let it feed itself: it needs cold water deep enough to dive in for ten minutes at a time, and Piplup will refuse hand-feeding.
Housing: Prinplup must be kept singly, Empoleon can live in a group with one leader. Never put two Prinplup together.
Handle with respect: it avoids disputes but will badly injure anything that threatens its pride, and its trainer must earn its attention.

niche.foraging: pursuit-diving predator; dives over ten minutes to hunt
niche.note: Prey never named; trophic level assumes it eats fish or other predators' prey.

relationships.note: Something it cuts through; whether it uses ice as a platform or obstacle is not said.

ecotypes.name: Long-dive hunter
ecotypes.reading: A lineage built for longer and faster dives: Aqua Ring wraps it in a veil of water that heals it a little each turn, Agility sharpens its speed, and Hydro Pump is a heavy strike at range. Together they extend the ten-minute dives of the canon. Fits deep, cold open water where prey is far down and scattered.
ecotypes.behavior: Dives longer and further offshore than others; rarely seen on land.

ecotypes.name: Shore peacemaker
ecotypes.reading: The adult's restraint made heritable: Feather Dance is a display that sharply lowers an opponent's attack, Yawn makes it drowsy, Supersonic confuses it. Ways to end a dispute without blood. Fits crowded shore colonies where proud animals must live close together.
ecotypes.behavior: Displays and lulls before it ever strikes; more tolerant of neighbours.

ecotypes.name: Tideflat prober
ecotypes.reading: A lineage of mud rather than ice: Mud-Slap and Mud Sport both use mud (one to blind, one to blunt electric attacks), and Double Hit strikes twice in quick succession, like rapid probing. Fits muddy estuaries and tidal flats, a warmer, shallower shore than the canon's icy seas.
ecotypes.behavior: Forages in the shallows at low tide; dives less.

open_questions: What does it eat? Prey is never named.
How does a solitary Prinplup become a group-living Empoleon? Do adults join a leader, or do groups form only at evolution?
How is the leader chosen: by horn size alone (395.1), or by fighting?
Where and how does it breed, given that Prinplup will not group?
Could it live on a highland lake, or does it need the sea?
Does a Piplup raised from an egg at Blackthorn still refuse food from people?

contradictions.text: Group life across the line: Prinplup can never form a group because each thinks it is the most important, but Empoleon have a leader, which implies groups.
contradictions.note: Different stages, so likely development rather than a true contradiction; worth confirming.

Espeon.summary: Espeon is the day form of Eevee, a 0.9 m, 26.5 kg Psychic type whose coat works as a sense organ. Its fine, velvety fur feels minute shifts in the air, and by reading air currents it predicts the weather and an opponent's next move; the tip of its forked tail quivers as it does. It is extremely loyal to any trainer it judges worthy, and it is said its foresight developed to protect that person. No Espeon is wild in Gen I–IV: the games make it only from an Eevee that is devoted to its trainer and levels up by day.

anatomy.text: A slender quadruped of 0.9 m and 26.5 kg, Psychic type.
Fine hair covers its body; the fur has the look and feel of velvet and is extremely sensitive.
A forked tail, whose tip quivers when it is predicting an opponent's next move.
An orb on its forehead that glows when it uses psychic power.

diet.text: No entry says what Espeon eats.
Its category is the Sun Pokémon and it learns Morning Sun (Lv 71), which restores health in sunlight; sunlight may matter to its energy budget, but nothing says it lives on light.
diet.note: The machine reading's 'psychotroph' came from its Psychic type alone.

habitat.text: Gen 3 Pokédex habitat: urban, the same as every Eevee form, which probably reflects where people get Eevee rather than a wild habitat.

Not found in the wild in any Gen I–IV game. Eevee is a gift in Celadon City, at Bill's house in Goldenrod City, a Game Corner prize in the Johto games, and a gift in Hearthome City; it is wild only in Sinnoh's Trophy Garden after the National Pokédex.
An animal that reads air currents would do best in open air, out of still rooms; whether it prefers open country is not recorded.
habitat.note: Follows from its senses, not from any habitat statement.

behavior.text: By reading air currents it predicts its foe's next move, and the weather.
Probably diurnal: it forms only by day in the games, its category is the Sun Pokémon, and Morning Sun is its own healing move.
No entry describes its daily routine.

social.text: It is extremely loyal to any trainer it considers worthy, which means it judges people and doesn't bond with just anyone.
Nothing is said about how Espeon live with their own kind.

reproduction.text: Field egg group, 35 egg cycles, 87.5% male.
Its eggs hatch as Eevee, so Espeon doesn't breed true; each young takes its adult form from its own circumstances.

defense.text: Early warning: its fur senses air currents so it can anticipate an enemy's actions.
defense.analogy: Crickets carry long, fine hairs on their cerci that respond to the faint air movement made by an approaching predator, triggering escape.

defense.text: Its level-up attacks are psychic: Confusion (Lv 15), Psybeam (Lv 36) and Psychic (Lv 64); Future Sight (Lv 43), an attack that lands two turns later, is the move form of foresight.
Synchronize passes poison, burns or paralysis back to an attacker.

senses.text: Its main sense is touch through the fur: it feels minute shifts in the air.

Predicting the weather from 'minute shifts in the air' implies sensitivity to small changes in air movement, and perhaps pressure or humidity, ahead of a change in weather; which of these it feels is not stated.
The tail-tip quiver while it predicts suggests the tail takes part in the sensing, or shows the effort of it.
senses.note: 196.3 describes the quiver, not its purpose.

life_cycle.text: Eevee (0.3 m, 6.5 kg) becomes Espeon on levelling up by day with high friendship; Espeon is about four times Eevee's mass.
Unlike Umbreon's entries, which credit moonlight, no Espeon entry explains how it forms. Eevee's entries say its form follows its surroundings.
The one origin story, that it developed foresight to protect its trainer, is reported as hearsay, but it matches the games' requirement that Eevee be devoted to a person before it becomes Espeon.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Its level-up set is built around psychic attack and anticipation: Confusion, Swift (Lv 29), Psybeam, Future Sight and Psychic, with Psych Up (Lv 57) and Power Swap (Lv 78) reading or exchanging an opponent's state.
Morning Sun (Lv 71) restores health in sunlight, the counterpart of Umbreon's Moonlight.
These describe what an Espeon could do on its own; no game has wild ones to observe.

ecology.text: Its role in a wild community is unknown: no diet, no wild population, no predators or prey named.

humans.text: Extremely loyal to a trainer it judges worthy.
In the games it exists only through people: it forms in an Eevee close to its trainer, and almost every Eevee comes from a person.

homestead.text: A weather forecaster for a mountain homestead: it predicts the weather from minute shifts in the air, which would give warning of storms or snow.
A bodyguard that sees trouble coming: it predicts an enemy's actions, and it is loyal to the person it has chosen.
Flash, a taught move, makes it a light source; its forehead orb also glows when it uses its powers.
It needs a person it considers worthy; an Espeon that hasn't chosen anyone may not stay or cooperate.

microhabitat: open air near people (Gen 3 habitat: urban)
niche.foraging: not described
niche.note: Diet is never stated, so no guild or trophic level is given.

relationships.note: As information: it reads them to predict foes and weather.
It is loyal to a trainer it judges worthy and, it is said, protects them. What the bond gives Espeon is not stated.

ecotypes.name: Foresight line
ecotypes.reading: Detect avoids an attack seen coming, Wish lays down healing that arrives a turn later, and Endure holds on through a blow.
