With Future Sight, the set describes a lineage that acts ahead of events, stepping out of the way and preparing recovery before it's needed. Fits exposed high meadows where weather and predators arrive fast and cover is scarce.
ecotypes.behavior: Moves out of the way before anything has happened.

ecotypes.name: Hearth companion
ecotypes.reading: Charm softens an attacker, Yawn makes it drowsy, and Tickle lowers its guard. A lineage that defuses trouble rather than fighting it, suited to living closely with people. Fits towns and homesteads, the urban habitat the Gen 3 Pokédex gives every Eevee form.
ecotypes.behavior: Ends a quarrel by making everyone too sleepy, or too charmed, to keep it up.

open_questions: What does Espeon eat?
Is its foresight sensory (air currents) or psychic precognition? (see contradictions)
What does it sense to predict the weather: air movement, pressure, humidity?
Could an Espeon form in the wild, without a bond to a person?
How does it decide a trainer is worthy?
Does sunlight feed it, or only trigger its development?

contradictions.note: Gold, Silver and Platinum (196.1, 196.2, 196.7) explain its predictions physically, by fur that reads air currents. Ruby, Sapphire and Emerald (196.4, 196.5) speak of precognitive powers, though only as something 'it is said'. Both can be true, but they are different mechanisms.

folklore.text: It is said that Espeon developed its precognitive powers to protect its trainer from harm.
folklore.note: Reported belief. Its loyalty in the same entries is stated as fact.

Feraligatr.summary: Feraligatr is the adult of the Big Jaw line: a 2.3 m, 89 kg predator of the water's edge, built around its bite. Most of the time it moves slowly; when it attacks it goes at blinding speed, clamps on and shakes its head to tear its victim apart. Out of water its weight is hard to carry, so it often drops to all fours, yet its thick hind legs can still launch a charge. No Gen I–IV game has a wild one: every Feraligatr in these games grew from a Totodile handed to a new trainer, so canon says nothing about where wild ones live or what they hunt.

anatomy.text: A large, upright, tailed reptile-like body: 2.3 m and 88.8 kg, Water type.
Massive, powerful jaws and a huge mouth that it can open wide.
Thick, powerful hind legs that drive fast movement even on the ground.
In the middle stage, Croconaw, the mouth holds 48 fangs whose tips slant backward like barbed fishhooks; lost fangs grow back quickly.
anatomy.analogy: Crocodilians also replace their teeth throughout life, each tooth position being refilled many times.

anatomy.text: No Feraligatr entry mentions fangs, but an animal that bites and tears as it does most likely keeps the replaceable, back-slanted fangs of Croconaw.
Its body is heavy enough that it struggles to support itself out of water, which suggests a body built to be carried by water most of the time.

diet.text: A predator: it bites prey, striking at blinding speed.
It kills or dismembers by biting hard, then shaking its head to tear the victim up.
diet.analogy: Crocodilians cannot chew, and tear pieces off prey too large to swallow by twisting and shaking it in their jaws.

diet.text: No entry names its prey. Its Water type and water's-edge habitat point to aquatic and bank-side animals, but that is a guess from habitat, not a diet record.
The juvenile bites anything that moves, so the line's feeding strike seems to be set off by movement rather than by recognising particular prey.

habitat.text: The Gen 3 Pokédex files the whole line under the water's edge.
It is hard for it to support its weight out of water, so it probably spends most of its time in water and comes ashore for short spells.

Not found in the wild in any Gen I–IV game. Totodile is only a starter gift: in New Bark Town in Gold, Silver, Crystal, HeartGold and SoulSilver, and in Littleroot Town in Emerald. Croconaw and Feraligatr are reached only by raising one.
Where wild populations live, at what altitude and in what kind of water, is not recorded anywhere.

behavior.text: Usually slow-moving, it switches to bursts of blinding speed when it attacks.
behavior.analogy: The pattern of an ambush predator such as a crocodile: long stillness or slow movement, then an explosive strike.

behavior.text: In a fight it kicks the ground hard with its hind legs and charges at great speed.
Out of water it often goes on all fours, but it can still move fast.
Its activity pattern is unknown: no entry mentions day or night, and there are no wild encounter tables to show it.

social.text: No entry describes groups, pairs or territory.
The juvenile nips at others in what it takes for play, which hints at play-biting with siblings or companions while young.
social.note: The entries describe its nips at people; play with its own kind is not stated.

social.text: The line is 87.5% male. The other starter lines checked here (Charmander, Squirtle, Bulbasaur, Mudkip) have exactly the same ratio, so it reads as a game convention for starters rather than a fact about its social life.

reproduction.text: Monster and Water 1 egg groups, 20 egg cycles, 87.5% male; the egg groups place it between land-living and water-living breeding pools.
Nothing in the Pokédex describes courtship, nests, eggs or care of young.

defense.text: Threat display: it opens its huge mouth to intimidate foes.
Once Croconaw clamps down it will not let go until it loses its fangs; the hooked tips make the bite impossible to pull free.
Its wild repertoire carries the same threat display: Leer at Lv 1, Scary Face at Lv 15 and Screech at Lv 45 are all level-up moves.
Torrent makes its Water moves stronger when it is close to defeat, the game's version of fighting harder when cornered.

senses.text: Totodile chomps at any moving object it sees, which points to sight, and specifically sensitivity to movement, as the trigger for the line's strike.
No entry describes the adult's senses: its eyesight, hearing, smell or any sense of vibration in water are all unrecorded.

life_cycle.text: Totodile (0.6 m, 9.5 kg) becomes Croconaw at level 18 (1.1 m, 25 kg) and Feraligatr at level 30 (2.3 m, 88.8 kg): about nine times the juvenile's mass.
The juvenile is small, rough and tough and bites anything that moves; its jaws can crush anything and even its trainer must be careful.

Read as development, the line goes from indiscriminate biting (Totodile), through a hooked, never-let-go grip (Croconaw), to a slow-moving adult that strikes fast and tears; and as the body grows, moving on land gets harder.
The adult gains Agility on evolving (Feraligatr learns it at Lv 30; Croconaw never does), matching the adult entries' stress on bursts of speed.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Feeding: its level-up moves are mostly jaw attacks, Bite (Lv 13), Ice Fang (Lv 21) and Crunch (Lv 32), matching the bite-and-tear entries; Slash (Lv 37) adds the claws.
Thrash (Lv 50), a frenzied attack that runs for several turns, is a fair reading of the head-shaking, tearing attack.
moves_in_the_wild.note: The move is about frenzy, not specifically head-shaking.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Travel and pursuit: Agility (Lv 30) and Aqua Tail (Lv 58) suit a fast swimmer with a strong tail; Hydro Pump (Lv 71) is its strongest water attack.
Surf, Waterfall, Strength, Dig and Rock Climb are machine moves, taught by people; they say what the body can be trained to do, not how wild ones live.

ecology.text: A large predator of the water's edge, probably near the top of its food web (trophic level about 4), though no entry names what it eats or what, if anything, eats it.
Because no wild population exists in these games, its effect on any real community is unrecorded.

humans.text: Its bite is a hazard from the start: Totodile's playful nips can cause serious injury, and even its trainer must be careful.
Turning your back on a Totodile is not recommended, because it chomps at anything moving.
In canon the line is known almost entirely as a trained animal: it reaches people as a starter given to new trainers, not from the wild.

homestead.text: A strong guard by presence alone: the open-mouth threat display, plus Leer, Scary Face and Screech, would keep most intruders back.

Better in water than on land: it could ferry people or loads across a lake or river (Surf and Waterfall are taught moves), but it is a poor draught animal on dry ground because its weight is hard to support out of water.
Strength, a taught move, and its powerful hind legs make short, heavy pulls possible, best done near water so it can rest its weight.
homestead.note: Untested: how long it can work out of water is not recorded.

homestead.text: It needs a pond or slow river deep enough to take its weight, and a meat diet the homestead would have to supply or let it hunt for.
Handling rule: keep children and livestock clear of its mouth, never turn your back on a young one, and expect bites to be serious even when meant as play.

microhabitat: shallows and banks of lakes and rivers
niche.foraging: slow movement or stillness, then a fast lunge and bite; large prey torn apart by head-shaking

relationships.with: prey animals (not named in any entry)

relationships.note: It struggles to carry its weight out of water.

ecotypes.name: Mudbank lurker
ecotypes.reading: Mud Sport and Water Sport both coat the body, in mud or water, and Aqua Jet is a strike that lands before the target can act. Together they suggest a lineage that lies coated in silt in shallow, muddy margins and takes prey with a first-strike lunge, the slow-then-sudden habit of the adult pushed further. Fits slow lowland rivers and marsh edges more than clear highland streams.
ecotypes.behavior: Lies half-buried at the edge; the first a prey animal knows of it is the lunge.

ecotypes.name: Boulder-river crusher
ecotypes.reading: Crunch and Metal Claw are hard-contact bites and strikes, and Rock Slide brings stones down. A lineage of rocky, fast-running water that works among boulders and crushes hard-bodied prey, using the line's jaws that can crush anything. Fits steep highland rivers of the kind around Blackthorn.
ecotypes.behavior: Pries and crushes among stones in the current instead of waiting in mud.

ecotypes.name: Thrashing displayer
ecotypes.reading: Dragon Dance raises speed and strength in the games, which reads as a vigorous display that also readies the body to charge; Thrash and Dragon Claw are the sustained, slashing fight that follows. A lineage where rivals settle contests by display and open charge rather than ambush. Fits crowded waters where many adults meet.
ecotypes.behavior: Dances and gapes before it charges; rivals fight in the open.

open_questions: Where do wild Feraligatr live? No Gen I–IV game has a wild population of any stage.
What does it eat? No entry names a single prey species.
On land, is it a quadruped or a biped? The entries disagree (see contradictions).
Does the adult keep Croconaw's 48 replaceable, hooked fangs?
Is the 87.5% male ratio biology, or a game convention for starter lines?
Is it diurnal or nocturnal? Nothing in canon or the encounter data says.
How does it breed: where are eggs laid, and does either parent guard them?

contradictions.note: Silver and FireRed (160.2) say that out of water it gets down on all fours; SoulSilver (160.8) softens this to 'sometimes'. Crystal (160.3) and Ruby, Sapphire and Emerald (160.4, 160.5) describe it running and charging on its powerful hind legs on the ground. They can be reconciled (all fours at rest, hind legs for a charge), but no entry says so.

Diamond, Pearl and Platinum (160.7) say it usually moves slowly and is fast only when it attacks; Silver and FireRed (160.2) and Crystal (160.3) simply say it moves fast. Probably the same animal at rest and in attack, but the earlier entries don't mention the slowness.

Garchomp.summary: A cave-born dragon that leaves the cave to become one of the fastest fliers in the Pokédex. Its young, Gible, are ambushers with huge mouths that nest in small horizontal holes in cave walls, kept warm by geothermal heat because the line, Pearl says, once lived in the tropics. Gabite digs out its nest and hoards the gems it finds. The adult folds its body, spreads its wings and flies like a jet, its drag cut by fine scales, and it never lets prey escape.

anatomy.text: A large upright dragon (1.9 m, 95.0 kg) that folds its body and extends its wings to fly; in that posture it looks like a jet plane.
Its body is covered in fine scales that reduce drag in flight.
anatomy.analogy: Shark skin is covered in tooth-like dermal denticles, and experiments suggest they can reduce drag in water; the line's category, Land Shark, invites the comparison.

anatomy.text: Gible attacks with a huge mouth.

diet.text: A predator at every stage: Gible pounces on prey that strays too close to its nest; Garchomp never lets its prey escape.
The prey is never named.
The line changes hunting style: an ambusher at the nest when young, a pursuit predator in the air as an adult.

habitat.text: Gible lives in caves warmed by geothermal heat to escape the cold, nesting in horizontal holes in the cave walls.
Pearl says the line once lived in the tropics; geothermal caves are where a warm-climate animal survives in a cold land.
Gabite hunts for treasure in caves and keeps a nest it expands by digging.

Garchomp is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game. Gible lives in the basement floor (B1F) of Wayward Cave in Sinnoh (15-20%); Gabite is rare in Platinum's Victory Road (5%). In HeartGold and SoulSilver, Gible is wild only in the Johto Safari Zone, rarely, and only with at least 49 peak and 49 plains blocks.

behavior.text: Garchomp flies at sonic speed, or at least at the speed of a jet fighter.
behavior.analogy: No real animal comes near the speed of sound; the fastest, the peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus), reaches roughly 300 km/h in a hunting dive.

behavior.text: Gabite digs habitually, expanding its nest, and keeps the gems it turns up; it loves sparkly things and seeks them out in caves.
Gible is clumsy: its attacks are powerful but it hurts itself too.
No entry gives an activity pattern.

social.text: Nothing is said about groups or pairs. Individual nests and hoards suggest solitary animals with a fixed home site, at least when young.

reproduction.text: Monster and Dragon egg groups, an even sex ratio, slow growth, and 40 egg cycles, twice the usual: a long time in the egg.
If the geothermally warmed nest holes also hold eggs, the heat would do the incubating.
reproduction.note: The entries call them nests but never mention eggs in them.
reproduction.analogy: The maleo (Macrocephalon maleo), a megapode bird of Sulawesi, buries its eggs in soil heated by geothermal activity or the sun and leaves them to incubate.

defense.text: Gible defends its nest by pouncing on and biting anything that gets too close; HeartGold and SoulSilver describe as defence the same pounce that Diamond describes as feeding.
Sand Veil, its only ability, makes it harder to hit in a sandstorm, and the line learns Sandstorm on its own (Gible Lv 13; Garchomp at Lv 1): it can make its own cover.
Adults rely on speed and size; nothing describes predators of Garchomp.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. A predator that never lets fast-flying prey escape must track it closely, probably by sight, but the entries don't say.
Gabite's love of sparkly things implies it notices and seeks out shine, so vision matters to it in caves.

life_cycle.text: Gible (0.7 m, 20.5 kg) becomes Gabite at level 24 (1.4 m, 56.0 kg) and Garchomp at level 48 (1.9 m, 95.0 kg). Growth is slow, the last evolution comes late.
Development runs from a nest-bound ambusher, to a digger and hoarder that roams caves for treasure, to an open-air flier.
Only Garchomp's entries mention wings; whether Gible and Gabite fly is not said.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Ground moves serve the cave life: Sand Attack, Sand Tomb (Lv 19, trapping prey in sand) and Dig (Gible Lv 31, Gabite and Garchomp Lv 40), the last matching Gabite's nest digging.
Crunch is learned on evolving into Garchomp (Lv 48), the adult form of Gible's huge-mouthed bite; Slash and Dragon Claw add claws.
Take Down (Lv 15) and Dragon Rush (Lv 37-55) are reckless charges, which sits with Gible's habit of hurting itself.
Outrage, Iron Head and Twister reach the line both as tutor and as egg moves, so a trained Garchomp with them was more likely taught than bred.

ecology.text: An apex aerial predator as an adult (trophic level about 4) and a cave ambusher as a juvenile.
Gabite's digging moves material and enlarges cave systems, and its hoarding concentrates gems in nests; both make it a small-scale engineer of cave interiors.
In Wayward Cave, Gible shares the basement with Zubat (35%), Bronzor and Geodude; Gabite shares Victory Road with Golbat, Graveler, Onix and Rhyhorn.

humans.text: People want what it hoards: its gem nest is constantly targeted by thieves.
A long-held belief that medicine made from Gabite's scales cures even incurable illness puts the line at risk from collectors; the belief itself is folklore.

homestead.text: It needs heat. A line that once lived in the tropics and hides from cold in geothermal caves will not winter outdoors at Blackthorn; it needs a warmed den, or the Glasshouse's Magcargo hearth for the young.
A prospector: Gabite digs habitually and turns up gems as it goes. That makes it useful for excavation and dangerous to anything sparkly left lying about.
Fast long-distance flight between Blackthorn and the outlying sites; no entry says it carries riders, and its speed would be dangerous for one.
Sandstorm is its own move and Sand Veil its own ability; it can make and use sand cover, which is a hazard to crops and people in the open.
Keep Gible away from walkways: it pounces on and bites anything that comes close to its nest hole, and is clumsy enough to hurt itself doing it.
Blackthorn should state plainly that it does not trade in shed scales, given the folk belief in scale medicine and the thieves its hoards draw.

microhabitat: geothermally warmed caves and nest holes (young)
niche.foraging: ambush from the nest hole when young; high-speed aerial pursuit as an adult

relationships.note: Hoarded, not eaten, as far as the entries say.
Its gem hoard is constantly targeted. Whether the thieves are people or Pokémon is not said.
Wayward Cave basement, Sinnoh.
Platinum's Victory Road, with Gabite.

ecotypes.name: Sand-trap lurker
ecotypes.reading: Three moves that all stop prey getting away: Sand Tomb traps it in sand, Mud Shot and Scary Face slow it. Gible's pounce-from-the-nest canon turned into a whole strategy. Fits sandy or silty cave floors where prey passes the nest mouth.
ecotypes.behavior: Stays at its nest hole longer than most Gible; holds what it catches rather than chasing.

ecotypes.name: Wind-cutter
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that attacks at range from the air: Twister whips up wind and Dragon Breath can paralyse. It is the move version of the Platinum folklore that its wings cut blades of wind. Fits open high country where prey is spotted and hit from a distance.
ecotypes.behavior: Strikes from the air without closing in; leaves flattened brush where it hunts.
ecotypes.note: Built partly on a folklore entry (445.3).

ecotypes.name: Clumsy rampager
ecotypes.reading: Gible's clumsiness made into a temperament: Thrash and Outrage are multi-turn rampages that leave it confused, and Double-Edge hurts the user. A lineage that wins by overwhelming force and pays for it. Fits crowded nesting caves where fights between neighbours are short and violent.
ecotypes.behavior: Fights in frenzies; often injured, rarely beaten.

open_questions: What does it eat? The prey is never named at any stage.
Do Gible and Gabite fly, or are wings only an adult trait?
Do the geothermal nest holes hold eggs as well as young?
Why hoard gems? Display, nest lining, or something else? And who are the thieves?
What does 'once lived in the tropics' (443.2) mean: an evolutionary history, a range contraction, or a migration?
Is there any truth in the scale-medicine belief (444.1)? It matters for how the line is protected.

contradictions.text: Gible's pounce: Diamond calls it a way to catch prey that strays too close; HeartGold and SoulSilver describe it as an attack on foes who get too close.
contradictions.note: Feeding versus defence. Both may be true; a sit-and-wait animal at its nest would do both.

contradictions.text: Garchomp's top speed: 'sonic speed' in Diamond, 'equal to a jet fighter plane' in Pearl.
contradictions.note: Close but not the same claim; neither is physically plausible for an animal.

folklore.text: It is said that when a Garchomp runs at high speed its wings create blades of wind that can fell nearby trees.
There is a long-held belief that medicine made from Gabite's scales will heal even incurable illnesses.
folklore.note: A belief, not a demonstrated effect.

Gengar.summary: A night-active shadow-dweller that feeds, by every account, on the warmth and life of other creatures. Gengar slips into its target's shadow and waits, absorbing heat until the victim shivers; a sudden chill is the classic sign that one is near. It also plays: on full-moon nights it mimics people's shadows and laughs at their fright, or runs past them under a streetlight pretending to be their shadow. Its line begins as Gastly, a body that is 95% gas, poisonous to breathe, and so light that strong wind blows it apart; in Johto they shelter in the old towers of Violet and Ecruteak and come out only at night.

anatomy.text: An upright, solid-bodied ghost (1.5 m, 40.5 kg), unlike its pre-evolutions, which weigh 0.1 kg.
Gastly's body is about 95% gas and contains poison; anyone engulfed in it faints.
Haunter has a tongue and hands made of gas, and can slip through any obstacle, including walls.
What Gengar's own body is made of is not said; the jump from 0.1 kg to 40.5 kg suggests it is no longer mostly gas.

diet.text: It takes heat: Gengar steals warmth from its surroundings and absorbs the heat of people whose shadows it hides in, leaving them shaking with cold.
It takes life: it slips into its prey's shadow and waits silently for the chance to steal its life force, lurking in the shadowy corners of rooms.
Haunter licks to sap its victim's life; the victim shakes until it dies.
Gastly kills more directly: it envelops prey of any size in gas, suffocating it or poisoning it through the skin, and can topple an elephant in two seconds.
Whether heat and 'life force' are the same thing, or whether the line eats any matter at all, is not said.

habitat.text: Shadows and darkness, often in human places: the shadowy corners of rooms, people's own shadows, streets lit by streetlights. Its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is cave.
Gengar is wild in only one Gen I-IV place: the Old Chateau in Sinnoh (one room, 4%), and only with a Gen 3 game in the DS's second slot. Elsewhere it exists only by trade evolution.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver, Gastly lives in the Sprout Tower (Violet City) and the Bell Tower (Ecruteak City), at night only and very common (80-85%); Haunter is on Kanto's Route 8 at night. Both also turn up at night in the Johto Safari Zone.
Across all the games the line favours old buildings and towers (Pokémon Tower, Lost Tower, Old Chateau, Sprout and Bell Towers) and caves; Gastly is 'said to appear in decrepit, deserted buildings'.

behavior.text: Night-active: it hides in shadows at night, and the full moon brings out its shadow mimicry.
Johto's Gastly and Haunter appear only at night in the encounter tables.
Playful in a way that looks like it enjoys fear: it mimics people's shadows and laughs at their fright, and runs past them pretending to be their shadow.
An ambusher: it waits silently in a shadow for its opportunity. Haunter does the same in total darkness, or beckons from the dark.

social.text: Gastly gather in groups under the eaves of houses to shelter from wind.
Nothing is said about Gengar living with others of its kind.

reproduction.text: Amorphous egg group, even sex ratio, 20 egg cycles. In the games it hatches from eggs like any other Pokémon.
Pearl and Platinum say Gastly is 'born from poison gases', which sits oddly with hatching from an egg.

defense.text: Concealment is its first defence: it hides in shadows, and Haunter lurks inside walls to watch its foes.
The young are fragile to weather: strong wind makes Gastly's gas body dwindle away, which is why they shelter under eaves.
Levitate, its only ability, makes it immune to Ground attacks. Its own level-up list holds several moves that punish an attacker: Spite, Curse, Destiny Bond (which takes the attacker down with it).

senses.text: It operates where nothing is visible: Haunter stalks in total darkness, and Gengar ambushes from shadow, so it does not seem to rely on light.
No sense organs are described.

life_cycle.text: Gastly (1.3 m, 0.1 kg) becomes Haunter at level 25 (1.6 m, 0.1 kg), and Haunter becomes Gengar (1.5 m, 40.5 kg) only when traded.
The line goes from a formless gas cloud, to a gas body with hands and tongue, to a solid-looking body four hundred times heavier.
The prey shifts with the body: Gastly suffocates and poisons, Haunter licks, Gengar draws heat and life from a victim's shadow without touching it.
Trade evolution has no obvious wild equivalent, which may be why wild Gengar are almost unknown.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Its own level-up moves describe a sleep-and-feed predator: Hypnosis (Lv 1), then Dream Eater (Lv 39), which restores the user by draining a sleeping target, and Nightmare (Lv 55), which harms a sleeper every turn.
Lick (Lv 1) is the canon life-sapping lick of Haunter; Mean Look (Lv 8) stops prey escaping; Sucker Punch (Lv 22) strikes first when the target is about to attack, a classic ambusher's move.
Confuse Ray, Night Shade, Shadow Punch and Shadow Ball make up its other natural attacks.
Fire, Ice and Thunder Punch reach the line as egg moves and as tutor moves, so a Gengar that knows them may have been taught.

ecology.text: A predator or parasite of warm-bodied animals, including people, taking heat or life rather than flesh. Its trophic position is hard to place because it may not consume matter.
In the Sprout Tower the same common slot holds Rattata by day and morning and Gastly at night: the tower is shared by time of day.
Gengar cools its surroundings when it hides; if true, it makes small cold spots in rooms and shadows.
ecology.note: Gold and HeartGold state the heat theft as fact; Diamond hedges the 10 °F figure.

humans.text: Dangerous to people: it hides in their shadows and takes their heat, and Haunter will try to lick you and steal your life. 'If one beckons you while floating in darkness, you must never approach it.'
Its harassment of people seems to be partly for amusement: it laughs at their fright.
It is tied to human places of the dead and the old: the towers of Violet and Ecruteak in Johto, and Kanto's and Sinnoh's grave towers.
Haunter gives people the feeling of being watched in the dark when no one is there.

homestead.text: Not for the nursery, clinic or bedrooms: it takes body heat and life from sleepers' shadows, and its own moves include Hypnosis and Dream Eater.
A cold source: it steals heat from its surroundings, so a resident Gengar in the Ice Path cold vault might help keep it cold. It would also chill anyone working there.
homestead.note: The cooling is canon; whether it can be directed is not.

homestead.text: A scout through walls: Haunter slips through any obstacle and watches from inside walls.
Moves freely in the dark: night travel is its normal state.
Gastly need wind shelter: Blackthorn's exposed highland would blow them apart. Eaves, towers or a cave are essential.
FireRed's mountain folklore (Gengar taking the lives of people lost in mountains) is the kind of story that will attach to any Gengar kept near the Ice Path; worth knowing, not worth believing.

microhabitat: shadows and dark corners of buildings
niche.foraging: ambush from a victim's shadow, draining heat and life force; sleep-inducing and dream-draining moves
niche.note: It may be thermotroph as much as psychotroph: the entries name heat and life force equally. Trophic level left null because it may take energy rather than matter.

relationships.note: Heat and life force, taken from their shadows.
Wind shelter for groups of Gastly.
Sprout Tower: Rattata by day, Gastly at night (HeartGold and SoulSilver).

ecotypes.name: Marsh lantern
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that lures and startles: Will-O-Wisp is a floating ghost-flame that burns, Astonish is a sudden fright that makes the target flinch. Together they look like the lights that draw travellers off a path. Fits open marsh and moor at night, away from buildings.
ecotypes.behavior: Shows a light, draws the curious close, then frightens them.
ecotypes.analogy: The will-o'-the-wisp of European folklore: lights seen over marshes at night, often attributed to burning marsh gas, though the explanation is still debated.

ecotypes.name: Still-air haze
ecotypes.reading: The gas body as a weapon in sheltered air: Haze spreads a black fog that wipes out every stat change, Disable shuts down an attacker's move, Psywave hits at variable strength. A lineage that fills enclosed spaces rather than drifting outdoors. Fits tower interiors, deep eaves and still caves, where no wind can break it up.
ecotypes.behavior: Stays indoors and fills a room; avoids open ground entirely.

ecotypes.name: Death-song haunt
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that makes itself too costly to kill: Perish Song dooms everything that hears it, Grudge strips the moves of whatever knocks it out, and Explosion takes the attacker with it. Defence by guaranteed retaliation. Fits haunts shared with strong predators, where hiding alone isn't enough.
ecotypes.behavior: Rarely fights; when cornered, ensures the attacker loses too.

open_questions: What does it actually take from its prey: heat, 'life force', or both, and are they the same?
Does it eat any matter at all, and what is Gengar's body made of, given that Gastly and Haunter weigh 0.1 kg?
How does a Gastly that is 'born from poison gases' (92.10) square with hatching from an egg?
Does a wild Gengar population exist, given that evolution needs a trade?
Why the full moon (94.1, 94.9)? Is it more active then, or just more visible?
Is its fright-and-laughter behaviour play, display, or a way to stress prey before feeding?

contradictions.text: Cooling: Gold and HeartGold say it steals heat and that a sudden chill means a Gengar is certainly there; Diamond only says it is 'said' to cool the area by nearly 10 °F; Yellow treats the chill as a sign it 'may' be cursing you.
What it takes from its victims: heat (Gold, Crystal) or life and life force (Silver, Pearl).
contradictions.note: Possibly the same thing described two ways.

contradictions.text: Gastly's origin: 'born from poison gases' in Pearl and Platinum, versus the egg it hatches from in the games.
contradictions.note: Entry versus breeding mechanic.

folklore.text: A sudden chill means a Gengar may be trying to lay a curse on you.
It is said to emerge from darkness to steal the lives of those who become lost in mountains.
It is said that a hiding Gengar cools the area by nearly 10 °F (about 5.5 °C).
The leer that floats in darkness belongs to a Gengar delighting in casting curses on people.
folklore.note: Curses are reported in Yellow and Platinum but never described working.

folklore.text: Haunter's ability to slip through walls has led people to say it comes from another dimension.
Gastly is said to appear in decrepit, deserted buildings.
folklore.note: The encounter data agrees: old towers and abandoned buildings.

Geodude.summary: A rock with arms. Geodude lives on mountain trails and in caves, looks so much like a boulder that hikers step on it, and swings its fists at them when they do. It hauls itself up steep paths with its arms, sleeps half-buried in the ground, and in the morning rolls downhill to look for food; its next stage, Graveler, is said to eat rock, preferring rock covered in moss. On Route 45 and at the Blackthorn end of Dark Cave it is one of the most frequent encounters, and one entry says there are many more around than people notice.

anatomy.text: A small, dense body: 0.4 m and 20.0 kg, a head-and-arms body plan, typed Rock and Ground.
Its arms are strong enough to climb steep mountain paths using only their power.
The longer a Geodude lives, the more its edges are chipped and worn away, so old ones are rounder; its heart stays hard and craggy.
anatomy.analogy: Rock fragments round off by abrasion as they are tumbled downslope or along a stream bed, a standard geological process.

anatomy.text: Its round form is easy to pick up.

diet.text: In the morning it rolls downhill in search of food.
No Geodude entry says what the food is. Graveler, its next stage, grows by feeding on rocks and prefers rocks covered in moss.
If it eats as Graveler does, the moss, lichen and microbial film on the rock could be the energy, and the rock the mineral supply.
diet.note: Graveler's moss preference is the only clue to where the energy comes from.
diet.analogy: Chitons and limpets rasp algal films off rock and swallow rock fragments with them; chiton teeth are capped with magnetite.

diet.text: Whether rock itself can supply energy is unknown.
diet.analogy: Chemolithotrophic bacteria get energy by oxidising iron and sulphur compounds in rock; no animal is known to do this.

habitat.text: Found in fields and mountains, and commonly near mountain trails.

In the highlands in HeartGold and SoulSilver: Route 45 (walk 30%, Lv 23) and the Blackthorn end of Dark Cave (walk 30%, Lv 23), with no time-of-day split; at the Violet City end of Dark Cave, walking 60% (Lv 2-4) and Rock Smash 10% (Lv 8-14); Route 46 walking 40% (Lv 2-3), plus 5% at night.

Across Johto and Kanto it is in most caves (Union Cave, Mt. Mortar, the Route 47 cave, Mt. Moon, Rock Tunnel, Victory Road, Cerulean Cave), in the Johto Safari Zone, and under every breakable rock outside the Ruins of Alph (Rock Smash 100%). The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is mountain.
It is met as often in the open (Route 45) as inside caves (Dark Cave); unlike most of the cave community, it is not a cave specialist.

behavior.text: When it sleeps deeply it buries itself halfway into the ground, and does not wake even if hikers step on it.
Many live on mountain trails, half buried, keeping an eye on climbers.
Stepped on by accident, it gets angry and swings its fists.
Morning foraging (74.7) suggests a day-active animal that sleeps buried at night.
behavior.note: One entry only; the highland tables don't split it by time.

social.text: Proud of their sturdy bodies, they bash against each other in contests to prove whose is harder.
social.analogy: Ritualised clashes such as the horn contests of bighorn rams (Ovis canadensis), which settle rank by head-on collision.

social.text: Most people may not notice, but there are many Geodude around: one of the few entries anywhere in this community that speaks to numbers, not just presence.

reproduction.text: Mineral egg group, 15 egg cycles, even sex ratio, and the highest possible catch rate (255). Nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding.

defense.text: It looks just like a rock at rest and is said to be impossible to tell from one; people mistake it for a boulder.
defense.analogy: Living stones (Lithops), succulent plants that pass for pebbles, are the familiar real case of looking like a stone.

defense.text: Sturdy (it can't be knocked out in one hit) and Rock Head; Defense Curl at Lv 1, and Self-Destruct (Lv 18) and Explosion (Lv 32) as last resorts.

senses.text: It keeps an eye on climbers from where it lies half buried, so it watches its surroundings; nothing more is said about its senses.

life_cycle.text: It becomes Graveler at Lv 25, and Graveler becomes Golem only when traded.
Trade is a game device; how wild Graveler become Golem is not explained.
Through the line the body is worn and renewed: Geodude rounds off with age, Graveler sheds pieces as it rolls, and Golem sheds its hide once a year, the old shell crumbling back into the soil.
Size through the line: 0.4 m and 20 kg, 1.0 m and 105 kg, 1.4 m and 300 kg.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Rolling and throwing: Rollout (Lv 22) matches its downhill roll for food, and Rock Throw (Lv 11) and Rock Blast (Lv 25) are the arm-and-rock moves. Magnitude (Lv 15) and Earthquake (Lv 29) are ground-shaking.
Rock Polish (Lv 8) is the game's version of smoothing its body to move faster, which echoes the rounding with age.
moves_in_the_wild.note: A reading of the move's name; no entry links them.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Strength, Rock Smash, Rock Climb and Dig are machine moves, taught by people.

ecology.text: A rock processor: if the line eats rock and wears away as it rolls, it turns bedrock into gravel and grit, and Golem's shed hide returns to the soil. That is a slow role in making highland soil.
ecology.note: Built from three stages' entries; the rate is unknown.
ecology.analogy: Lichens and burrowing animals speed the weathering of rock into soil.

ecology.text: A grazer of moss and lichen on rock, if Graveler's preference holds for Geodude.
ecology.note: Only Graveler's entry names moss.

ecology.text: No predator of Geodude is named.

humans.text: Mistaking them for boulders, people often step or trip on them.
Some people have picked them up and thrown them at each other in snowball fights.

homestead.text: Strong arms that pull a 20 kg body up steep paths; taught Rock Smash and Strength it could help clear stones from fields and tracks.
A hand in dry-stone walling: an animal the size and weight of a building stone, with arms, that likes sitting still among rocks.
homestead.note: Whether it would place stones rather than eat them is the open question.

homestead.text: It needs loose ground to bury itself in at night and rock to roll on; its food is uncertain.
Mark the paths it sleeps on, and don't let children throw them: being stepped on or picked up angers them.

niche.foraging: rolls downhill in the morning to find food; by its line, rock, preferably mossy. Trophic level 2 assumes the moss and microbial film supply the energy

relationships.note: Stated for Graveler, not Geodude.
Graveler's preference; untested for Geodude.
It sleeps half buried.
Route 45 and the Blackthorn end of Dark Cave.
Blackthorn end of Dark Cave.
Blackthorn end of Dark Cave.
Violet City end of Dark Cave; both are found by Rock Smash there.
Route 45 (HeartGold).

ecotypes.name: Quarry fist
ecotypes.reading: Two heavy arm strikes: a lineage that breaks rock into pieces it can eat or move. Fits bare bedrock and cliff walls with little loose stone, such as the walls of Dark Cave.
ecotypes.behavior: Breaks rock where others graze its surface.

ecotypes.name: Trail sitter
ecotypes.reading: Block stops passage, and Curse (for a non-Ghost) trades speed for strength and toughness. A sedentary lineage that sits half buried on a path and holds its ground; fits busy mountain roads such as Route 45.
ecotypes.behavior: Rarely rolls; stays put and lets the path come to it.

ecotypes.name: Scree runner
ecotypes.reading: Brings rock down and fights hardest when worn down. A lineage of steep, loose slopes and talus below cliffs, where rockfall is the everyday weather.
ecotypes.behavior: Sets off small rockfalls; desperate when cornered.

open_questions: Does Geodude eat rock, as Graveler does, and what does it get from it? If the answer is moss and lichen, the energy base of the highland rock community is the film on the rocks.
What does it do at night: sleep buried, as 74.7 implies?
How do wild Graveler become Golem without trade?
Do Geodude have blood? It matters for whether Golbat, which punctures 'however hard' a hide (42.3), can feed on them.
How many are there? 74.3 says there are many more than people notice; the encounter tables can't say.

Golbat.summary: The blood-drinking bat of the highland caves. Golbat's four fangs puncture even thick hide, it takes in more than ten ounces of blood at a time, and some entries say it will not stop feeding even when it is too heavy to fly. It hunts people and Pokémon at night, approaching unseen and striking from behind. In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is common on every floor of the Ice Path and rare at the Blackthorn end of Dark Cave, which makes it the most likely predator of the warm-bodied animals in the Ice Path, though no entry names its prey.

anatomy.text: A winged body, 1.6 m and 55.0 kg, typed Poison and Flying.
It bites with four fangs.
The fangs puncture even the toughest hides and have small holes for sucking blood.
anatomy.analogy: Hollow fangs are known from vipers, where they inject venom rather than draw fluid; vampire bats instead cut a small wound with sharp incisors and lap the blood.

diet.text: It drinks the blood of living things, people and Pokémon both.
It draws and gulps down more than ten ounces of blood at once.
Once it starts, it does not stop until it is full; in other entries it will not stop draining energy from the victim even when too heavy to fly.
Ten ounces is about 0.3 litres, roughly half a percent of a 55 kg Golbat, too little to ground an animal that size. Either it drinks repeatedly, or the 'too heavy to fly' entries exaggerate.
diet.analogy: Common vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus) take a blood meal that is large for their small bodies and begin excreting its water within minutes so they can fly.

diet.text: Its level-up moves include Leech Life (Lv 1), Bite (Lv 13) and Poison Fang (Lv 39): the feeding bite in game form.

habitat.text: In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is on all four Ice Path floors (1F, B1F, B2F, B3F) at 30% at any time of day, Lv 22-23, and at the Blackthorn end of Dark Cave at 5% (Lv 23). Gold and Silver had the same 30% in the Ice Path; Crystal had more, 55-60% on 1F to B2F.

Elsewhere it is in most caves of Johto and Kanto (Union Cave, Slowpoke Well, Whirl Islands, Mt. Mortar, Seafoam Islands, Mt. Silver, Victory Road, Tohjo Falls, Cerulean Cave), and in the Johto Safari Zone only at night. The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is cave.
It hunts in the open: it flits around in the night skies seeking fresh blood.
Its young form roosts by day, hanging from the ceilings of caves and old buildings and avoiding sunlight.
The Ice Path is probably its roost rather than its only feeding ground: it rests in the cave and hunts outside at night, as the young do and as most bats do.

behavior.text: Nocturnal: particularly active in the pitch black of night, and on inky, moonless nights.
It attacks stealthily and without warning, flitting about in darkness and striking from behind, in search of neck veins.
If it drinks too much, it gets heavy and flies clumsily.

social.text: Zubat form colonies in perpetually dark places and gather to hang from ceilings by day.
Whether adult Golbat keep to colonies is not stated.

reproduction.text: Flying egg group, 15 egg cycles, even sex ratio; nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding or roosts with young.

defense.text: Inner Focus (it can't be made to flinch), the Poison type, and a set of moves that disorient rather than wound: Supersonic, Confuse Ray (Lv 21), Mean Look (Lv 33), Haze (Lv 45).
No predator is named; flight and darkness are its evident protection.

senses.text: Zubat have no eyes and find their way by echolocation, emitting ultrasonic cries from the mouth.
senses.analogy: Most small bats find obstacles and prey by echolocation, calling through the mouth (some families through the nose).

senses.text: Golbat's own entries say nothing about its senses; Supersonic and Screech at Lv 1 suggest it keeps the ultrasonic calls of Zubat.

life_cycle.text: It evolves from Zubat at Lv 22 and into Crobat through high friendship, a bond with people that no wild animal has a clear analogue for.
Size through the line: 0.8 m and 7.5 kg, 1.6 m and 55 kg, 1.8 m and 75 kg. The jump from Zubat to Golbat is more than sevenfold in mass.
Crobat grows a second pair of wings on its hind legs for faster, quieter flight, and sneaks up on prey with wings that barely make a sound.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Its level-up kit reads as a hunting sequence: sound and confusion to approach and disorient (Supersonic, Screech, Astonish, Confuse Ray), Mean Look to stop the victim leaving, and fangs to feed (Leech Life, Bite, Poison Fang). Wing Attack, Air Cutter and Air Slash are its flying strikes.

ecology.text: The Ice Path's main predator, as a blood-feeder: the likely hosts are the warm-bodied animals that share its floors, Swinub, Jynx and (in SoulSilver) Delibird.
ecology.note: Its diet is canon; the hosts are inferred from co-occurrence only.

ecology.text: If Golbat and Zubat roost in the caves and feed outside, their droppings would carry energy from outside into the Ice Path and Dark Cave, possibly the main energy input for whatever lives on the cave floor.
ecology.note: No entry mentions droppings. This is the strongest candidate for an energy base in the caves, and it is untested.
ecology.analogy: In many real caves, bat guano is the main food input, supporting specialised invertebrates and fungi.

ecology.text: A blood-feeder takes a meal without necessarily killing; whether its victims survive is not stated, so it may act more like a parasite than a predator.

humans.text: It attacks people: it flies around on dark nights attacking people and Pokémon, and loves the blood of humans.
Travellers crossing the Ice Path or camping near it at night are at risk.

homestead.text: A risk to livestock and sleeping people at night; stock near cave mouths needs closed housing after dark.
A tame one is a feeding problem: nothing says it will take anything but blood.
An echolocating night flier could scout the slopes after dark, if it can be trusted around stock.
homestead.note: Untested; its own entries are about hunting, not ranging.

homestead.text: It needs a dark roost out of sunlight, judging by the young form's habits.
Fly is a machine move; taught, it gives a trainer air travel in the games.

microhabitat: ice-cave ceilings (roost, by analogy with Zubat)
niche.foraging: night-flying blood-feeder: approaches unseen, bites from behind, drinks until full

relationships.note: Shares every Ice Path floor; no entry names it as prey.
Shares every Ice Path floor; untested.
SoulSilver only; untested.
Described for Zubat.
Blackthorn end of Dark Cave.
Blackthorn end of Dark Cave.

ecotypes.name: Sleep-feeder
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that puts its victim to sleep and approaches unseen, a refinement of striking from behind. Fits caves full of resting animals, like the Ice Path with its Swinub and Jynx.
ecotypes.behavior: Feeds on sleepers; rarely has to fight.
ecotypes.analogy: Common vampire bats feed mostly on sleeping animals at night.

ecotypes.name: Open-air pursuer
ecotypes.reading: Moves that hit a fleeing target, strike first and dive hard: a chasing lineage for the open night sky over Route 45 and the cave mouths rather than tight passages.
ecotypes.behavior: Hunts outside; returns to roost before dawn.

ecotypes.name: Roost holder
ecotypes.reading: Wind moves that blow rivals away: a lineage that defends roost space in crowded colonies. Fits the high-ceilinged chambers of the Ice Path, where Zubat and Golbat roost together.
ecotypes.behavior: Drives others off the best ceiling spots.

open_questions: What does Golbat actually feed on in the highlands? No entry names a prey species.
Do its victims survive? If so, it is closer to a parasite than a predator.
Does it roost in the Ice Path and hunt outside, and do its droppings feed the cave floor?
Do Geodude and Graveler have blood? 42.3 says it punctures 'however hard' a hide.
Does Golbat have eyes? Zubat does not (41.9); Golbat's entries don't say.
In HeartGold, Zubat takes the 20% Ice Path slot that Delibird holds in SoulSilver. Is the Zubat-Golbat colony larger in the HeartGold reading of the community?

contradictions.text: Red/Blue (and LeafGreen) say it will not stop draining its victim even if it gets too heavy to fly; Silver/SoulSilver says that if it has too much it gets heavy and flies clumsily; Pearl says it stops when full.
contradictions.reading: The entries disagree on whether it stops when full, and on whether overfeeding grounds it or just slows it. The stated volume (over ten ounces, 42.4) is small for a 55 kg animal, which favours 'clumsy' over 'grounded'.

Goldeen.summary: A river fish with a single sharp horn, admired for fins that billow like a ballgown. Goldeen are strong swimmers that hold a steady five knots up fast streams, and at spawning time they swim up rivers and waterfalls in schools. The elegance is deceptive: it rams hard enough with its horn to shatter aquarium glass. In the highlands it is the common fish of Dark Cave's water, caught there with every rod, and nothing records what it eats.

anatomy.text: A fish, 0.6 m and 15.0 kg, typed Water.
Its tail, dorsal and pectoral fins billow and wave in the water; the dorsal and pectoral fins are strongly developed, like muscles.
It has a single sharp horn that it can ram or jab with, powerfully.

diet.text: No entry says what Goldeen eats.
Its first level-up move is Peck (Lv 1), and later Fury Attack (Lv 31): pecking strikes that might double as the way it picks at food, though nothing says so.
diet.note: A reading of moves only.

habitat.text: Rivers and ponds, and fast streams it can swim up nonstop.

In the highlands in HeartGold and SoulSilver it is only in Dark Cave's water, at both ends: Old Rod 15% (Lv 10), Good Rod 60% (Lv 20), Super Rod 70% (Lv 40). Surfing there gives Magikarp, not Goldeen. The waters of Blackthorn City, Dragon's Den and Routes 44 and 45 hold Poliwag, Magikarp, Remoraid and the Dratini line, but no Goldeen.

Elsewhere it is one of the commonest fish in Johto and Kanto: Union Cave, Slowpoke Well, Route 42, Mt. Mortar, Mt. Silver, Tohjo Falls, the Kanto routes around Cerulean, Cerulean Cave and the Johto Safari Zone. The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is waters-edge.
Its entries describe running water; in the highlands the games put it in cave water. Whether Dark Cave's water connects to streams outside is not recorded.

behavior.text: A strong swimmer that holds a steady five knots (about 9 km/h), even up fast streams.
behavior.note: 118.13 says 'five knots per hour', a slip: a knot is already a speed.

behavior.text: It loves swimming wild and free; put in an aquarium, it will shatter even thick glass with one ram of its horn and escape.
If it senses danger, it strikes back with its horn.
Activity pattern isn't stated; the fishing tables don't split it by time.

social.text: It schools: in spring, schools of Goldeen swim up falls and rivers, and at egg-laying time they travel upstream in large groups.
During spawning season they search for their 'perfect mate', which implies mate choice.

reproduction.text: It migrates upstream to spawn, swimming up rivers and waterfalls in large groups.
reproduction.analogy: Salmon (Salmo, Oncorhynchus) migrate upriver to spawn, leaping falls on the way.

reproduction.text: Its evolution, Seaking, bores nests in riverbed boulders and guards the eggs for over a month. Goldeen's own entries describe spawning but not nests, so both stages may breed.
Water 2 egg group, 20 egg cycles, even sex ratio.

defense.text: The horn: it rams and jabs when threatened.
Swift Swim (faster in rain) and Water Veil (it can't be burned); Agility (Lv 47) and Aqua Ring (Lv 27) for escape and recovery.

senses.text: It 'senses danger', but how is not described.

life_cycle.text: It evolves into Seaking at Lv 33, from 0.6 m and 15 kg to 1.3 m and 39 kg.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Waterfall is a natural level-up move for it (Lv 37), matching its runs up falls; Horn Attack (Lv 11), Horn Drill (Lv 41) and Megahorn (Lv 51) are the horn. Supersonic (Lv 7) and Water Pulse (Lv 17) are its ranged moves.

ecology.text: Its diet, and so its trophic level, is unknown.
If schools crowd into small streams to spawn, eggs and spawning fish would be a seasonal food pulse for anything that eats fish.
ecology.note: No predator of Goldeen is recorded in the highlands.
ecology.analogy: Salmon runs feed bears and eagles, and nutrients from salmon carcasses reach streamside forests.

ecology.text: Dark Cave's water holds Goldeen, Seaking and Magikarp. What the base of that food chain is, and what eats Goldeen there, are both unrecorded.

humans.text: Nicknamed the Water Queen and the water dancer for its fins; it has the look of a queen.
People keep it, and are warned: don't let your guard down, it could ram you powerfully with its horn.

homestead.text: It needs a stream, or a pond fed by one, with a riffle or fall; a glass tank won't hold it.
It senses danger and reacts; a Goldeen in the water intake pool might warn of something in the water, if its reactions can be read.
homestead.note: Untested.

homestead.text: Handle with care: the horn.
The homestead's stream pool, where the spring run of Goldeen is the first sign the thaw has reached the high ground.

niche.foraging: unknown; nothing records what it eats

relationships.note: Spawning runs.
Dark Cave water, both ends.

ecotypes.name: Silt-bottom
ecotypes.reading: Two mud moves: a lineage of still, muddy water that stirs up silt to hide in or to forage through. Fits cave pools like Dark Cave's, where there is no current to run.
ecotypes.behavior: Stays low; clouds the water when disturbed.

ecotypes.name: Torrent runner
ecotypes.reading: Two powerful water attacks in a lineage built for the fastest water, the strong swimmers that run up falls to spawn. Fits steep highland streams.
ecotypes.behavior: First up the falls in spring.

ecotypes.name: Murk-caster
ecotypes.reading: A psychic beam to disorient and Haze to clear the field: a lineage for murky or lightless water, where disorientation matters more than sight. Fits cave water.
ecotypes.behavior: Defends itself without seeing its attacker.

open_questions: What does Goldeen eat? Nothing is recorded.
When does it spawn: spring (118.8) or autumn (Seaking's entries)?
Do Dark Cave's Goldeen run out to streams to spawn, and where?
What eats Goldeen in the highlands? No predator is recorded in Dark Cave's water.
What is the energy base of Dark Cave's water: plant matter washed in, droppings from the bats above, something else?

contradictions.text: Emerald puts Goldeen's spawning runs in the springtime; the Seaking entries (Red/Blue, Crystal, Ruby, LeafGreen, Platinum) put the line's spawning in autumn.
contradictions.reading: Either the two stages spawn in different seasons, populations differ, or the entries disagree. Not resolved here.

Golduck.summary: The adult of Psyduck, and the strongest swimmer in the Ilex Forest community. Golduck has long limbs ending in webbed flippers and a streamlined body; the entries call it the fastest swimmer among Pokémon, faster than any human champion, and it copes with rough seas as well as the quiet lakes and slow rivers it prefers. It appears by waterways at dusk, and its forehead glows when it swims flat out or uses its psychic power. People have mistaken it for the kappa, and it has rescued sailors from wrecks. In Ilex Forest it is the rarer of the pond's two surfing encounters (10%).

anatomy.text: A large, blue, upright duck (1.7 m, 76.6 kg) with slim, long limbs ending in broad, webbed flippers on fore- and hind legs, and a streamlined body.
Its forehead glows or shimmers when it swims at full speed and when it uses psychic or telekinetic power.
Its well-developed limbs and flippers give it its speed.

diet.text: Not stated in any entry.
Its speed suggests a pursuit hunter, and the pond's fish make the obvious prey: Magikarp (0.9 m, 10.0 kg) and Poliwag (0.6 m, 12.4 kg) share its water and are far smaller.
diet.note: Rests on speed, size and shared water; no entry says it hunts.

habitat.text: Lakes and lakeshores, and the quiet, slow-moving rivers it is fond of; it also swims easily in rough, stormy seas.
In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is surfed on Ilex Forest's pond (10%), Route 35 and Route 6, and walks in Seafoam Islands and inside Mt. Silver.
The Mt. Silver records put it on land inside a high mountain, well away from water.

behavior.text: It swims elegantly, gracefully and dynamically, using its limbs and flippers.
Crepuscular: it appears by waterways at dusk.
The surfing tables have no time of day; on Mt. Silver it is in the walking tables at every hour.

social.text: Nothing is said about other Golduck. Its sociability is described only towards people (see People).

reproduction.text: Water 1 and Field egg groups, 20 egg cycles, an even sex ratio. Nothing in the Pokédex describes nesting or young.

defense.text: No entry describes a defence; speed in the water is the obvious one.
Its abilities are Damp and Cloud Nine; Disable, Confusion and Screech are among its moves.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses.

life_cycle.text: It evolves from Psyduck at level 33. Psyduck's headaches and forgetting give way to power tied to the glowing forehead.
Its egg moves sit with Psyduck, the line's first stage; the ecotypes below use them.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Aqua Jet (Lv 1) is a fast first strike in water, apt for the fastest swimmer; Water Gun, Water Pulse and Hydro Pump (56) are water force, Fury Swipes (27) its claws.
Confusion (18), Zen Headbutt (44), Psych Up and Disable are the psychic side, which the entries link to the glowing forehead.

ecology.text: The pond's largest resident and probably its top predator (trophic level about 3.3), if it hunts the fish its speed suggests.
ecology.note: Its diet is undescribed.

ecology.text: At dusk by the water it overlaps Noctowl's hunting hours at the pond edge.
ecology.note: Rests on activity times only.

humans.text: It is often mistaken for the kappa (see Folklore).
It sometimes rescues people from wrecked ships floundering in high seas.
It sometimes joins competitive swimmers in training, and swims faster than any human champion.
The fastest and best swimmer among Pokémon, by two entries.

homestead.text: Water rescue: it has rescued people from wrecks in high seas, and it is sociable with swimmers.
Water travel: a large, fast swimmer could carry a person across Blackthorn's waters. Surf is a TM, but the swimming is its own.
Watering and garden work, as for Psyduck: the capability records credit its upright body with handling objects, and Water Gun is in its wild repertoire.
It needs open water to swim in. Cold tolerance is unknown, though the Mt. Silver records put it on a high mountain.

microhabitat: open water of lakes and slow rivers
niche.foraging: unknown; a fast pursuit swimmer, so probably chases fish
niche.note: No entry gives its diet; the guild rests on its speed and on the fish that share its water. Activity rests on 55.4.

relationships.note: The weakest fish in the pond, easy prey by its own entries, in the same water as the fastest swimmer.
Same water; but Poliwag's skin is so flexible that sharp fangs bounce off it.
If both take Magikarp at the surface around dusk; neither diet is described.

ecotypes.name: Shallows brawler
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that fights hand to hand and flings mud. Fits muddy rivers and marshes where visibility is poor and prey or rivals are met at close range.
ecotypes.behavior: Wades and grapples instead of sprinting.

ecotypes.name: Hypnotic hunter
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that stuns or confuses with its power before the chase, saving the sprint. Fits big lakes where prey is spread out and chases are long.
ecotypes.behavior: Forehead glowing, it stalks before it swims.

ecotypes.name: Sentinel
ecotypes.reading: A watchful lineage: it sees through evasion, strikes later, and shakes off status conditions. Fits rough coasts where its rescues are described (55.7) and danger is frequent.
ecotypes.behavior: Patrols shorelines and comes to trouble rather than avoiding it.

open_questions: What does it eat?
Lakes or seas: is it a freshwater animal that copes with the sea, or both by nature?
What makes the forehead glow?
Why does it appear at dusk?
Are its rescues deliberate?

contradictions.text: Freshwater or sea? Diamond says it lives in lakes (55.11) and Crystal that it is fond of quiet, slow rivers and lakes (55.5); Sapphire has it swimming easily in rough, stormy seas and rescuing people from wrecks in high seas (55.7).
contradictions.note: Compatible if it lives in lakes and can cope with the sea; recorded because the habitat matters for where it belongs.

folklore.text: It is often mistaken for the kappa, a monster of Japanese folklore.
folklore.note: The entries record a mistaken identity, not that Golduck is a kappa.
folklore.analogy: In Japanese legend the kappa is a water creature said to live in rivers and ponds.

Graveler.summary: The heavy, rolling middle stage of the Geodude line, and the only animal in the highlands community whose diet is plainly stated as rock. Graveler eats a ton of rock a day and prefers rock covered in moss; it climbs a mountain eating as it goes, then rolls back down, flattening whatever is in its way. It makes its home in rows of horizontal holes it gouges in sheer cliffs. On Route 45 it has the highest encounter rate of any Pokémon in both HeartGold and SoulSilver.

anatomy.text: 1.0 m and 105.0 kg, a bipedal body with no tail, typed Rock and Ground.
Pieces of its body break off as it rolls, and it doesn't mind.

diet.text: It grows by feeding on rocks, its favourite food, and eats its way through a ton of rock a day.
It apparently prefers rocks covered in moss.
diet.note: Hedged ('Apparently').

diet.text: It feeds as it climbs: from the base of a mountain to the summit, crunching rocks all the way, then rolls back down.
A ton a day is roughly ten times its body weight, so it must pass most of what it swallows and extract only a small part of it.
diet.analogy: Earthworms swallow soil in bulk, digest the organic matter in it and pass the mineral fraction as casts.

diet.text: The moss preference suggests the energy comes from the moss, lichen and microbes on the rock, with the rock itself supplying minerals and bulk.
diet.note: If rock alone fed it, it would need a metabolism no animal is known to have.

habitat.text: Mountains: trails, steep slopes and the paths it rolls down.
It makes its homes on sheer cliff faces by gouging out numerous horizontal holes.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver: Route 45 walking 40% (HeartGold, Lv 23-27) or 55% (SoulSilver, Lv 23-25), the highest rate on that route; the Blackthorn end of Dark Cave 20% (Lv 25); no time-of-day split. Also Mt. Mortar's upper cave, the Route 47 cave (4% by day and morning), Mt. Silver 1F, Victory Road and Cerulean Cave (Rock Smash).
Crystal's Route 45 table had it at 30% by day and morning and 50% at night.
The open mountain road of Route 45 is its main highland ground; Dark Cave is the edge of its range rather than its centre.

behavior.text: A slow walker, it rolls to move.
It rolls over obstacles without slowing or changing direction, paying no attention to what is in its path; once it has momentum, no Pokémon can easily stop it.
Read together, the entries give a daily round: it walks slowly uphill eating, and rolls down when it reaches the top.
Activity pattern isn't stated; only Crystal's Route 45 table leans to night.

social.text: Entries speak of Graveler in the plural ('They descend from mountains') but say nothing about groups. Whether the hardness contests of Geodude continue is unknown.

reproduction.text: Mineral egg group, 15 egg cycles, even sex ratio; the line's egg moves sit on Geodude. Nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding.

defense.text: Sturdy and Rock Head; Defense Curl, Self-Destruct (Lv 18) and Explosion (Lv 38).
Its main defence is mass: few things in the highlands could hurt 105 kg of rolling rock.

senses.text: It pays no attention to objects in its path; nothing is said about how it perceives.

life_cycle.text: It evolves from Geodude at Lv 25 and into Golem by trade.
Golem sheds its hide once a year to grow larger; the shed hide crumbles and returns to the soil.
Across the line the body is constantly worn and renewed: chipped with age (Geodude), shedding pieces as it rolls (Graveler), moulting yearly (Golem).

moves_in_the_wild.text: Rollout (Lv 22) is its way of travelling; Magnitude (Lv 15), Earthquake (Lv 33), Rock Blast (Lv 27) and Double-Edge (Lv 44) fit an animal that smashes trees and boulders aside with its tackles.
Dig is a machine move; its cliff holes are described, but how it gouges them is not.

ecology.text: An engineer: its rows of cliff holes are cavities other animals could use once made.
ecology.note: Nobody is recorded using them. Delibird, which nests at the edge of sharp cliffs (225.2), is a candidate.

ecology.text: A disturber: it smashes trees and boulders aside on the way down, so it clears and breaks up slopes as it goes.
Eating rock by the ton and shedding pieces as it rolls, the line turns bedrock into gravel and grit on a large scale: the community's main living agent of weathering, if the entries are literal.
ecology.note: Scale is the entries'; whether a ton a day is meant literally is unknown.

ecology.text: A grazer of moss on rock, which puts it at trophic level 2 if the moss is its real food.
ecology.note: One hedged entry.

humans.text: A hazard on mountain trails: it may come rolling down the path without slowing.
People engineer around the line: grooves have been dug into mountainsides to steer rolling Golem away from homes downhill.

homestead.text: Keep buildings and paths out of a Graveler's downhill line, or cut a diversion groove as people do for Golem.
It would eat the dry-stone walls: rock, preferably mossy, by the ton.
A land-clearer, if it can be steered: it smashes aside trees and boulders on the way down.
homestead.note: Nothing suggests it can be pointed anywhere; 75.2 says it goes straight over obstacles.

homestead.text: Taught Strength, a 105 kg bipedal body could haul stone.
A Graveler that cuts storage niches into the rock face behind the homestead, the way it cuts its own homes.

niche.foraging: grazes rock while climbing, preferring mossy rock; rolls back down. Trophic level 2 assumes moss is the real food

relationships.note: 'Apparently' prefers mossy rock.
Cliff holes as possible nest sites for a cliff-nesting bird; neither entry mentions the other.
Route 45, HeartGold.
Route 45, SoulSilver.
Blackthorn end of Dark Cave.

ecotypes.name: Cliff-cutter
ecotypes.reading: Heavy arm strikes in a lineage that gouges horizontal homes into sheer cliffs (75.10): a burrowing specialist of hard rock faces, such as the cliffs above Route 45.
ecotypes.behavior: Spends more time cutting than rolling; colonies of holes in one face.

ecotypes.name: Avalanche
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that sends rock ahead of itself on the steepest slopes and fights hardest when battered. Fits scree and talus where its rolling sets off rockfalls.
ecotypes.behavior: Rolls in a shower of stones.

ecotypes.name: Roadblock
ecotypes.reading: Block and Curse (slower, stronger, tougher) in a lineage that has given up rolling for holding ground: a Graveler that sits on the trail instead of thundering down it. Fits gentler slopes where rolling gains little.
ecotypes.behavior: Grazes in place; rarely rolls.

open_questions: How much of a ton of rock is food? What does the moss contribute?
Is 'a ton a day' (75.6, 75.11) meant literally? At ten times body weight it would make Graveler the community's biggest earth-mover by far.
What lives in the cliff holes, during or after Graveler's use of them?
Does it eat building stone?
Is it night-active? Crystal's Route 45 table leans that way; the others don't split by time.

contradictions.text: Crystal says that if it gains too much speed it stops by running into huge rocks; Emerald says it smashes aside obstructing trees and massive boulders.
contradictions.reading: The entries disagree on whether a big rock stops a rolling Graveler or is knocked aside by it. Perhaps size of rock or speed decides; not resolved here.

Hoothoot.summary: A small owl with a perfect sense of time. Hoothoot stands on one foot, switching feet too fast to see, and begins to hoot at precisely the same time every day, thanks to an internal organ that tracks the Earth's rotation; some trainers use it as a clock. No entry says what it eats or when it is active, but HeartGold and SoulSilver meet it in grass only at night, and in Ilex Forest it is the animal most often shaken out of the Headbutt trees.

anatomy.text: A small owl (0.7 m, 21.2 kg) that always stands on one foot.
It switches its standing foot so quickly that the movement can rarely be seen.
anatomy.analogy: Many real birds rest on one leg, which is thought to cut heat loss from the bare legs.

anatomy.text: It has an internal organ that senses and tracks the Earth's rotation.

diet.text: Not stated in any entry.
Its evolved form catches prey in darkness, and Hoothoot's own moves include Peck (Lv 9) and Foresight (Lv 1), so it is most likely a small predator.
In Ilex Forest the larvae and pupae of its common Headbutt trees are the obvious candidates (see Relationships).
diet.note: Rests on sharing the same trees and on size; no entry links them.

habitat.text: A forest animal. In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is in Ilex Forest's common (60%) and rare (50%) Headbutt trees, in Headbutt trees across Johto from New Bark Town to Ecruteak City, and in grass at night on Routes 29 to 31 and 35 to 37 and in National Park.
Its nearest records to Blackthorn are the Headbutt trees of Route 43 and the Lake of Rage.
It lives in the trees, in both kinds of Headbutt tree, which puts it alongside every other tree-dweller in the forest.

behavior.text: It begins to hoot at precisely the same time every day.
Whatever happens, it keeps rhythm by tilting its head precisely in time.
Nocturnal by the encounter tables: every grass record of Hoothoot in HeartGold and SoulSilver is at night. Headbutt records have no time of day, and no entry states its activity.

social.text: Nothing is said about groups or pairs. Its daily hoot at a fixed time might be a signal to others, but no entry says who hears it.
social.note: A reading of the hooting; untested.

reproduction.text: Flying egg group, 15 egg cycles, an even sex ratio. Nothing in the Pokédex describes nesting or young.

defense.text: Even when attacked it doesn't brace itself on both feet.
Its abilities are Insomnia (it can't be put to sleep) and Keen Eye (its accuracy can't be lowered); Hypnosis (Lv 5) and Reflect (17) are its defensive moves.

senses.text: A perfect sense of time, from an organ that senses the Earth's rotation.
senses.analogy: Real animals keep time with internal circadian clocks that run on their own and are reset each day by light, not by sensing the Earth's rotation; in birds the pineal gland is part of that clock.

senses.text: Keen Eye and Foresight suggest sharp sight, and its evolved form sees in near darkness.

life_cycle.text: Hoothoot becomes Noctowl at level 20; the adult is larger (1.6 m, 40.8 kg), sees in near darkness and flies silently onto prey.

The timekeeping entries all belong to Hoothoot and Noctowl's are all about vision, silent flight and thought: read as development, the young owl is described by its clock and the adult by its hunting.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Peck (9) and Take Down (25) for attack; Uproar (13) is a loud, sustained call; Confusion (21), Zen Headbutt (33) and Extrasensory (37) are psychic.
Foresight (Lv 1) lets it hit targets that evade, which reads as a knack for finding hidden prey.
Dream Eater (49) works only on a sleeping target and follows Hypnosis, but Hoothoot evolves at 20, so a wild one almost never has it.

ecology.text: Probably a small nocturnal predator of the canopy (trophic level about 3), though its diet is undescribed.
Being in both Headbutt tables, it overlaps every other tree-dweller: the larvae and pupae of the common trees, and Pineco, Butterfree or Beedrill, and Noctowl in the rare ones.
Bird Pokémon peck Pineco by mistake; Hoothoot and Noctowl are Ilex Forest's only birds, so they are the likely culprits.

humans.text: Some trainers use them in place of clocks.
Platinum says it marks time precisely, and that some countries regard it as a wise friend (see Folklore).

homestead.text: A living clock: it hoots at precisely the same time every day, which would mark a daily routine with no equipment.
Night watch: a night-active bird with keen eyes in the trees around the homestead would notice movement after dark; a Noctowl would do it better.
homestead.note: Its night activity rests on encounter tables only.

homestead.text: Local: it lives in the Headbutt trees of Route 43 and the Lake of Rage, the nearest records to Blackthorn. It needs trees to perch in and a quiet day roost.

niche.foraging: unknown; probably a perch-based hunter of small animals, as its evolved form hunts in darkness

relationships.note: HeartGold: both in the common Headbutt trees, and a 0.3 m larva is within reach of a 0.7 m owl. Caterpie is day-active and Hoothoot night-active, so it would be a larva resting in foliage, and Caterpie's stench (10.3) is aimed at exactly such enemies.
SoulSilver: same trees and sizes as for Caterpie; Weedle's warning colours and barb make it a risky meal.
An immobile pupa in the same trees; whether a peck gets through an iron-hard shell is doubtful.
As for Metapod, plus a poison barb.
Attempted only: birds peck Pineco by mistake and its shell protects it.
Same rare Headbutt trees, same nights; Noctowl is more than twice the size, so they may take different prey.
Rare Headbutt trees, HeartGold.
Rare Headbutt trees, SoulSilver.

ecotypes.name: Sound hunter
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that hunts by sound in deeper darkness: an ultrasonic call and an attack out of the dark. Fits dense, dark forest like Ilex, where sight alone fails.
ecotypes.behavior: Calls more and hunts later into the night.

ecotypes.name: Canopy ambusher
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that drops onto prey from a perch without warning. Fits closed-canopy forest with plenty of perches and prey on the branches.
ecotypes.behavior: Waits motionless on one foot, then strikes from above.

ecotypes.name: Display mimic
ecotypes.reading: A lineage given to social display: copying others' actions and showy feather displays. Fits dense owl populations where neighbours have to be told apart and territories advertised.
ecotypes.behavior: Mirrors rivals and fluffs its feathers at them.
ecotypes.analogy: In real birds, ritualised feather displays are mostly for courtship and territory.

open_questions: What does it eat?
Is it nocturnal? Only the encounter tables say so.
What is the time-sensing organ, and what is the daily hoot for: territory, contact, courtship?
At what time does it hoot, and does the time shift with the seasons?
Why does it stand on one foot, even under attack?

folklore.text: Some countries consider it a wise friend, versed in the world's ways.
folklore.note: A belief people hold about it, not a description of the animal.

Infernape.summary: A fast, fire-crowned primate of high crags that fights with all four limbs. The line starts as Chimchar, which climbs sheer cliffs to live on craggy mountaintops and burns gas made in its belly as a flame at its rear; that flame is a signal as well as a weapon, weakening when the animal is sick and, in Monferno, showing rank in the pack. Infernape carries its fire as a crown and on its hands and feet, and its fire never goes out. Nothing in the Pokédex says what any stage eats, and no game has it in the wild.

anatomy.text: An upright, primate-like animal (1.2 m, 55.0 kg) with a crown of fire on its head and fire on its hands and feet.
In Chimchar the fuel is a gas made in the belly, burned at the rear end.
anatomy.analogy: Mammal guts do make flammable gases (methane and hydrogen from microbial fermentation), though no real animal burns them.

anatomy.text: Whether Infernape's head and limb fires run on the same belly gas is not said.

diet.text: No entry for any stage says what the line eats.
Whatever it eats has to feed both the animal and a fire that never goes out, so its food needs are probably high for its size.

habitat.text: Chimchar climbs sheer cliffs to live on top of craggy mountains.
Monferno uses ceilings and walls to launch attacks from above, which fits overhangs, caves or cliff faces.
It is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game. Chimchar is a starter gift at Lake Verity in Diamond and Pearl and on Route 201 in Platinum; no Johto game offers it.
No Gen 3 habitat is given, because the line is from Generation 4.

behavior.text: Extremely fast and agile: beaten by none in quickness, and it throws its enemies around.
Bold to the point of recklessness: it will take on any opponent.
Chimchar puts out its tail flame when it sleeps; Platinum says it does so on purpose, to prevent fires.
No entry gives a time of day for activity.

social.text: Monferno lives in packs with ranks: a bigger tail fire and a brighter blue pattern on the face mean higher rank.
social.analogy: Male mandrills (Mandrillus sphinx) show rank the same way: dominant males have brighter red and blue facial colour.

social.text: A fire that burns weakly when the animal is sick makes the flame an honest signal of condition, which is the kind of signal a ranked pack can rely on.
Whether Infernape still lives in packs is not said; the entries describe it only as a fighter.

reproduction.text: Field and Human-Like egg groups, 20 egg cycles, 87.5% male (the usual starter ratio). Nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding or young.

defense.text: Monferno manages distance with fire: it stretches its tail flame to look bigger and intimidate attackers, and controls the flame's intensity to keep foes at the range it wants.
Infernape's defence is attack: a martial art using all four limbs, with fire on its hands and feet.
Chimchar's fire survives rain.
Blaze, its only ability, strengthens its Fire moves when it is badly hurt.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. Reading rank from flame size and the brightness of a blue face pattern implies good colour vision in Monferno.

life_cycle.text: Chimchar (0.5 m, 6.2 kg, Fire) becomes Monferno at level 14 (0.9 m, 22.0 kg, Fire/Fighting) and Infernape at level 36 (1.2 m, 55.0 kg).
The fire moves through development: at the rear in Chimchar, on the tail in Monferno (as a weapon and a rank badge), then a crown on the head and flames on the hands and feet in Infernape.
The young can put the fire out; the adult cannot, or does not: Chimchar's flame goes out in sleep, Infernape's never goes out.
Read as development, the line shifts from a climber that avoids trouble to a pack animal that displays, to a fighter that seeks out opponents.

moves_in_the_wild.text: No wild Infernape exists in the games, so the level-up list is the species' own repertoire, not observed behaviour. Provocation first: Leer, Taunt (Lv 1 and 9), and in Chimchar, Torment; then speed, with Mach Punch (Lv 14), which matches 'beaten by none in quickness'.
Flame Wheel (Lv 21), a rolling charge wrapped in fire, and Close Combat (Lv 41) fit an animal that fights with all its limbs; Fire Spin (Lv 45) traps an opponent in flame.
Chimchar (Lv 39) and Monferno (Lv 46) learn Slack Off, a rest-and-recover move, which sits well with a young animal that puts its fire out to sleep; Infernape does not learn it.
