Fire Punch and Thunder Punch reach this line both as egg moves and as tutor moves; when a trained Infernape uses them, they are more likely taught than inherited.

ecology.text: Its role in a food web is unknown, because its diet is.

A permanent fire on an animal living on dry mountain crags is a wildfire risk; Chimchar's habit of putting out its flame before sleep 'to prevent fires' shows the line's fire can and does ignite its surroundings.

humans.text: Its line reaches people as a Sinnoh starter, handed to new trainers at Lake Verity or on Route 201.
No entry describes a working relationship with people; the record is entirely about fighting.

homestead.text: A heat source that doesn't need fuel from the woodpile: Infernape's fire never goes out, and Chimchar's survives rain.
That same fire needs managing: keep it away from hay, timber and the Glasshouse's dry stores. A young Chimchar puts its flame out to sleep; an adult cannot be relied on to.
A free health check: Chimchar's flame burns weakly when it feels sick.
At home on Blackthorn's crags: the line climbs sheer cliffs and lives on craggy mountains, so steep ground is its habitat, not an obstacle. Rock Climb is a taught move, but the climbing is its own.
A guard that will take on anything, with hands that can grip; whether that boldness can be trained into deterrence rather than picking fights is untested.
homestead.note: Boldness is canon; its usefulness as a guard is a guess.

homestead.text: Hauling and clearing would be taught: Strength, Rock Smash and Cut are machines, not its own moves.
If several are kept, expect a rank order: in Monferno the size of the tail fire and the face pattern decide it.

niche.foraging: unknown; no entry says what any stage eats
niche.note: Guild guessed from the primate-like body plan and Human-Like egg group only. The machine reading's 'thermotroph' comes from the Fire type alone.

relationships.with: gas made in its own belly
relationships.note: Its fuel, at least in Chimchar.

ecotypes.name: Four-limb striker
ecotypes.reading: The canon fighting style made heritable: burning fists, a burning kick, and a two-footed kick. A lineage that commits to close striking with hands and feet rather than flame at range. Fits narrow ledges where there's no room to keep distance.
ecotypes.behavior: Closes in fast and strikes with every limb; uses its fire as a glove, not a torch.

ecotypes.name: Troop helper
ecotypes.reading: A cooperative lineage: Helping Hand strengthens a packmate's attack, Assist borrows a packmate's move, and Fake Out makes an attacker flinch so the group can act first. Fits the ranked packs Monferno lives in, on crags where a troop defends one stretch of cliff together.
ecotypes.behavior: Fights alongside others and covers them; low-ranked animals that make themselves useful.

ecotypes.name: Cliff trickster
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that wins by reading its opponent: Encore locks an attacker into repeating its last move, Counter returns physical blows, and Focus Energy readies a decisive hit. Together they make fights short and predictable. Fits crowded cliff colonies where conflicts are frequent and must not be costly.
ecotypes.behavior: Baits, waits and punishes; rarely the first to commit.

open_questions: What does any stage eat, and what in the diet becomes the belly gas that fuels the fire?
Do Infernape's head, hand and foot fires run on the same gas as Chimchar's rear flame?
Can an Infernape put its fire out at all, or does 'never goes out' (392.1) mean it can't?
Does Infernape still live in a ranked pack, and does its crown fire signal rank as Monferno's tail does?
Where does a wild population live? The games give it only as a Sinnoh starter.
Is it diurnal? Chimchar's sleep habits are described but never their timing.

contradictions.text: Chimchar's flame and sleep: Diamond says its fire is put out when it sleeps, as if passively; Platinum says it puts the flame out itself before sleeping, to prevent fires.
contradictions.note: Probably compatible (a deliberate act that happens at sleep), but the two entries describe different agency.

contradictions.text: Across the line: Chimchar's fire goes out when it sleeps, but Infernape's never goes out.
contradictions.note: Different stages, so this may be development (the adult loses or gives up control of the flame) rather than a true contradiction.

Jolteon.summary: Jolteon is the Thunder Stone form of Eevee, a 0.8 m, 24.5 kg Electric type that makes its own lightning. Its cells give off weak charges, which it concentrates and amplifies through the static of its fur to drop thunderbolts of 10,000 volts. When it is charged, angered or startled every hair stands up into sharp, charged needles that pierce attackers, and Platinum has it launching them in small bunches. A sensitive animal, it charges up with every change of mood, and its fur crackles constantly. Like every Eevee form it is never wild in Gen I–IV.

anatomy.text: A light quadruped of 0.8 m and 24.5 kg, Electric type.
Its cells generate a low level of electricity, which it concentrates into lightning bolts.
anatomy.analogy: Electric eels (Electrophorus) work the same way in principle: thousands of modified muscle cells, each producing a small voltage, discharge together to deliver several hundred volts.

anatomy.text: Its fur amplifies that power with static electricity, and the bristling fur is made of electrically charged needles.
Negatively charged ions generated in its fur make a constant sparking noise.

diet.text: No entry says what Jolteon eats.

It can take in electricity: Volt Absorb heals it when it is hit by an Electric move, and the Red, Blue and LeafGreen entries have it gathering negative ions from the atmosphere. That is energy uptake, but nothing shows it replaces food.
diet.note: The machine reading's 'electrotroph' came from its type; these are the only pieces that bear on it.

habitat.text: Gen 3 Pokédex habitat: urban, the same as every Eevee form, which probably reflects where people get Eevee rather than a wild habitat.

Not found in the wild in any Gen I–IV game. Eevee is a gift in Celadon City, at Bill's house in Goldenrod City, a Game Corner prize in the Johto games, and a gift in Hearthome City; it is wild only in Sinnoh's Trophy Garden after the National Pokédex.

behavior.text: A sensitive animal that easily becomes sad or angry, and every change of mood charges it up.
Its fur sparks audibly all the time.
Its activity pattern is unknown.

social.text: No entry describes how it lives with its own kind.
An animal whose charge rises with its mood would be unpredictable company; close quarters with others of its kind, or with people, may keep it charged.
social.note: An extension of 135.2, not a described behaviour.

reproduction.text: Field egg group, 35 egg cycles, 87.5% male.
Its eggs hatch as Eevee, so Jolteon doesn't breed true; each young takes its own adult form.

defense.text: If angered or startled, the fur all over its body bristles like sharp needles that pierce attackers.
defense.analogy: Porcupine quills are modified hairs that the animal raises when threatened.

defense.text: When agitated it uses electricity to straighten its fur and launch it in small bunches.
defense.analogy: Many New World tarantulas defend themselves by kicking clouds of barbed hairs off the abdomen at an attacker.

defense.text: Every hair stands sharply on end when it becomes charged, so the needle defence and the charge are linked.
Pin Missile (Lv 36), a volley of needles, is its needle fur in move form; Thunder Wave (Lv 57) paralyses, and Volt Absorb turns an opponent's electricity to its own benefit.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. 'Sensitive' in 135.2 refers to its temperament.

life_cycle.text: Eevee (0.3 m, 6.5 kg) becomes Jolteon when exposed to a Thunder Stone; Jolteon is nearly four times Eevee's mass.
Eevee's entries describe this as mutation caused by radiation from evolutionary stones acting on its irregular genetic code.
Unlike Espeon and Umbreon, Jolteon needs no bond with a person to form, only a stone. Like the other stone forms, it could in principle arise wherever an Eevee meets the right mineral.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Electric attacks by level-up: Thunder Shock (Lv 15), Thunder Fang (Lv 43), Thunder (Lv 71) and Discharge (Lv 78).
Speed: Quick Attack (Lv 22) and Agility (Lv 64), with Double Kick (Lv 29) as a hind-leg strike.
These describe what a Jolteon could do on its own; no game has wild ones to observe.

ecology.text: Its role in any wild community is unknown: no diet, no wild population and no predators or prey are named.

humans.text: Its thunderbolts are described at 10,000 volts, enough to make it dangerous to handle when upset.
Almost every Jolteon in these games comes from an Eevee given to someone and a stone a person provides.

homestead.text: An electricity source: it generates charge in its own cells. Whether it could charge a battery steadily, and how often, is untested.
homestead.note: The capability records list battery-charging as gear, not as anything an entry describes.

homestead.text: A deterrent: bristling needle fur, a crackling coat and thunderbolts would keep most wild animals off.
Flash, a taught move, makes it a light source for the Glasshouse or a barn.
Keep it calm and keep it away from hay and kindling: its fur sparks constantly and its charge rises with every upset.
Groom with care: startling it raises the needles, and in Platinum's account it can launch them.

niche.foraging: not described
niche.note: Diet is never stated, so no guild or trophic level is given. It can take in electricity (Volt Absorb, 135.1), but that is not shown to be food.

relationships.note: Only the Red, Blue and LeafGreen entries say this; later entries put the source in its cells (see contradictions).
Needed for Eevee to become Jolteon.

ecotypes.name: Last-spark sprinter
ecotypes.reading: Detect sidesteps an attack, Endure survives one that should fell it, and Flail hits harder the closer the user is to defeat. With Jolteon's speed (Quick Attack, Agility), the set describes a lineage that relies on escape first and a desperate counterattack second. Fits open, exposed ground with little cover.
ecotypes.behavior: Runs at the first sign of trouble; cornered, it is at its most dangerous.

ecotypes.name: Mood-charger
ecotypes.reading: Fake Tears and Charm are both emotional displays, one of distress and one of appeal. If every change of mood charges Jolteon, a lineage that displays its feelings often would also stay charged. Fits life in groups, or close to people, where displays get answered.
ecotypes.behavior: Sulks, pleads and sparks in turn; never quite discharged.

open_questions: Where does its electricity come from: the air, its cells, or its moods? (see contradictions)
What does it eat?
Can it shed or regrow its needle fur, and how quickly after launching it?
Could it charge a battery or light a lamp steadily without harm?
Does the constant sparking make it a fire risk around dry material?
Could Jolteon arise in the wild where Eevee and Thunder Stones occur together?

contradictions.note: Red, Blue and LeafGreen (135.1, 135.9) say it gathers negative ions from the atmosphere; Gold, HeartGold, Ruby, Sapphire and Emerald (135.3, 135.6, 135.7) say its own cells produce weak charges that it concentrates and amplifies; Yellow (135.2) says it charges up with every change of mood. Crystal (135.5) has the ions generated in its fur. These may be parts of one system, but each entry names a different source.

Jynx.summary: A humanoid Ice and Psychic Pokémon, every one of them female, that moves as if dancing and appears to use the dance to communicate. Its cries sound like human speech and come in several patterns that seem to carry different meanings, but nobody has worked out what it says. The dancing is contagious: people who watch it find themselves swaying along without meaning to. Nothing in the Pokédex says what it eats or how a species without males reproduces. In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is an uncommon find on every floor of the Ice Path, met more often by day.

anatomy.text: A humanoid body, 1.4 m and 40.6 kg, typed Ice and Psychic; the games give it no males (0% male).
It rocks its body rhythmically and wiggles its hips as it walks.
In the young form, Smoochum, the lips are the most sensitive part of the body and the first thing used to examine anything; the Jynx entries don't say whether this persists.

diet.text: No entry says what Jynx eats.

Its wild moves are close-contact ones: Pound, Lick (Lv 5), Double Slap (Lv 15), Ice Punch (Lv 18), Body Slam (Lv 39), Wring Out (Lv 44), with Lovely Kiss (Lv 8), which puts a target to sleep, and Mean Look (Lv 21), which stops it escaping. If it takes animal food, the kit fits capture at arm's length.
diet.note: Moves explain biology but don't define a diet; nothing says Jynx hunts.

diet.text: Smoochum tests everything by touching it with its lips, which remember what it likes and dislikes: a taste-led animal that learns its foods.

habitat.text: In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is on all four Ice Path floors (1F, B1F, B2F, B3F): 5% at any time plus another 5% by day, Lv 22-23. It is also on Seafoam Islands B4F (12%, Lv 38-40).

Gold and Silver had the same pattern (10% by day, 5% morning and night); Crystal has it only on B1F-B3F, by day and morning. Platinum puts it in Snowpoint Temple. In Red, Blue, FireRed and LeafGreen it is only an in-game trade in Cerulean City (for a Poliwhirl).
Wherever it is wild, it is inside a cold cave or ice-bound building: the Ice Path, Seafoam Islands' lowest floor, Snowpoint Temple.
Its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is 'urban', which fits none of its wild locations; it may reflect its humanlike form or the Cerulean trade rather than where it lives.

behavior.text: It moves to a rhythm of its own, sashaying as if it were dancing.
It appears to alter the rhythm depending on how it is feeling.
The Ice Path tables lean to daytime in every Johto game, which hints at a day-active animal.
behavior.note: Time-of-day slots are a weak guide inside a cave.

social.text: It seems to use dancing to communicate.
social.analogy: Honeybees (Apis mellifera) communicate the direction and distance of food with the waggle dance.

social.text: It has several different cry patterns, each of which seems to have its own meaning.
social.analogy: Vervet monkeys give acoustically distinct alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes, and listeners respond to each differently.

social.text: Its cries sound like human speech; it is said to speak a language similar to that of humans, but it is impossible to tell what it is trying to say.
Group size is not described.

reproduction.text: Human-Like egg group, 25 egg cycles, and no males. Smoochum, its young form, is a baby Pokémon in the Undiscovered egg group.
How an all-female population reproduces in the wild is not described anywhere.
reproduction.analogy: Some real vertebrates are all-female and reproduce by parthenogenesis, such as several whiptail lizards (Aspidoscelis).

defense.text: Forewarn lets it determine what moves a foe has: an early warning of what it is facing. It also has Oblivious.
Its dancing compels people to dance in unison with it; if that works on would-be attackers too, it is a defence by distraction, as Lovely Kiss is in game terms.
defense.note: The entries describe the effect on people only.

defense.text: Fake Tears (Lv 25) and Perish Song (Lv 49) round out a defence built on display and sound more than strength.

senses.text: Forewarn reads as a sense: it perceives what an opponent can do before the opponent acts.
Smoochum's lips remember what it likes and dislikes; touch and taste are its first senses as a juvenile.

life_cycle.text: It evolves from Smoochum at Lv 30, growing from 0.4 m and 6.0 kg to 1.4 m and 40.6 kg, keeping Ice and Psychic.
Smoochum runs about actively but falls often, and checks its reflection on a lake's surface to see its face isn't dirty: the juvenile lives near still water.
Smoochum has no wild encounters in HeartGold and SoulSilver, so the highlands have no recorded juveniles.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Lovely Kiss (Lv 8) puts others to sleep by contact, and Smoochum examines everything with its lips: the kiss is the line's way of meeting the world, in moves as in entries.
Powder Snow (Lv 11), Avalanche (Lv 33) and Blizzard (Lv 55) are its cold-weather moves; Perish Song (Lv 49) is a song, fitting a vocal animal.

ecology.text: At 40.6 kg it is one of the larger animals in the Ice Path, and nothing records what it eats; it is one of the community's biggest unexplained energy demands.
No predator of Jynx is named. Golbat, which drinks the blood of people and Pokémon, shares every Ice Path floor.
ecology.note: Co-occurrence and Golbat's stated diet only.

humans.text: Its motions are so alluring that people who see it are compelled to shake their hips without noticing, and it can cause people to dance in unison with it.
Research is under way to work out what its humanlike language says.
People trade for it: in the Kanto games it is obtained from a trader in Cerulean City.

homestead.text: A humanoid body with hands; in principle it could handle tools.
homestead.note: Nothing describes Jynx using objects.

homestead.text: Ice-typed, with Powder Snow and Icy Wind: possibly a way to keep a cold store cold in summer.
homestead.note: Untested whether its cold is controllable or lasting.

homestead.text: A hazard to plan for: people near it may be compelled to dance, which matters around tools, ledges and livestock.
Its distinct cries could become shared signals with the household, if their meanings can be learned.
homestead.note: Researchers haven't decoded them (124.8).

homestead.text: At the homestead a Jynx keeps the rhythm for long work days, and nobody can say quite why the hay gets in faster.

niche.foraging: unknown; the level-up moves are close-contact, with a sleep-inducing kiss

relationships.note: Its cries resemble human speech. Resemblance only; nothing says it imitates people deliberately.
Shares every Ice Path floor; Golbat drinks the blood of people and Pokémon. Untested.
SoulSilver only.

ecotypes.name: Mirror troupe
ecotypes.reading: Psych Up copies another's state and Wish sends help to whoever is there a moment later: a social lineage that synchronises with and supports others, the move-level echo of making others dance in unison. Fits the larger chambers of the Ice Path, where several could gather.
ecotypes.behavior: Dances in groups; tends the hurt.

ecotypes.name: Clear-eyed
ecotypes.reading: Miracle Eye sees through evasion and Meditate is focus. A perceptive lineage that finds what hides, on top of Forewarn; fits the dark lower floors of the Ice Path.
ecotypes.behavior: Watches more than it dances; the first to notice an intruder.

ecotypes.name: Cold fist
ecotypes.reading: A contact lineage that strikes first and hits with cold fists. Fits passages it shares with Golbat, where it has to defend itself rather than charm.
ecotypes.behavior: Less dance, more fist.

open_questions: What does Jynx eat?
How does an all-female species reproduce in the wild?
What do the dances and the distinct cries mean? Is the 'language similar to that of humans' (124.4) a language at all?
How does its dancing compel people to move (124.6): a psychic effect, or contagious behaviour?
Where are the young? No wild Smoochum appear in HeartGold or SoulSilver.
Why does the Gen 3 Pokédex give its habitat as urban?

contradictions.text: Silver/SoulSilver says it speaks a language similar to humans' but seems to use dancing to communicate; FireRed says it speaks a language that sounds human and research is under way; Diamond/Pearl/Platinum says only that its cries sound like speech and that it is impossible to tell what it means.
contradictions.reading: The entries differ on whether this is a language or just speech-like sound, and on whether speech or dance is how it communicates. Not resolved here.

Kakuna.summary: The pupa of the Beedrill line. Kakuna clings to or leans against stout trees, or hides under leaves and in the angles of branches, almost unable to move while its body is remade inside a hardening shell. It is not defenceless: it can move a little and push out a poison barb if attacked. The shell grows hot to the touch from the work going on inside. In SoulSilver it is met in Ilex Forest's grass in the morning and by day and in the common Headbutt trees.

anatomy.text: A yellow shell (0.6 m, 10.0 kg) that hardens on the outside while the body within grows softer.
A poison barb or stinger that it can extend from the shell.
The shell becomes hot to the touch.
FireRed calls it 'a temporary stage while making its body'.

diet.text: It doesn't feed. No entry mentions food, and every entry describes it waiting, nearly immobile, for evolution.
diet.analogy: Real insect pupae do not feed; they live on reserves laid down by the larva.

habitat.text: On trees: it clings to a tree or leans against stout trees.
Under leaves and in nooks of branches, where it hides from predators.

In SoulSilver it is in Ilex Forest's grass (30% in the morning and by day, none at night) and common Headbutt trees (10%), on Routes 30 and 31, in National Park, in Route 47's secret Headbutt trees, and in Kanto on Route 2 (including a night record, 11%) and in Viridian Forest. In HeartGold it appears only in the Bug-Catching Contest.

behavior.text: Virtually immobile: almost completely unable to move on its own, though it can move a little.
Still on the outside, extremely busy on the inside as it prepares for evolution.
The time-of-day pattern in its tables reflects where and when pupae are found, not activity.

social.text: Nothing is said about other Kakuna. The machine reading's 'solitary' isn't backed by any entry.

reproduction.text: In the games Kakuna is in the Bug egg group (15 egg cycles) and can breed; a pupa isn't a reproductive stage, so this is a game convention.

defense.text: Hardening its shell is its main protection from predators.
When attacked or endangered it may stick out its stinger and poison the attacker.
defense.analogy: Real pupae aren't always helpless: many wriggle when touched, and some beetle pupae pinch attackers with 'gin traps' between their abdominal segments.

defense.text: Concealment: it hides under leaves and in nooks of branches.
Its only level-up move is Harden, so the barb is described but not given as a move; its ability, Shed Skin, may heal its own status problems.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses, though extending its barb 'if it is attacked' and hardening 'when it is in danger' imply it can tell when it is threatened. The capability records turn this into danger sense.

life_cycle.text: From this form it will grow into an adult: Weedle becomes Kakuna at level 7, and Kakuna becomes Beedrill at level 10.
As its body softens the shell hardens: the outside sets while the inside is reorganised.
life_cycle.analogy: Complete metamorphosis: inside a real pupa much of the larval body is broken down and the adult is built from small clusters of cells (imaginal discs) carried over from the larva.

life_cycle.text: If the heat of the shell is metabolic, the pupal stage is expensive and runs on reserves built by Weedle's leaf-eating.
life_cycle.note: The entries give the heat as evidence of activity inside but don't say where it comes from.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Harden is all a wild Kakuna does. Its tutor moves (String Shot, Iron Defense, Bug Bite) are taught by people.

ecology.text: A non-feeding stage that takes nothing from the forest: a store of energy defended by shell, barb and hiding.
It uses trees as anchors and cover: stout trunks to lean on, branch nooks and leaves to hide in.
It has predators: two entries say its defences are against them, though none names one.

humans.text: Anyone handling one will find the shell hot, and it can push out its barb if it feels attacked.

homestead.text: It needs a stout tree or post to lean on, leaf cover, and to be left alone until it emerges.
Not a heater. The capability records list it as a heat source because the shell gets hot, but that heat is a by-product of a few levels' development, not a supply anyone could plan around.
Keep it away from curious hands: it can extend a poison barb when it feels attacked.

niche.foraging: none: a non-feeding pupa living on reserves from the larva
niche.note: No feeding guild applies. Trophic level 2 is its position as food: its body is built from Weedle's leaf-eating.

relationships.note: Trunks to lean on and cling to; branch nooks and leaves for cover.
It hides and hardens against predators; none is named.
Both in Ilex Forest's common Headbutt trees in SoulSilver; Hoothoot pecks (Peck, Lv 9). Shell and barb make it a poor target.
Version counterparts in Ilex Forest; together only in National Park's Bug-Catching Contest.

open_questions: What makes the shell hot, and how hot does it get?
Is the pupa wrapped in silk, as Caterpie's is (10.8)? No Weedle-line entry mentions silk.
Which predators does it hide from (14.1, 14.10)?
How long is the pupal stage in real time?
Can it extend the barb repeatedly, and is its poison Weedle's or Beedrill's?
The line has no HeartGold-SoulSilver egg moves, so no ecotypes can be read from breeding.

contradictions.text: Red/Blue and LeafGreen say it can only harden its shell to protect itself (14.1, 14.9); Yellow and Gold say it can stick out its stinger and poison an enemy (14.2, 14.3).
contradictions.note: The movement claims agree (almost immobile, or able to move a little); the disagreement is over whether hardening is its only defence.

Lapras.summary: A large, gentle sea animal that carries people across the water and has been hunted almost to extinction for its trouble. Lapras understands human speech, is said in one entry to read minds, and sings an enchanting cry when it is in a good mood; Hoenn's entries add that in the evenings it is said to sing plaintively, searching for the few others of its kind still left. Because it rarely fights, many were caught, and the games reflect that scarcity: in Johto a single Lapras surfaces in Union Cave, only on Fridays. Nothing in the Pokédex says what it eats.

anatomy.text: A large swimming animal (2.5 m, 220.0 kg) with a body shape the games class as fish-like, and a back broad enough to carry people and Pokémon.
Its ability Shell Armor (it can't suffer critical hits) implies a protective shell; the Pokédex never describes one.
Water and Ice types, which fit a cold-sea animal.

diet.text: No entry says what it eats.
The machine reading's 'aquatic grazer or filter feeder' comes from its Water type alone and should not be relied on.

habitat.text: The sea: it ferries people across it, and its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is sea.

Yet nearly every wild Lapras in the games is in enclosed or inland water: one in Union Cave's lowest floor, only on Fridays (Gold to SoulSilver); rarely at the Icefall Cave waterfall (FireRed, LeafGreen, 1%); in the water inside Victory Road (Diamond to Platinum, 10%); and on the Johto Safari Zone's water.
The cave records could mean a hunted sea animal surviving in refuges people rarely reach.
habitat.note: A reading of the encounter pattern against the overhunting canon; nothing says Lapras retreat into caves.

behavior.text: Gentle and non-aggressive: they rarely fight.
It likes, even loves, carrying people and Pokémon across the water, and is a very comfortable ride.
It may sing an enchanting cry when it is in a good mood.
behavior.analogy: Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) sing long, structured songs, mostly males on the breeding grounds.

behavior.text: Evenings bring singing in the Hoenn accounts; no activity pattern is otherwise stated. The Johto Safari Zone has it morning, day and night.

social.text: It seeks out others of its kind: in the evenings it is said to sing plaintively, searching for the few that remain.
social.note: Reported as hearsay ('is said to'); see folklore.

social.text: If the song is a contact call, a population thinned by hunting would depend on it to find mates.

reproduction.text: Monster and Water 1 egg groups, even sex ratio, slow growth, and 40 egg cycles (twice the usual). It is a single-stage species.
Long incubation and slow growth mean a population recovers slowly once reduced, which makes overhunting all the more damaging.
reproduction.analogy: The same life history (large, slow-breeding, long-lived) is why great whale populations took decades to recover from commercial whaling.

defense.text: Its gentleness is a liability: because it rarely fights, many have been caught.
defense.analogy: Steller's sea cow (Hydrodamalis gigas), a slow, unaggressive marine mammal, was hunted to extinction within about 27 years of its discovery in 1741.

defense.text: Its own moves are mostly non-violent defences: Sing (Lv 1) and Perish Song (Lv 27) use its voice, Mist and Safeguard protect, Confuse Ray disorients. Sheer Cold (Lv 55) is the exception.
Water Absorb lets it heal from Water attacks; Shell Armor stops critical hits.

senses.text: Intelligent enough to understand human speech.
Yellow says it can read the minds of people.
senses.note: A single entry; stated as fact.

life_cycle.text: Lapras does not evolve; it has no pre-evolution and no later stage.
Nothing is said about how young Lapras grow or how long Lapras live.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Voice is central: Sing is its first move, and Perish Song, a song that makes every listener faint in three turns unless it leaves, comes at Lv 27. Both fit the singing canon.
Its attacks are water and ice: Water Gun, Ice Shard, Water Pulse, Ice Beam (Lv 32), Brine, Hydro Pump (Lv 49).
Rain Dance (Lv 22) is its own move as well as a machine move.
Surf, Waterfall and Strength, behind its transport and hauling records, are machine moves. The ferrying itself is canon; the field moves are taught.

ecology.text: Its food-web role is unknown because its diet is.
A species reduced by people to a remnant: its ecological role in the sea, whatever it was, is now played by very few animals.

humans.text: People drove it almost to extinction: overhunted (Red, Blue, LeafGreen; Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald) and over-caught because it rarely fights (Gold, HeartGold).
It is also the classic water transport for people.
Kanto's games give one away in Saffron City; Johto's let you meet the Union Cave Lapras only on Fridays.

homestead.text: Water transport: it loves to carry people and Pokémon and is a very comfortable ride, suited to the Transport facility's water routes.
A calming presence: a gentle animal whose good-mood song is enchanting.
Easy to direct: it understands spoken instructions.
Its Ice type and sea habitat suggest Blackthorn's winters won't trouble it, but it needs open water: a frozen lake is no use to it.
Needs: large, deep, clean water, and others of its kind if it is to breed; one alone may sing for company.
Blackthorn could keep a small breeding group as a conservation effort for an overhunted species, with long hatching times planned for.

microhabitat: cave lakes and inland water (game records)
niche.foraging: unknown; no entry says what it eats
niche.note: Guild left empty: the machine reading's aquatic grazer comes from the Water type alone.

relationships.note: Overhunted almost to extinction; why it was hunted is not said.
People benefit; Lapras seems to enjoy it, but no benefit to Lapras is stated.

ecotypes.name: Pack-ice breaker
ecotypes.reading: Two one-hit moves that drill and split: Horn Drill with a horn, Fissure by cracking the ground beneath a target. In an Ice-type sea animal they read as tools for breaking ice. A lineage of polar seas, keeping breathing holes and channels open through pack ice.
ecotypes.behavior: Rams and splits ice; travels where others are frozen out.

ecotypes.name: Sleeping voyager
ecotypes.reading: A long-distance lineage: Sleep Talk lets it act while asleep, Refresh clears its own poison, burns and paralysis, and Whirlpool traps a pursuer in a current. An animal that can keep going for days at sea. Fits open ocean crossings far from shore.
ecotypes.behavior: Travels without stopping, resting on the move.
ecotypes.analogy: Dolphins rest one half of the brain at a time (unihemispheric sleep), which lets them keep swimming and surfacing while asleep.

ecotypes.name: Gentle evader
ecotypes.reading: The canon's gentleness as a survival strategy: Substitute leaves a decoy to take the hit, Tickle weakens an attacker without harming it. A lineage that avoids capture and conflict instead of fighting. Fits waters still hunted by people, where the animals that survived are the ones that slipped away.
ecotypes.behavior: Rarely fights; disappears behind a decoy when approached.

open_questions: What does Lapras eat?
Why was it hunted, and for what? The entries only say it was.
Is the evening song (131.6, 131.7) a contact call? Does it work?
Why does every wild Lapras in the games live in caves or inland water when the entries say it lives at sea?
Is the Union Cave Lapras one individual returning each Friday, or several?
Can it really read minds (131.2), or is that an interpretation of its sensitivity to people?
How large must a population be for it to breed successfully, given 40 egg cycles and slow growth?

contradictions.text: Why its numbers fell: Red, Blue and LeafGreen say it was overhunted; Gold and HeartGold say it was caught, because it rarely fights.
contradictions.note: Killing versus capture. Both are human causes; they are not the same pressure.

contradictions.text: Habitat: every entry that names a place says the sea, but the games' wild Lapras are in caves, a waterfall pool, Victory Road and the Safari Zone.
contradictions.note: Entries versus encounter data.

folklore.text: In the evenings, Lapras is said to sing plaintively as it seeks the few others of its kind that remain.
folklore.note: The near-extinction in the same entries is stated as fact; the song is hearsay.

Lucario.summary: A lean, upright fighter defined by a sense no other animal in this set has: it perceives the 'aura' given off by living things, and through it reads their feelings, thoughts and movements. A well-trained Lucario can pick out the feelings of creatures more than half a mile away, and it understands human speech. Its young, Riolu, use aura to talk to one another and to raise the alarm when afraid, and can run all night across mountains and canyons. Nothing says what it eats, and the only wild Riolu in these games are in the Johto Safari Zone.

anatomy.text: An upright, tailed animal (1.2 m, 54.0 kg); its types, Fighting and Steel, are all the games say about its build.
Riolu's body is lithe yet powerful, built to cover ground.
Aura emanates from the body itself: Riolu's grows stronger when it is afraid or sad.
No organ for sending or receiving aura is described.

diet.text: No entry for Riolu or Lucario says what it eats.
A sense that reads other animals' movements, plus all-night running across mountains, are traits of a hunter; if it hunts, aura would let it track prey it cannot see.
diet.note: The traits fit predation but the entries never connect them to food.

habitat.text: No entry describes its habitat. Riolu crests mountains and crosses canyons, which implies rugged country.
Lucario is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game.

Riolu is a one-off egg given on Iron Island in Diamond, Pearl and Platinum. In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is wild only in the Johto Safari Zone, rarely, at any time of day, and only once the zone holds at least 28 forest and 42 mountain-peak blocks.
The Safari Zone requirement, forest plus a lot of peak, is the closest the games come to describing its habitat: wooded high mountains.

behavior.text: Riolu are tireless travellers: they can run through the whole night, cresting three mountains and crossing two canyons.
Activity pattern is mixed: Riolu runs at night, evolves by day, and the Safari Zone has it morning, day and night.
Lucario understands human speech.

social.text: Riolu communicate with one another using their auras.
A frightened or sad Riolu's aura intensifies to alert others: an alarm signal.
An alarm signal only pays if others are near, so Riolu probably live in groups or stay close to adults; the plural 'they' in HeartGold points the same way.
Nothing is said about whether adults live alone or together.

reproduction.text: Field and Human-Like egg groups for Lucario, 25 egg cycles (longer than most of this set), 87.5% male. Riolu is a baby Pokémon in the Undiscovered group and can't breed.

defense.text: Hard to surprise: it reads others' movements through their aura and can detect foes it could not otherwise see.
Its abilities are both about not being thrown off: Inner Focus (it can't be made to flinch) or Steadfast (flinching makes it faster).
Detect (Lv 1), which dodges an attack, and Counter (Lv 6), which returns one, are what reading an opponent's movement looks like in the games.

senses.text: It senses the aura of all things, and from others' auras reads their thoughts and movements.
Range depends on training: a well-trained Lucario can identify creatures and take in their feelings over half a mile (about 800 m) away.
Riolu perceives emotions such as joy and rage as waves, which suggests aura is read as something like a signal with intensity and pattern.
Aura sensing works on foes it can't see, so it does not depend on light or line of sight.
senses.note: The HeartGold entry frames the full claim, that no foe can stay invisible to it, as hearsay; see folklore.

senses.text: What aura physically is, and whether it has a real-world counterpart, is unknown.

life_cycle.text: Riolu (0.7 m, 20.2 kg, Fighting) evolves into Lucario (1.2 m, 54.0 kg, Fighting/Steel) when it levels up by day with high friendship.
The aura sense matures: the young sees emotions as waves and broadcasts its own fear; the adult reads thoughts and movements and, with training, works at half a mile.
That evolution needs a close bond suggests a slow-maturing, social animal whose development depends on its relationships.
life_cycle.note: A friendship trigger is a game mechanic; reading it as social dependence is speculative.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Sensing moves come first in its level-up list: Foresight and Detect at Lv 1, then Me First (Lv 29), which uses the opponent's chosen move before it can, the closest thing in the games to reading thoughts.
Aura Sphere (Lv 37) is its signature attack and never misses, which matches the canon that no foe can hide from it.
Speed moves bracket the list: Quick Attack at Lv 1 and Extreme Speed at Lv 51, fitting the young's all-night running.
Bone Rush (Lv 19) is odd: it implies striking with a bone or bone-like object, which nothing in the Pokédex mentions.
Riolu's own list adds Endure, Reversal and Copycat (Lv 29): survive, hit back hardest when nearly beaten, and imitate what it sees.

ecology.text: Its place in a food web is unknown, because its diet is.
A wide-ranging animal: one night's run covers three mountains and two canyons, so a Riolu's home range, if it has one, is probably large.

humans.text: It understands human speech, and training extends its senses, so people and Lucario have a working relationship in canon.
In Sinnoh, Riolu reaches people as an egg given on Iron Island; it evolves only with a strong bond.

homestead.text: Search and rescue on the mountain: a well-trained Lucario can find creatures and read their state over half a mile away, which suits finding lost walkers on the Ice Path or the crags around Blackthorn.
An early warning: it detects foes it cannot see and reads their movements.
A Riolu in the nursery would announce its own fear or distress: its aura intensifies to alert others.
A fast night courier between Blackthorn and the outlying sites: Riolu run all night across mountains and canyons.
Easy to work with: it understands spoken instructions.
It may pick up the moods of everyone around it, people included; a tense household could be hard on it.
homestead.note: An extrapolation from emotion sensing; nothing describes stress in Lucario.

homestead.text: Needs: a strong bond (its evolution depends on one), room to run, and training to develop its range.

niche.foraging: unknown; a long-range sense for other animals' movements and long-distance running would suit a pursuit or tracking hunter
niche.note: No entry gives its diet; the machine reading's predator comes from the Fighting type alone. Habitat is read from Riolu's travel and the Safari Zone block requirement.

relationships.note: Not a material resource, but the information it lives by.
Riolu's travel country.

ecotypes.name: Canyon runner
ecotypes.reading: Riolu's three-mountains-in-a-night canon made into a lineage: Agility for speed, High Jump Kick for clearing gaps and ledges, Low Kick for taking down heavy animals at the legs. Fits broken canyon country where ground is crossed at a run and in leaps.
ecotypes.behavior: Covers enormous ground every night; strikes from a jump.

ecotypes.name: Reading jaw
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that hunts with its jaws: Mind Reader makes the next move certain to land, and Bite and Crunch put the jaws, otherwise absent from the line's own list, behind it. Aura reading plus a sure bite is the shape of an ambush hunter. Fits forest edge where prey moves under cover.
ecotypes.behavior: Waits until it has read the animal's next movement, then bites once.

ecotypes.name: Pack shield
ecotypes.reading: A guardian lineage: Follow Me draws attacks onto itself, Detect dodges them, and Iron Defense hardens it to take what gets through. It pairs with Riolu's aura alarm: one animal hears the fear and stands in front. Fits open mountainside where a group with young must cross exposed ground.
ecotypes.behavior: Moves toward a frightened groupmate and takes the threat on itself.

open_questions: What does it eat? Neither Riolu nor Lucario has a diet entry.
What is aura physically, and does Lucario sense it with an organ or the whole body?
Do adults live in groups, as Riolu's aura communication implies for the young?
Why does Bone Rush appear in its own level-up moves, when no entry mentions bones?
Where do wild Lucario live? The games give only Iron Island's egg and the Johto Safari Zone.
How much of the half-mile range is training and how much is innate (448.3)?

folklore.text: It is said that no foe can remain invisible to Lucario, since it can detect auras, even of foes it could not otherwise see.
folklore.note: The ability to sense unseen foes is consistent with the other entries; the absolute 'no foe' is the hearsay part.

Machamp.summary: Machamp is a four-armed, 130 kg mountain fighter: its arms react faster than it can think and can throw a thousand punches in two seconds, and once it pins a foe's limbs the fight is all but over. It is strong enough to hurl almost anything aside, yet hopeless at careful work with its fingers, which tangle when it tries. The line lives for training: Machop lifts boulders and even Graveler as weights in the mountains, and Machoke, which wears a belt to hold its power in check, willingly does heavy work for people. Machamp forms only when a Machoke is traded, so it is never wild in Gen I–IV.

anatomy.text: A humanoid body of 1.6 m and 130 kg, Fighting type, with four arms.
Heavy, rugged muscles on four arms that can launch 1,000 punches in two seconds.
Its arms react more quickly than it can think.
It is terrible at delicate work with its fingers; anything needing care and dexterity gets its arms tangled.
In the juveniles the whole body is muscle that never gets sore or cramps however much it is used, and Machoke's toned muscles have the hardness of steel.

diet.text: No entry for any stage says what the line eats.
An animal that is almost all muscle and trains all day must eat a great deal; what it eats is not recorded.

habitat.text: Gen 3 Pokédex habitat for the whole line: mountain. Machop lives in the mountains away from humans and trains by lifting rocks there.
Machamp is never wild in Gen I–IV, because it forms only when a Machoke is traded.

Machop and Machoke live in mountain caves and passes: in HeartGold and SoulSilver, Mt. Mortar, Rock Tunnel, the cave on Route 47 and the Johto Safari Zone, with Machoke also in Cerulean Cave; elsewhere Victory Road, Mt. Ember, Jagged Pass, Fiery Path and Mt. Coronet.
Trades link it with the Abra line: Crystal's Goldenrod City trade gives a Machop for an Abra, and Sinnoh's Oreburgh City trade gives an Abra for a Machop. Both lines finish evolving only by trade.

behavior.text: It tends to leap into action before it thinks.
Its fighting spirit flares when it faces a tough opponent.

The line trains constantly: Machop passes time lifting boulders, is never satisfied however hard it trains, and some travel the world to master martial arts; Machoke never tires and its muscles thicken after every battle.

Probably diurnal: Crystal lists Machop and Machoke only in the morning and day, while the Geodude and Graveler in the same caves also appear at night; HeartGold's Cerulean Cave has Machoke at 20% by day and 2% at night.

social.text: No entry describes how Machamp live with their own kind.
'Some Machop travel the world' to master martial arts, which reads as dispersal by young animals away from where they were raised.

reproduction.text: Human-Like egg group, 20 egg cycles, 75% male.
Nothing describes breeding or care of young.

defense.text: Its punches and chops from four arms are impossible to defend against.
It grapples: it pins a foe's limbs with its four arms, and once it has hold the battle is all but over; the foe is thrown far over the horizon.
No Guard, which makes every attack by or against it land, is the game form of 'impossible to defend against'; Guts makes it hit harder when it is hurt by a status condition.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. Foresight (Lv 13), a level-up move that sees through evasion, hints at a watchful fighter, but that is a move reading only.

life_cycle.text: Machop (0.8 m, 19.5 kg) becomes Machoke at level 28 (1.5 m, 70.5 kg), and Machoke becomes Machamp (1.6 m, 130 kg) only when traded. The last step nearly doubles its mass and adds a second pair of arms.
Read biologically, the four-armed adult depends on exchange between people: no Machamp can arise in a wild population, which fits its absence from every encounter table.
Machoke wears a belt that holds back its power so it can regulate its movements; it is so dangerous without it that no one has ever removed one.
Where Machoke's belt comes from, and whether wild Machoke wear one, is not stated.
Even standing still, Machoke gives off a strong sense of power, and it always stays focused.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Throws: Seismic Toss (Lv 19), Vital Throw (Lv 25) and Submission (Lv 32) are the 'thrown over the horizon' of its entries in move form.
Strikes: Karate Chop (Lv 10), Cross Chop (Lv 40) and Dynamic Punch (Lv 51), matching its punches and chops.
Focus Energy (Lv 7), Revenge (Lv 22) and Scary Face (Lv 44) round out a fighter's set; Wake-Up Slap (Lv 36) is an open-handed blow.

ecology.text: Machop uses Graveler and Geodude as training weights: it hefts Graveler like a barbell and can throw several Geodude at once.
The encounter data agree: Machop and Geodude share every floor of Mt. Mortar, and Graveler shares the upper cave with Machoke.
Its trophic position is unknown because its diet is never given.

humans.text: Machoke willingly does hard work for people, moving heavy goods and helping with demanding labour; it can lift a dump truck with one hand, and on days off it goes to the fields and mountains to train.
The arrangement benefits both sides: people get the labour and Machoke gets the training it wants ('it happily carries heavy cargo to toughen up').
Machop has the strength to hurl a hundred adult humans and to hoist a sumo wrestler; Machamp can knock a train flying.

homestead.text: Heavy hauling: the line moves heavy goods for people by choice, and Machamp can hurl anything aside.
Clearing boulders and fallen timber: one arm alone can move mountains, and Rock Smash is a taught move it can use.
Construction labour, but only the lifting: it can raise beams and stones, not fit them, because careful work tangles its arms.
Keep it away from the Glasshouse panes, eggs and anything fragile.
It needs work and exercise every day: the line is never satisfied with its training, and idle strength is the risk.

The capability records list it as a calming presence (from its Sapphire entry) and for air travel (from LeafGreen). Neither is supported: 68.7 is about mastering martial arts and throwing foes, and 68.10 about knocking victims flying.

niche.foraging: not described
niche.note: Diet is never stated. Machamp has no wild niche in these games; the habitat and activity come from Machop and Machoke.

relationships.note: Machop lifts Graveler as a training weight. The interaction is canon; whether it harms Graveler is not stated, so 'commensalism' is a guess.
Machop throws several Geodude at once; effect on Geodude unstated.
Every floor of Mt. Mortar, and Rock Tunnel.
Mt. Mortar's upper cave, with Machoke.
Machoke works for people and treats the work as training.
As training weights.

ecotypes.name: Quarry lifter
ecotypes.reading: Rock Slide brings stone down, and Power Trick swaps the user's attack and defence, turning a body hardened by lifting into a weapon. A lineage built around working rock, the boulder-lifting habit of Machop made into a way of life. Fits rocky caves and quarry-like scree such as Mt. Mortar.
ecotypes.behavior: Moves rock all day, whether or not anything needs moving.

ecotypes.name: Patient counterstriker
ecotypes.reading: Meditate builds strength calmly, Counter returns a physical blow twice as hard, and Light Screen blunts special attacks. A lineage that waits and returns force rather than leaping in first, the opposite of 68.6's 'leaps into action before it thinks'. Fits narrow passes where foes come one at a time.
ecotypes.behavior: Stands still and lets the other animal make the first mistake.

ecotypes.name: Flurry boxer
ecotypes.reading: Bullet Punch is a jab that lands first, Close Combat an all-out exchange that leaves the user open, and Rolling Kick a spinning strike. A lineage built entirely on speed and volume of blows, the thousand punches in two seconds of 68.9. Fits open slopes where fights are short and decided at once.
ecotypes.behavior: Wins in the first second or not at all.

open_questions: What does the line eat, and how much?
Where does Machoke's belt come from, and do wild Machoke wear one?
Could Machamp ever arise without people trading it?
Does lifting Graveler and Geodude harm them, or do they tolerate it?
Is the line diurnal? Crystal's tables say so; Gold, Silver and HeartGold mostly don't split by time.
Machop 'lives in the mountains away from humans' (66.11), yet Machoke works willingly for people (67.12). When does the line move from shy to tame?

contradictions.topic: Over the horizon: fact or saying
contradictions.note: Red, Blue, Silver, SoulSilver and Sapphire (68.1, 68.4, 68.7) state that it throws or punches victims over the horizon; LeafGreen (68.10), rewording Red and Blue, makes it something 'said'.

contradictions.topic: Shy of people or eager to work for them
contradictions.note: Pearl (66.11) says Machop lives in the mountains away from humans; Sapphire and Platinum (67.7, 67.12) say Machoke helps people willingly and happily. Different stages, so not strictly a contradiction, but the shift is never explained.

folklore.text: Its punches are said to knock the victim flying clear over the horizon.
folklore.note: Other entries state it as fact (see contradictions).

Magcargo.summary: A lava snail whose shell is its own skin, cooled and hardened, and so brittle it crumbles at a touch; flames escape through the gaps. Its entries give a body temperature of about 18,000°F, a figure hard to square with a shell that is simply cooled skin. No game puts Magcargo or its young form Slugma anywhere near Blackthorn, so its place in the highlands community is Blackthorn's own choice: a possible heat source in a frozen, energy-poor landscape, and a test of whether hot ground exists there at all. Swinub's habit of rooting out hot springs is the only canon hint that it might.

anatomy.text: A slug-like body (squiggle shape) with a shell, 0.8 m and 55.0 kg, typed Fire and Rock.
The shell on its back is just skin that has cooled and hardened, also described as hardened magma. It is very brittle and crumbles if touched.
Its body is as hot as lava and always billowing; flames burst from gaps in the shell and circulate through its body.
Its body temperature is given as roughly 18,000°F.
That figure can't be taken literally alongside a shell of cooled skin that people can touch; read it as 'extremely hot', not as a measurement.
anatomy.analogy: Basaltic lava erupts at roughly 1,100-1,200 °C (about 2,000-2,200 °F). 18,000 °F is about 10,000 °C, hotter than the visible surface of the Sun (about 5,500 °C).

anatomy.text: In the young form, Slugma, there is no blood: magma circulates through the body instead, carrying nutrients and oxygen to the organs.

diet.text: No entry says it eats anything.
It returns to its original size by dipping itself in magma, so magma restores its body.
Slugma slithers in a constant search for warm places and sleeps near magma.
Taken together: it seems to take its heat from hot ground and its substance from magma, a thermotroph in the project's terms.
diet.note: Nothing says how heat becomes energy for it.
diet.analogy: Real hydrothermal-vent communities run on chemical energy (bacteria oxidising hydrogen sulphide), not on heat itself; no known organism uses heat directly as its energy source.

habitat.text: Volcanic craters, where Magcargo have lived for tens of thousands of years; Slugma are a common sight in volcanic areas.

Magcargo is not wild anywhere in HeartGold or SoulSilver. Slugma is on Kanto Routes 16 and 18 (5%) and Route 17 (5%, 30% by day), and comes as a gift Egg in Violet City's Pokémon Center with a password. Wild Magcargo appear only on Mt. Ember B3F (FireRed, LeafGreen, by Rock Smash) and Stark Mountain (Diamond, Pearl, Platinum).
No game places Magcargo or Slugma in the Blackthorn highlands. It is part of this community by Blackthorn's choice, as the geothermal member.
If it lives in the highlands at all, it can only be where there is geothermal heat. Swinub's entries say Swinub roots out hot springs, which is the only canon sign of such heat in the community.
habitat.note: The Swinub entries aren't tied to Blackthorn specifically.

behavior.text: Slugma never sleeps: it has to keep moving because if it stopped, its magma body would cool and harden. The Magcargo entries don't say whether the adult shares this.
If it is caught in rain, the raindrops turn to steam on contact and cloak the area in thick fog.
Activity pattern isn't stated.

social.text: Slugma group together in places hotter than normal: aggregations at heat, not necessarily social bonds.

reproduction.text: Amorphous egg group, 20 egg cycles, even sex ratio. Nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding.
The capability records list both its abilities, Flame Body and Magma Armor, as egg care in the overworld.

defense.text: Flame Body (contact may burn the attacker) and Magma Armor (it can't be frozen); in the highlands the second matters as much as the first.
The shell gives little protection: it crumbles at a touch. Heat is the real defence.
Harden (Lv 16), Recover (Lv 23) and Amnesia (Lv 31) are its defensive level-up moves; Recover fits an animal that must keep rebuilding a crumbling body.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses. Slugma's constant search for warm places implies it can sense heat.

life_cycle.text: It evolves from Slugma at Lv 38, from 0.7 m and 35 kg to 0.8 m and 55 kg, gaining the Rock type with the shell.
Cold costs the line its body: a chilled Slugma's magma hardens, turns brittle and falls off in chunks, reducing its size, and Magcargo regains its size by dipping in magma.
In a cold place that loss would be constant, so a highland Magcargo would need regular access to magma or something like it to stay whole.
Tens of thousands of years living in volcanic craters have turned Magcargo's bodies into magma: the entry gives an origin, not a development.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Its level-up moves are heat and rock: Smog and Ember (Lv 1), Rock Throw, Lava Plume (Lv 40), Rock Slide (Lv 45), Flamethrower (Lv 61), Earth Power (Lv 66). Yawn (Lv 1) is its oddity, a move that makes others drowsy.

ecology.text: If it lives in the highlands, it is a moving heat source: it would melt snow and ice around it and turn rain to fog, opening warm, wet patches in frozen ground.
ecology.note: Rests on its canon heat; its presence in the highlands is Blackthorn's choice.

ecology.text: Its crumbling shell and Slugma's shed chunks are rock, and would add mineral fragments to the ground where it lives.
ecology.note: As with Golem's shed hide returning to soil (76.8); untested.

ecology.text: No predator and no prey are recorded.

humans.text: Dangerous to touch: its body is as hot as lava and contact may burn.
In HeartGold and SoulSilver trainers meet the line only through Slugma on Kanto Routes 16-18 or the Violet City gift Egg.

homestead.text: A living heater for a highland winter, if it can be kept somewhere safe. In practice treat it as a fire that moves: stone floors, nothing flammable nearby.
The capability records list it for egg care (Flame Body, Magma Armor in the overworld).
The cold is the obstacle: a chilled body hardens and crumbles, and rebuilding it takes magma. Unless there is geothermal heat near the homestead, keeping one through winter is an open problem.
Keep it out of the rain near buildings: rain on it becomes thick fog.
The homestead's forge, built around a Magcargo's corner of the workshop.

microhabitat: geothermal ground, if any exists in the highlands (unconfirmed)
niche.foraging: seeks heat and dips in magma to restore its body; no food recorded

relationships.note: Stated for Slugma.
Hot springs that Swinub roots out would be warm ground for Magcargo; no entry links them, and Magcargo's presence in the highlands is Blackthorn's choice.

ecotypes.name: Heat banker
ecotypes.reading: Three moves for storing something inside and releasing it later: read as banking heat or molten material so it can range away from a hot spot for longer. The lineage most likely to cope with a cold highland.
ecotypes.behavior: Charges up at a hot spot, then ranges out into the cold.

ecotypes.name: Fumarole
ecotypes.reading: Smoke and broad hot air rather than flame: a lineage of steaming vents and hot-spring margins rather than lava. Fits the cooler, wetter end of geothermal ground, the kind of place a Swinub's hot spring would offer.
ecotypes.behavior: Sits in steam; vents heat in waves.

ecotypes.name: Molten
ecotypes.reading: Acid Armor melts the body to toughen it, and Curse (for a non-Ghost) trades speed for strength and toughness. A lineage that stays soft and molten instead of relying on a brittle crust; fits only the hottest ground.
ecotypes.behavior: Barely moves; never crusts over.

open_questions: Is there any geothermal heat in the Blackthorn highlands? Swinub's hot springs (220.1) are the only hint; without it, Magcargo has no habitat there.
Should Magcargo be in the highlands community at all, given that no game places it or Slugma near Blackthorn?
What does it actually take in: heat, magma, minerals? How does heat become energy for it?
How can a shell of cooled skin sit on an 18,000°F body (219.1, 219.5)?
Magma Armor says it can't be frozen, but Slugma's body hardens and immobilises when it cools (218.6). How does that play out in a highland winter?
Does the adult, like Slugma, have to keep moving and never sleep?

contradictions.text: Gold/HeartGold and Ruby say the shell is skin that has cooled and hardened and crumbles when touched; Sapphire and Diamond/Pearl/Platinum give a body temperature of about 18,000°F.
contradictions.reading: A body that hot could not keep a cooled skin, and nothing could touch it. Not strictly entry against entry, but the two claims can't both be literal. Read the temperature as hyperbole unless Zack prefers otherwise.

Magikarp.summary: A fish that does almost nothing but flop and splash, and the Pokédex's favourite example of weakness. Its swimming muscles are weak, so currents push it along and wash it into pools in numbers, and it jumps for no reason, which makes it easy for predators like Pidgeotto to catch. Yet it is hardy enough to survive in any body of water, however polluted, and it lives in seas, lakes, rivers and puddles alike. In Ilex Forest it is the commonest catch on an Old Rod, and it is in Blackthorn City's water too.

anatomy.text: A red fish (0.9 m, 10.0 kg).
Its swimming muscles are weak.
It may jump high on rare occasions, but never (or usually not) more than seven feet.

diet.text: Not stated in any entry, and none of its moves concerns feeding.
A fish that can't swim against even slow currents probably eats whatever it can reach without chasing: drifting food, plants or small animals.
diet.note: Untested.
diet.analogy: Real carp (Cyprinus carpio) are omnivorous bottom-feeders, taking plants, seeds and invertebrates.

habitat.text: Seas, lakes, rivers and shallow puddles: any body of water, however polluted.
Currents carry it: strong currents push it along rivers, and many Magikarp are deposited wherever water pools.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is fished from Ilex Forest's pond (85% on the Old Rod, 40% Good Rod, 20% Super Rod) and from almost every water in Johto, including Blackthorn City (where it is also 100% of surfing encounters), Dragon's Den and the Lake of Rage.

behavior.text: It flops and splashes about, for no reason anyone can see.
It can't swim against even slow-moving currents.
Its activity pattern is unknown: Ilex Forest's fishing tables have no time of day.

social.text: Many gather where currents deposit them, but that is passive aggregation, not described social life.

reproduction.text: Water 2 and Dragon egg groups, 5 egg cycles (the shortest there is), slow growth, an even sex ratio.

Quick-hatching eggs and its presence in nearly every body of water fit a fish that survives by numbers rather than strength, a possible answer to Diamond's 'no one knows why it has managed to survive'.
reproduction.note: Egg cycles are a game mechanic; how many eggs a Magikarp lays is never stated.
reproduction.analogy: Many real fishes withstand heavy predation by producing very large numbers of young.

defense.text: Practically none: it is virtually worthless in both power and speed, and its jumping makes it easy for predators like Pidgeotto to catch mid-jump.
Hardiness instead: it is a very hardy Pokémon that can survive in any body of water, however polluted.
Its ability is Swift Swim (faster in rain); Splash does nothing, Tackle (15) and Flail (30) are its only attacks.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses.

life_cycle.text: Magikarp becomes Gyarados at level 20: from the weakest Pokémon to a huge, vicious one that can destroy cities in a rage.
When it evolves, its brain cells undergo a structural transformation, which is said to cause Gyarados's violent nature.
In the distant past it was somewhat stronger than its horribly weak descendants today.
A Magikarp living for many years can leap a mountain with Splash; the move stays useless (see Folklore and Contradictions).

moves_in_the_wild.text: Splash (Lv 1), Tackle (15) and Flail (30) are its whole level-up list; Bounce is a tutor move taught by people. A wild Magikarp splashes, bumps and thrashes.
It evolves at 20, so a wild Magikarp has Splash and perhaps Tackle; Flail at 30 belongs to one kept from evolving.
The line has no egg moves in HeartGold and SoulSilver.

ecology.text: Prey: its entries name one predator, Pidgeotto, and describe it as easy to catch.
A fish this weak and this widespread is probably food for many larger animals; in Ilex Forest, Golduck and Noctowl are the candidates.
ecology.note: Pidgeotto isn't in Ilex Forest's tables.

ecology.text: Its diet is unknown, so its trophic level is a guess: 2 if it grazes, nearer 3 if it takes small animals.
Carried by currents and tolerant of pollution, it would be among the first fish to reach new or degraded water.
ecology.note: An inference from two entries; no entry describes colonisation.

ecology.text: In Ilex Forest it dominates the Old Rod catch (85%) and Poliwag the Super Rod (80%).

humans.text: Its constant flopping and splashing prompted scientists to research it.
It is famous for being very unreliable, and called an underpowered, pathetic Pokémon, the weakest and most pathetic in the world.
The capability records list scouting (from 129.1) and water travel (from 129.8); neither is supported by what the entries say it can do.

homestead.text: Local: it lives in Blackthorn City's water, Dragon's Den and the Lake of Rage.
No use as a water-quality indicator: it survives in any water, however polluted, so its presence says little, though its absence would be alarming.
A Gyarados in waiting: raising a Magikarp past level 20 produces Gyarados, whose entries describe rampages and burned villages. Don't raise one near the homestead without a plan.
It needs only water, and even polluted water will do.

niche.foraging: unknown; a weak swimmer that cannot chase, so probably takes drifting or bottom food
niche.note: No entry gives its diet; the guild is a placeholder for a carp-like fish.

relationships.note: Named as a predator that catches it mid-jump. Pidgeotto isn't in Ilex Forest's tables.
The pond's fastest swimmer and its weakest fish share the water. Golduck's diet is undescribed.
A splashing fish at the surface is the kind of target 129.4 says birds take; Noctowl hunts the forest at night.
Its dispersal: currents carry it and deposit it where water pools.

open_questions: What does it eat?
Why does it splash 'for no reason'? No purpose is recorded.
How has it survived (129.10)? Numbers, hardiness, or something else?
How high can it jump: never more than seven feet (129.3), usually not more (129.13), or over a mountain (129.12)?
What does 'stronger in the distant past' (129.1) rest on?
The line has no HeartGold-SoulSilver egg moves, so no ecotypes can be read from breeding; is there variation between populations anyway?

contradictions.text: How high does it jump? Gold says never more than seven feet (129.3); HeartGold, rewording the same entry, says usually not more than seven feet (129.13); Platinum says a long-lived Magikarp can leap a mountain (129.12).

Weak or hardy? Sapphire says it is considered weak but is actually very hardy (129.7); FireRed calls it the weakest, most pathetic Pokémon in the world (129.9), and Diamond says no one knows how it has survived (129.10).
contradictions.note: Compatible if 'weak' means in battle and 'hardy' means in tolerance; recorded because the entries frame it differently.

folklore.text: It is said to be the world's weakest Pokémon, and is considered weak because it can only splash.
folklore.note: Given as reputation ('is said to be', 'is considered'); Sapphire immediately qualifies it.

folklore.text: A Magikarp that lives for many years can leap a mountain using Splash.
folklore.note: Stated as fact in Platinum, but it contradicts the seven-foot limit (129.3, 129.13); best read as legend.
folklore.analogy: It echoes the Chinese legend of the carp that leaps the Dragon Gate and becomes a dragon, which the Magikarp-to-Gyarados line plainly draws on.

Magnezone.summary: A floating, magnetic Steel-and-Electric Pokémon that exists only because of where its parent was standing. Magnezone forms when a Magneton is exposed to a special magnetic field, which the HeartGold and SoulSilver Pokédex says changes its molecular structure; a group that tried to make it happen by scientific means failed. Its line feeds on electricity, hovers on electromagnetic waves, and in numbers disrupts radios, televisions and machinery, and Magneton is said to be three Magnemite linked by magnetism. Few animals in the Pokédex sit so far from ordinary biology: genderless, without egg moves, and impossible to evolve anywhere in Johto.

anatomy.text: A heavy, hovering body (1.2 m, 180.0 kg) with three units that generate its magnetism.
In Magnemite the side units do the work: they emit electromagnetic waves that keep it aloft, act as powerful magnets, and generate more magnetic force the faster they spin.
Magneton is a linked cluster of Magnemite, held by a strong magnetic force; most entries say three, older ones say 'several'.
The weights don't add up: three Magnemite are 18 kg, Magneton is 60 kg and Magnezone 180 kg. Whatever linking does, it is not simple addition of bodies.

diet.text: The line feeds on electricity; Magnemite attach to power lines to feed.
diet.analogy: Some real bacteria, such as Geobacter, can take electrons directly from an electrode, which microbiologists call electrotrophy; nothing larger than a microbe does.

diet.text: Its energy store is finite: a Magnemite whose internal electrical supply runs out can no longer fly.
No entry says what Magnezone itself eats; electricity is the obvious inference from the line.

habitat.text: Magnezone is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game.

It forms only at a special magnetic field: the archive gives Mt. Coronet (Sinnoh) and Chargestone Cave. Neither is in Johto or Kanto (Chargestone Cave is not a Gen I-IV location at all), so a HeartGold or SoulSilver Magneton cannot become Magnezone.

The line favours electrical and industrial places: Kanto's Power Plant, Hoenn's New Mauville and Sinnoh's Fuego Ironworks. In Johto, Magnemite lives on the pasture of Routes 38 and 39 at any hour, and on Kanto's Routes 6 and 11; Magneton lives in Cerulean Cave. Its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is rough terrain.
Gold and Silver also have a Magnemite swarm on Route 38.

behavior.text: It hovers constantly; Magnemite is born able to defy gravity.
It approaches electromagnetic sources: Magnemite is attracted to electromagnetic waves and may approach trainers using a PokéGear.
Magneton appear in numbers when sunspots flare up.
Johto and Kanto tables have Magnemite morning, day and night, so it is active around the clock.

social.text: Aggregation is the line's social life: Magnemite gather in large numbers on breaker boxes; Magneton is several Magnemite linked; many Magneton together raise a magnetic storm.
Whether the linked units of a Magneton are still individuals, or become one animal, is not said; Magnezone's three units raise the same question.
social.analogy: Siphonophores, such as the Portuguese man o' war (Physalia), are colonies of specialised individuals (zooids) that function as one animal.

reproduction.text: Genderless, in the Mineral egg group, 20 egg cycles. In the games a genderless Pokémon breeds only with Ditto.
No stage of the line has any egg moves in HeartGold and SoulSilver, so lineages can't carry inherited specialisations the way other species here can.
Magnemite is 'born' able to defy gravity, the only word in the record about its beginnings.

defense.text: Sturdy (it can't be knocked out in one hit) or Magnet Pull (Steel-type opponents can't escape it).
Its magnetic force is fatal to mechanical devices, electronics and precision instruments, and Magneton dries all moisture around it; standing close to one gives you earache.
Magnezone starts with Barrier and Mirror Coat (Lv 1), a defensive screen and a move that reflects special attacks back.

senses.text: It detects electromagnetic waves, as its approach to PokéGear users shows.
Lock-On (Lv 27), which makes its next attack certain to hit, is the closest the games come to describing how it targets.
No eyes, ears or other sense organs are described.

life_cycle.text: Magnemite (0.3 m, 6.0 kg) becomes Magneton at level 30 (1.0 m, 60.0 kg), and Magneton becomes Magnezone (1.2 m, 180.0 kg) only by levelling up in a special magnetic field.
The final change is environmental, not age- or size-driven: exposure to a special magnetic field alters Magneton's molecular structure.
It can't be forced: a group that tried to make Magnezone evolve by scientific means failed.
The canon and the mechanic disagree about Magneton: the entries say three Magnemite link up, but in the games one Magnemite levels up into one Magneton.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Thunder Wave (Lv 17) is in the canon itself: Magnemite appears without warning and uses Thunder Wave and similar moves, discharged from its side units.
Its sound moves, Supersonic (Lv 11), Sonic Boom (Lv 14), Screech (Lv 33-34) and Metal Sound (Lv 1), fit the earaches Magneton causes.
Magnet Rise (Lv 46-50) is the levitation of the canon in move form, and Gyro Ball (Lv 49-54) fits units that spin.
Discharge and Zap Cannon are its own electrical attacks; Thunderbolt and Thunder are taught by machine.

ecology.text: Outside the carbon food web: it takes energy from electricity, not from other organisms, and nothing is recorded eating it.

Magneton changes its surroundings: its radio waves raise the temperature by 3.6 °F (about 2 °C) within 3,300 feet (about 1 km), and its magnetism dries the moisture around it. A group could alter a local microclimate.
On Routes 38 and 39, Magnemite shares the pasture with Miltank and Tauros, and the trees with Pineco.

humans.text: A pest of electrical systems: Magnemite feed on power lines, and in a power cut you may find many clinging to the breaker box.
A public hazard in numbers: large cities sound sirens for big Magneton outbreaks; their magnetic storms disrupt radio and stop televisions displaying properly.
Kanto's Power Plant offers a Magneton in trade for a Dugtrio in Crystal, HeartGold and SoulSilver.

homestead.text: Electricity: an Electric type whose capability records include charging a storage battery. Whether it gives power as readily as it takes it is untested; the record says it feeds on electricity.
It will drain the homestead's own supply if it can: keep it off the power lines and away from the breaker box.
Keep it far from the clinic's instruments, the radios, the PokéGear and anything with a circuit: the line's magnetism is fatal to electronics and precision instruments.
A magnetic retriever: Magnemite can draw iron objects from over 300 feet (about 90 m) away, useful for recovering lost tools, nails and wire.
Drying: Magneton dries the moisture around it, which could serve seed and berry storage in the Ice Path cold vault, if its effect on everything else in the vault can be managed.
homestead.note: An extrapolation from a canon side effect; untested and possibly harmful to stored samples.

homestead.text: Blackthorn can't produce its own Magnezone: there is no special magnetic field in Johto, so one has to come from Sinnoh.
Light is a taught move here (Flash is a machine), not its own.

niche.foraging: attaches to electrical sources to feed; drawn to electromagnetic waves
niche.note: Trophic level is left null: it feeds on electricity, not on organisms, so it sits outside the usual food-chain count.

relationships.note: It draws them in; whether it uses them for anything is not said.
A correlation in the entries (Magneton appear when sunspots flare), not a stated dependency.
Required for Magnezone to form at all.
Routes 38 and 39 pasture, HeartGold and SoulSilver (Magnemite).

open_questions: No ecotypes are possible from the games: the line is genderless (it breeds only with Ditto) and has no egg moves at any stage in HeartGold and SoulSilver.
Is a Magneton three individuals or one? The entries say three Magnemite link; the games evolve one Magnemite into one Magneton.
Why do the weights jump (6 kg, 60 kg, 180 kg) if Magneton is just three linked Magnemite?
What makes a magnetic field 'special' enough to trigger Magnezone, and why did the scientific attempt fail (462.2)?
Does Magnezone feed on electricity as Magnemite does?
Why do Magneton appear when sunspots flare? Is solar activity a food source, a trigger, or a cue?
Is Magnemite on Johto's pasture routes for a reason (power lines, fencing wire), or is that a game convenience?

contradictions.text: How many Magnemite make a Magneton: 'several' in Red, Blue, FireRed and LeafGreen; exactly three in Gold, Emerald, Diamond and Pearl.
How Magnemite floats: anti-gravity energy that blocks gravity (Red, Blue, LeafGreen, Silver, SoulSilver, Sapphire) versus floating on electromagnetic waves (Yellow, Diamond and Pearl).
contradictions.note: Sapphire reconciles them: electromagnetic waves that block gravity.

folklore.text: It is said that some towns warn people to keep Magneton inside a Poké Ball because of its effect on electronics.
folklore.note: The effect on electronics is stated as fact; the town warnings are hearsay.

Mamoswine.summary: A huge, shaggy, ice-tusked survivor of an ice age. Mamoswine flourished worldwide while the ice lasted and declined as it melted; a frozen one dug out of 10,000-year-old ground is said to have woken up. Its young are Swinub, small rooting pigs with noses sensitive enough to find mushrooms, berries and even hot springs under ice, and they are common in the Ice Path, right beside Blackthorn. In between comes Piloswine, so shaggy it can't see, which finds its way by smell and sound and just keeps charging.

anatomy.text: A massive quadruped (2.5 m, 291.0 kg) with impressive tusks made of ice.
Piloswine's coat of long hair lets it endure freezing cold; its short legs end in rugged hooves that grip icy ground, and its ice tusks thicken when it snows.
Swinub's nose is tough enough to dig into frozen ground.
Tusks that grow with snowfall suggest they are built from or added to by ice from outside, rather than grown like tooth.

diet.text: Swinub roots for food by rubbing its snout on the ground; its favourite food is a mushroom that grows under dead or dried grass.
diet.analogy: Pigs are used to find truffles (Tuber) by smell, which is the same rooting-by-nose foraging.

diet.text: It also finds berries, and mushrooms buried under ice.
Piloswine digs up food buried under ice with its tusks.
No entry says what Mamoswine eats; the line's foraging suggests it still digs for plant and fungal food under snow.

habitat.text: An ice-age animal: it flourished worldwide during the ice age and thinned out when the climate warmed and the ice dwindled.
habitat.analogy: The woolly mammoth (Mammuthus primigenius) followed a similar course: widespread in the cold, it retreated as the climate warmed after the last glacial period, with a last population on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.

habitat.text: Mamoswine is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game, and Piloswine only by Poké Radar on Route 217 in Platinum.

Swinub lives in the Ice Path between Mahogany Town and Blackthorn City, on every floor and common (40%): at any hour in HeartGold and SoulSilver, by day and morning only in Crystal. Its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is cave.
Elsewhere Swinub keeps to ice: Icefall Cave in FireRed and LeafGreen, and the snowy north of Sinnoh (Route 217, Acuity Lakefront).

behavior.text: Swinub follows its nose: if it smells something enticing it dashes off headlong after it.
Piloswine, unable to see past its hair, just keeps charging repeatedly; the hairs on its back stand up when it charges.
behavior.analogy: Raising the hair along the back (piloerection) is a common mammal threat display, as in a dog's raised hackles.
