life_cycle.text: It becomes Forretress at level 31, and the bark case becomes a steel-hard shell: the type changes from Bug to Bug/Steel.
The adult is even more sedentary, immovably rooted to its tree, usually on a fat trunk; it opens the shell only to catch prey, too fast for the inside to be seen.

Read as development, the move from layered bark to a steel shell suggests the case is mineralised or replaced as the animal matures, and the adult trades the juvenile's branch-hanging life for trunk-clinging.
life_cycle.note: No entry describes the change itself.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Feeding: Bug Bite. Defence: Protect, Iron Defense, Self-Destruct, Explosion. Rapid Spin (Lv 17) and Gyro Ball (Lv 42) fit a round body that falls and rolls; Spikes (Lv 28) matches the adult scattering pieces of its shell to drive enemies away.
Natural Gift (Lv 23) needs a held Berry, which hints that it handles fruit, but nothing in the Pokédex says it eats or stores Berries.
moves_in_the_wild.note: A level-up move, so it's the wild form's own repertoire; treat as a lead, not a diet item.

ecology.text: A canopy insectivore (trophic level about 3: it eats insects, which mostly eat plants), probably a minor control on flying insects in the trees it occupies.
It strips or collects tree bark for its case, so it uses the trees as a building material as well as a perch; whether it takes living bark (harming the tree) or shed bark is unknown.
Its explosion when a tree is shaken makes it a hazard to anything that shakes trees for food, such as foragers using Headbutt.

humans.text: People meet it by shaking trees, which is exactly the disturbance that the Ruby, Sapphire and Emerald entries say makes it explode. The Johto games' only way of finding it is the way most likely to set it off.

homestead.text: A natural perimeter deterrent: as Forretress it scatters shell fragments to drive enemies away, and Spikes is the game form of that.
Free insect control in an orchard or around the Glasshouse, if it will settle in the trees there; it needs trees to hang from and flying insects to eat.
homestead.note: Untested: whether it targets pest insects or just whatever flies past.

homestead.text: Don't put it in trees people shake for fruit or Apricorns, and keep it away from Headbutt foraging: a shaken tree is the trigger for its explosion.
Its bark-glue fluid, which sets in air, is an interesting material for repairs if it can be collected without stressing the animal.

niche.foraging: sit-and-wait ambush of flying insects from a hanging position

relationships.note: Birds peck it by mistake, taking it for food or for a cone; the shell protects it. Attempted predation, not a successful one.
Same Ilex Forest headbutt trees in HeartGold and SoulSilver; Hoothoot and Noctowl are the forest's bird Pokémon and the likely mistaken peckers.

ecotypes.name: Barbed bark
ecotypes.reading: A lineage whose defence is chemical and projectile rather than explosive: barbs in the bark case and a toxic litter of shed fragments beneath its tree. Fits dense woods where predators approach from below.
ecotypes.behavior: Explodes less, sheds more; leaves a poisoned ring of debris under its roost.

ecotypes.name: Ground-fall brawler
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that turns the drop from the branch into a fight: retaliation moves (Counter, Revenge) for the animal that shook its tree, and Sand Tomb for burying in sand or leaf litter once down. Fits dry, sandy woodland edges where falling is common and climbing back is slow.
ecotypes.behavior: Falls, digs in and hits back rather than exploding.

ecotypes.name: Mirror shell
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that leans into the armour: a defensive screen, and Power Trick, which swaps attack and defence, as the habit of turning that heavy case into the weapon (rolling and ramming).
ecotypes.behavior: Rolls into attackers with its case; the most Forretress-like juvenile.

open_questions: What is inside the shell? The Forretress entries call it a total mystery (205.1, 205.7).
Does it take bark from living trees, harming them, or gather shed bark?
What, if anything, does it eat besides flying insects? Natural Gift hints at Berries.
Does it survive its own explosion, and how often can it do it?
How does it breed, and where are eggs laid: in the canopy, in the case?
Is it diurnal or nocturnal? Ilex Forest's tree tables don't say.

Poliwag.summary: A tadpole that has just grown legs and can't use them yet. Poliwag's skin is thin, damp and so transparent that its coiled insides show through as the swirl on its belly, clearer after it has eaten; yet the skin is so flexible that sharp fangs bounce off it. It lives in water and swims rather than walks. In Ilex Forest it is caught only by fishing, and it lives in Blackthorn City's water too. The direction of the belly spiral is said to differ from region to region.

anatomy.text: A tadpole (0.6 m, 12.4 kg) with newly grown legs.
anatomy.analogy: Real tadpoles grow their hind legs first and their forelegs later, then absorb the tail at metamorphosis; a two-legged tadpole like Poliwag is at the hind-leg stage.

anatomy.text: Very thin, slick, damp black skin through which its internal organs can be seen.
The swirl on its belly is its insides showing through the skin: part of its internal organs, seen as a spiral.
anatomy.analogy: Many real tadpoles have a long, coiled gut that shows through the belly skin; it is long because they digest plant food.

diet.text: It eats, and its belly swirl looks clearer afterwards.
What it eats isn't stated. A long, coiled gut points to plant food or detritus rather than prey.
diet.note: An inference from gut shape that leans on real tadpoles; the entries don't say the spiral is the gut, only 'insides' and 'internal organs'.
diet.analogy: Most real tadpoles graze algae and detritus, and carnivorous tadpoles, such as the meat-eating form of spadefoot toad tadpoles, have shorter guts.

habitat.text: Water: because it is inept at walking on its new legs, it always swims around in water.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is fished from Ilex Forest's pond (15% on the Old Rod, 60% Good Rod, 80% Super Rod) and never surfed there; it is fished from ponds and rivers across Johto, including Blackthorn City and Routes 43 to 45, and surfed on Routes 30, 31 and 44 and in Violet and Ecruteak Cities.
Being caught by rod rather than met surfing in Ilex Forest suggests it stays below the surface.

behavior.text: It prefers swimming to standing or walking, and is more adept at it.
Its activity pattern is unknown: Ilex Forest's fishing tables have no time of day.

social.text: Poliwag gather from far and wide when they hear Politoed's echoing cry, and Politoed's cries make them obey: the line's adult leads groups of young.
So Poliwag live within earshot of, and respond to, adults of their own line; whether they form groups without one isn't stated.

reproduction.text: Water 1 egg group, 20 egg cycles, an even sex ratio, medium-slow growth. As a tadpole it is the line's juvenile; nothing says where eggs are laid.

defense.text: Its skin, though thin, is so flexible that even sharp fangs bounce off it.
Hypnosis (Lv 8) is the belly spiral in game form: in its evolved form the spiral puts a foe to sleep so it can escape, and staring at it causes drowsiness.
Its abilities are Water Absorb (water attacks heal it) and Damp.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses.

life_cycle.text: Poliwag becomes Poliwhirl at level 25; Poliwhirl becomes Poliwrath with a Water Stone, or Politoed if traded holding a King's Rock.
Read as tadpole to frog: the new legs become Poliwhirl's well-developed legs, and Poliwhirl can live in or out of water, though it prefers water.
life_cycle.analogy: Amphibian metamorphosis: an aquatic, tailed larva becomes a semi-aquatic or land-living adult.

life_cycle.text: The two adult forms divide: Poliwrath is a powerful swimmer that nonetheless lives on dry land, and Politoed is a leader whose cry gathers Poliwag.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Water Sport (Lv 1), Bubble (5), Water Gun (11), Bubble Beam (25), Hydro Pump (38): water. Mud Shot (28) and Mud Bomb (41): mud.
Hypnosis (8) is the spiral; Rain Dance (18) calls rain. A wild Poliwag evolves at 25, so its working repertoire stops at Body Slam (21).

ecology.text: If it grazes, it is a primary consumer of the pond (trophic level 2), and food for larger pond animals.
ecology.note: Its diet is undescribed.

ecology.text: Its fang-proof skin is a defence against biting predators, which implies they exist.
In Ilex Forest it shares the fishing tables with Magikarp, and the share shifts by rod: mostly Magikarp on the Old Rod, mostly Poliwag on the Super Rod.

humans.text: Easy to catch (catch rate 255) and fished all over Johto.
People have noticed that the spiral's direction varies by area and have a theory about why (see Folklore).

homestead.text: Local: it lives in Blackthorn City's water and on Routes 43 to 45, so it is at home in the highland ponds.
If it grazes algae, a Poliwag in a cistern or garden pond might help keep the water clear.
homestead.note: Untested; rests on the grazing hypothesis.

homestead.text: Water Gun (Lv 11) is in its wild repertoire, so it can spray water on plants.
homestead.note: A move, read as a practical ability.

homestead.text: It needs clean water to live in: its thin, damp skin means it can't stay out of water for long.

microhabitat: pond and slow water, below the surface
niche.foraging: unknown; probably grazing, judging by its coiled gut
niche.note: No entry gives its diet.

relationships.note: From gut shape; no entry gives its diet.
Same water; Golduck is the pond's fastest and largest animal. Poliwag's fang-proof skin argues against.

ecotypes.name: Cold-water
ecotypes.reading: Three Ice-type egg moves: a lineage at home in cold, high water. Fits highland ponds and streams like Blackthorn City's and Route 44's, where Poliwag is in fact found.
ecotypes.behavior: Stays active in cold water and under thin ice.

ecotypes.name: Mud-bottom
ecotypes.reading: A lineage of silty, shallow ponds: mud as weapon and cover, and resistance to the infections and fouling of stagnant water (Refresh cures status problems).
ecotypes.behavior: Lives on and in the muddy bottom.

ecotypes.name: Splash-escape
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that leaps clear of the water to escape, and fights hardest when badly hurt. Fits ponds with many fast predators, where a last-ditch escape matters.
ecotypes.behavior: Jumps when chased; turns on an attacker when cornered.

open_questions: What does it eat?
Does the belly spiral really differ by area, and if it does, why?
Where are its eggs laid, and how long is the tadpole stage?
Does it hatch with legs, or grow them later?
Does it ever come onto land?

folklore.text: The direction of its belly spiral differs by area, and the equator is thought to have an effect on this.
folklore.note: The regional difference is stated as fact; the equator explanation is given as a belief ('is thought to').
folklore.analogy: The popular idea that water drains swirl opposite ways in the two hemispheres is a myth at the scale of a basin. And in real tadpoles the gut coils the same way in nearly every individual, as part of the body's fixed left-right asymmetry.

Psyduck.summary: A pond duck with a constant headache and powers it can't remember using. When the headache peaks, Psyduck shows psychic or telekinetic power, apparently in an altered state like deep sleep, and afterwards it has no memory of it, which is why it always looks puzzled. Not one entry says what it eats or where it lives. HeartGold and SoulSilver put it on the water: it is 90% of what is met surfing Ilex Forest's pond.

anatomy.text: A yellow duck (0.8 m, 19.6 kg) that stands upright.
When it uses its power it produces brain waves otherwise seen only in sleepers, a discovery that caused controversy among scholars.
It can use its psychic power only when its sleeping brain cells happen to wake.

diet.text: Not stated in any entry.

Its moves suggest a scratching, splashing forager (Scratch at Lv 1, Water Gun 9, Fury Swipes 27), and a duck at the water's edge suggests water plants and small animals; but that is a guess from its body plan.
diet.note: No entry or capability record gives a diet.
diet.analogy: Real dabbling ducks eat a mix of water plants, seeds and invertebrates.

habitat.text: Water's edge by Gen 3 habitat. In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is surfed on Ilex Forest's pond (90%), Route 35 and Route 6, walks in Seafoam Islands, surfs in Cerulean Cave, and is in the Johto Safari Zone.
Golduck's entries put the line on lakes and quiet, slow rivers.
In Crystal it also walked Ilex Forest's grass at night (10%); HeartGold and SoulSilver keep it on the water.

behavior.text: It is constantly tormented by headaches, and when a headache peaks or worsens it starts using strange powers.
It can't remember using its powers, so it always looks puzzled and tilts its head.
During an episode it goes into an altered state much like deep sleep, and so forms no memory of it.
Activity is unknown: surfing tables have no time of day, and its land records (Crystal's Ilex Forest, HeartGold-SoulSilver's Safari Zone) are at night only.

social.text: Nothing is said about other Psyduck.

reproduction.text: Water 1 and Field egg groups, 20 egg cycles, an even sex ratio. Nothing in the Pokédex describes nesting or young.

defense.text: It lulls enemies with its vacant look while it uses psychokinetic powers: a 'wily' animal, in the oldest entry.
Its abilities are Damp (no one can self-destruct near it) and Cloud Nine (weather has no effect); Disable (14), Confusion (18) and Screech (31) are its disruptive moves.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses.

life_cycle.text: Psyduck becomes Golduck at level 33: the yellow, puzzled duck becomes a blue, fast, graceful swimmer whose forehead glows when it uses its power.
The headaches and forgetting belong to Psyduck alone; Golduck's entries describe its power as tied to a glowing forehead, not to pain or blackouts.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Water Sport (Lv 1), Water Gun (9), Water Pulse (22) and Hydro Pump (48): water used with growing force.
Confusion (18) and Zen Headbutt (40) are its psychic episodes in game form; Psych Up (35) and Amnesia (44) are status moves with no counterpart in the entries.

ecology.text: By surfing rate the pond's commonest surface animal, so probably its main large consumer, whatever it eats.
With no described diet, the pond's commonest surface animal has no food link at all; water plants, invertebrates, and the smaller Poliwag and Magikarp are the candidates.
ecology.note: A gap in the reconstructed web.

ecology.text: Damp stops anything near it from self-destructing, and Pineco, which explodes when its tree is shaken, lives in the same forest. The interaction is a game mechanic only.

humans.text: Its psychic episodes interest scholars: the sleep-like brain waves caused controversy.
The capability records say it could use hand tools and garden tools, because of its upright, handed body; that rests on body shape, not on any entry.

homestead.text: Watering: Water Gun is in its wild repertoire from level 9, and the capability records credit its upright body with handling objects, so it could carry water too. It could water the Glasshouse rows, which need heavy watering.
homestead.note: Untested; depends on it being calm enough for routine work.

homestead.text: Its headaches and the powers that come with them are unpredictable; keep it away from eggs and fragile equipment when it is visibly suffering.
homestead.note: No entry says its episodes are dangerous, only that they happen and it can't remember them.

homestead.text: It needs water to live by: a pond, a stream, or at least a large tub.
Damp is an odd but real benefit near anything that self-destructs, such as Pineco.

niche.foraging: unknown; probably dabbling and scratching at the pond margin
niche.note: No entry gives its diet; the guild is a guess from a duck body at the water's edge.

relationships.note: A guess from body plan and habitat; no entry gives its diet.
Ilex Forest's surfing table is Psyduck (90%) and Golduck (10%).

ecotypes.name: Seer
ecotypes.reading: A lineage in which the power is stronger and steadier, with a flavour of anticipation (Future Sight, Foresight). Fits waters with many threats, where early warning pays.
ecotypes.behavior: Fewer blackouts, more deliberate use of its power.

ecotypes.name: Drowsy lure
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that disarms threats by making them sleepy or confused, turning the 'vacant look' that lulls enemies (54.1) into a real tactic. Fits ponds with many predators and few hiding places.
ecotypes.behavior: Stares, yawns, and lets attackers lose interest.

ecotypes.name: Mud-bank brawler
ecotypes.reading: A physical lineage of muddy pond margins, flinging mud and striking with its arms, using its upright body. Fits shallow, silty ponds and marsh.
ecotypes.behavior: Fights on the bank rather than retreating to open water.

open_questions: What does it eat?
Where does it live, by the entries? None say; its habitat comes from game data and from Golduck.
What causes the headaches, and are the powers involuntary or deliberate?
Is it active by day or by night?
Does it nest at the pond margin?

contradictions.text: Deliberate or involuntary? Red/Blue calls it wily and has it lull enemies before using its power (54.1); Yellow says no one knows whether it means to use it (54.2), and later entries say it can't even remember using it (54.3, 54.7).

Roserade.summary: A small, flower-handed predator that lures with scent and kills with poison. Roserade attracts prey with a sweet aroma, then strikes with poison-thorned whips hidden in its arms; HeartGold and SoulSilver add that the more toxic it is, the sweeter it smells. Its line starts as Budew, a bud that waits out winter closed and opens in spring sun beside clear pools, and passes through Roselia, whose scent relaxes people and whose flowers carry poisoned thorns. Roserade itself is never found in the wild; it is made by touching a Roselia with a Shiny Stone.

anatomy.text: A small upright animal (0.9 m, 14.5 kg) with a flower on each hand and thorny whips hidden in its arms; the whips are densely lined with poison thorns.
Each hand carries a different toxin, and both can jab with near-fatal power.
It also spews poison, a third delivery route beside whips and jabs.
Two separate toxins in two hands suggests either two glands or two sources of toxin; nothing says which, or what the toxins do.

diet.text: A predator: it draws prey in with a sweet aroma, then downs it with its whips or poison.
diet.analogy: Carnivorous plants such as pitcher plants (Sarracenia, Nepenthes) also lure prey with scent and nectar, while still photosynthesising; prey mainly supplies nitrogen and phosphorus.

diet.text: The prey is never named. A lure based on sweet scent suggests insects or other nectar seekers, but that is a guess.
diet.note: Sweet-scent lures attract nectar feeders in real systems; nothing in the entries says what Roserade catches.

diet.text: As a Grass type with Mega Drain at Lv 1 (and Synthesis and Giga Drain in the line), it probably also lives partly on sunlight and drains what it catches.
Roselia's flowers respond to the water it drinks: nutritionally rich springwater or clean water gives lovely, vivid blooms.

habitat.text: Roserade is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game, and no entry says where it lives.
Budew lives alongside clear ponds and pools; Roselia's Gen 3 habitat is grassland.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver the line is barely present: Budew only through the Sinnoh Sound radio in Ilex and Viridian Forests, and Budew and Roselia only in the Johto Safari Zone once enough plains or forest blocks are placed. It is common in Sinnoh (Eterna Forest, Routes 204 and 212, Trophy Garden, Great Marsh).
Water quality matters to the line: Budew picks clear water, and Roselia's flowers show what it drinks.

behavior.text: It fights with the movements of a dancer.
A lure-and-strike forager: it lets scent do the searching and the prey come to it.
Probably day-active: Budew opens in the sun's warmth and evolves by day, and Sinnoh tables add day and morning slots for Budew and Roselia. Nothing is said about Roserade's own hours.

social.text: No entry describes groups, pairs or interactions with its own kind.

reproduction.text: Roselia and Roserade are in the Fairy and Grass egg groups, with an even sex ratio and 20 egg cycles; Budew is a baby Pokémon in the Undiscovered group and can't breed.
Budew's bud opens in spring to release pollen, which in a plant is reproductive. Oddly, the stage that releases pollen is the one the games say cannot breed.
reproduction.note: Pollen is described only as an irritant and a seasonal release; no entry ties it to breeding.

defense.text: Chemical and mechanical at once: poison-thorned whips, toxic jabs, sprayed poison, and Poison Point (contact may poison an attacker).
Roselia defends its flowers: it shoots sharp thorns at anything trying to steal them, the thorns on its head carry a vicious poison, and its arm flowers have toxic thorns.
Roselia's fragrance makes its foes careless, a softer defence that disarms rather than injures.
Natural Cure, its other possible ability, clears its status problems when it withdraws from a fight.

senses.text: Budew is sensitive to temperature and opens its bud when it feels the sun's warmth.
senses.note: Platinum (406.3) hedges the same thing as 'said to'; see folklore.

senses.text: Nothing is said about how Roserade detects prey that its scent has drawn in.

life_cycle.text: Budew (0.2 m, 1.2 kg) becomes Roselia (0.3 m, 2.0 kg) when it levels up with high friendship by day, and Roselia becomes Roserade (0.9 m, 14.5 kg) when exposed to a Shiny Stone. The archive lists the line as Roselia, Budew, Roserade, but Budew is the first stage.
Budew spends winter as a closed bud enduring the cold, and opens in spring to release pollen.
The line goes from a bud, to flowers on the arms, to a bouquet on each hand with whips inside the arms; the defensive thorns of Roselia become the predatory weapons of Roserade.
The scent changes meaning: in Roselia a stronger aroma means a healthier animal; in Roserade a sweeter aroma means a more toxic one. Both may be the same thing, if a healthy animal makes more toxin.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Roserade's own level-up list in HeartGold is short, all at Lv 1: Sweet Scent (the lure), Poison Sting (the thorns), Mega Drain and Magical Leaf. Sweet Scent is the canon hunting method in move form.

Roselia's level-up list holds most of the line's natural repertoire: Stun Spore, Leech Seed, Grass Whistle, Toxic Spikes, Ingrain, Toxic, Aromatherapy and Synthesis, which together read as a plant that drugs, drains and poisons rather than chases.
Budew learns Water Sport (Lv 7), which fits a pond-edge animal.

ecology.text: A small ambush predator using scent as bait (trophic level about 3 if its prey are herbivores or nectar feeders).
Budew's pollen goes into the air in spring and causes harsh sneezing and runny noses, so the line affects the animals around clear ponds as an allergen source.
ecology.analogy: Hay fever in people is mostly caused by wind-dispersed pollen, from grasses, birch and the like.

ecology.text: Because Roselia's flowers track water quality, the line could serve as a living indicator of clean water.
ecology.note: The entries say water changes the flowers; whether poor water dulls them is not stated.

humans.text: Its flowers tempt people, which is dangerous: 'Don't even think about picking those flowers.'
Roselia's scent deeply relaxes people and brings serenity to living things.
People make Roserade: it comes only from a Roselia exposed to a Shiny Stone.

homestead.text: A handling hazard: near-fatal toxins in both hands, poison-lined whips and Poison Point. Keep it away from children, grazing animals and the nursery, and handle with gloves.
A possible pest trap for the Glasshouse: it lures and kills small animals with scent. Whether it takes pests rather than pollinators is untested and important.
homestead.note: Prey identity is unknown; a lure that works on pollinators would harm the berry beds.

homestead.text: Keep Budew out of the house and the Glasshouse in spring: its pollen causes harsh sneezing.
Budew survives winter by closing up, which suits Blackthorn's cold season without heated housing; whether Roserade is as hardy is not said.
A Roselia's flowers as a check on the water it is drinking.
homestead.note: Unproven as an indicator.

homestead.text: Sweet Scent, its own move, draws wild Pokémon out, which a forager can use and a guard should know about.
Needs: clean water, sun, and a pond edge for the young.

niche.foraging: sit-and-wait lure predator: draws prey with a sweet scent and strikes with poison-thorned whips; probably also photosynthetic
niche.note: Prey never named; activity read from Budew and Roselia, not Roserade.

ecotypes.name: Thorn thicket
ecotypes.reading: Roselia's thorn-shooting made heritable and extended: Pin Missile fires a volley of thorns, Spikes scatters barbs on the ground. A lineage that defends a fixed patch, like a dense flowerbed, from browsers and flower thieves rather than hunting. Fits crowded meadow and garden edges where its blooms draw trouble.
ecotypes.behavior: Holds a patch, fires at anything that reaches for a flower, and litters the approach with barbs.

ecotypes.name: Sleeping lure
ecotypes.reading: The scent lure with a sedative behind it: Sleep Powder puts the animal it has drawn in to sleep, Cotton Spore slows anything that tries to leave, and Mind Reader makes the next strike certain. A sit-and-wait trap that needs no venom to work. Fits sheltered pond margins where prey come to drink.
ecotypes.behavior: Lures, drugs and only then strikes; rarely needs to chase.

ecotypes.name: Sun-fed bloom
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that leans on sunlight rather than prey: Synthesis for recovery in the sun, Razor Leaf for everyday defence, Leaf Storm as a single all-out burst that costs it afterwards. Fits open, sunny grassland where prey is scarce and light is not.
ecotypes.behavior: Basks more and lures less; hits hard once when threatened, then retreats to recover.

open_questions: What does Roserade catch? Its prey is never named.
What are the two toxins in its two hands (407.3), and does it choose between them?
If sweeter means more toxic (407.4), what tells prey to keep coming? Is the scent a lure, a warning, or both?
Is Budew's spring pollen reproductive, given that Budew itself cannot breed in the games?
Where does a wild Roserade live? Shiny Stones are the only route the games give.
Does Roserade keep Budew's winter dormancy?

contradictions.text: Water and flower colour: Diamond states as known fact that Roselia raised on clean drinking water grow vividly coloured flowers; HeartGold and SoulSilver say only that Roselia drinking rich springwater are 'said to' reveal rare coloration; Emerald states that springwater gives lovely flowers.
contradictions.note: Vivid versus rare colour, and fact versus report. The rare-colour version is filed as folklore.

contradictions.text: Budew's bloom on the sun's warmth: HeartGold and SoulSilver state it plainly; Platinum says the bud is 'said to' bloom that way.

folklore.text: On extremely rare occasions a Roselia is said to appear with its flowers in unusual colours.
folklore.note: Reported as hearsay. Likely the games' rare colour variants described in-world.

folklore.text: Roselia that drink nutritionally rich springwater are said to show rare colouring when they bloom.
Budew's bud is said to bloom when it feels the sun's warm touch.
folklore.note: Hedged in Platinum, stated as fact in HeartGold and SoulSilver (406.4).

Scizor.summary: A steel-hard, red insect that has traded its parent's camouflage and flight for armour and a bluff. Scizor's pincers carry eye-like markings that it raises to make itself look three-headed, and they contain steel enough to crush any hard object. Its wings no longer fly; it flaps them fast to regulate its body temperature. It develops from Scyther, a green, grass-hiding ambusher with scythes that cut logs, and in the games only a Scyther traded while holding a Metal Coat becomes one.

anatomy.text: A heavy, winged insect (1.8 m, 118.0 kg) with a body as hard as steel.
Two pincers that contain steel and can crush any hard object they grip; they carry eye-like markings.
Its wings are not used for flying; they are flapped at high speed to adjust body temperature.
anatomy.analogy: Bumblebees and many moths warm up by shivering their flight muscles before they can fly; whether Scizor's flapping warms it or cools it is not said.

anatomy.text: If its steel-hard body conducts heat the way metal does, it would warm and cool quickly, which may be why it needs the wing-flapping.
anatomy.note: A physical guess linking two canon facts; no entry connects them.

diet.text: No entry says what Scizor eats.
Scyther is a predator: it leaps out of tall grass to slice prey, and tears and shreds it with its scythes.
diet.analogy: Praying mantises (Mantodea), which Scyther's category names, are sit-and-wait predators that seize prey with raptorial forelegs.

diet.text: Crushing pincers suit hard-shelled prey, which Scyther's slicing scythes would not; Scizor may take different food from its parent.
diet.note: Built on anatomy alone.

habitat.text: Its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is grassland; Scyther hides in tall grass.
Scizor is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game.

In HeartGold and SoulSilver, Scyther appears only during the National Park Bug-Catching Contest (5%), and after the National Pokédex only on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday contests. In Platinum it is on Routes 210 and 215, commoner in the morning; in Kanto, in the Safari Zone or as a Game Corner prize.

behavior.text: Threat display: it raises its eye-patterned pincers to intimidate, which makes it look three-headed, and it can swing them down dangerously.
Scyther relies on speed: too fast for the eye, leaving only a blur, so fast its opponent doesn't know what hit it, and very proud of it.
Scyther rarely flies; Scizor doesn't fly at all.
Platinum's Scyther are commoner in the morning; no activity pattern is stated for Scizor.

social.text: No entry describes groups. Scyther's speed can create the illusion of more than one, which is a solitary animal looking like many, not a group.

reproduction.text: Bug egg group, even sex ratio, 25 egg cycles (a little longer than most). Nothing is said about breeding or young.

defense.text: A deimatic bluff: the eyespots on its raised pincers make it look like a three-headed animal.
defense.analogy: The peacock butterfly (Aglais io) flashes large eyespots on its wings when disturbed, which experiments show deters small birds.

defense.text: Armour: its steel-hard body is not easily fazed by ordinary attacks.
Scyther's defence was concealment instead: its protective colouring makes it invisible in grass.
Iron Defense (Lv 37) is in Scizor's own level-up list; Swarm or Technician are its abilities.

senses.text: Nothing is said about Scizor's senses. An eyespot display only works on predators that see well, so its enemies are probably visual hunters.

life_cycle.text: Scyther (1.5 m, 56.0 kg, Bug/Flying, green) becomes Scizor (1.8 m, 118.0 kg, Bug/Steel, red) when traded holding a Metal Coat.
The change swaps strategies: from camouflage, speed and slicing scythes to bright colour, a bluff display, crushing pincers and armour; from rare flight to wings used only for heat.
The weight doubles while the height grows only 0.3 m, which fits a body that becomes metal-hard.
Scyther's scythes grow sharper by cutting hard objects; whether that habit feeds into Scizor's steel is not said.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Scizor's level-up list mixes speed and steel: Quick Attack and Bullet Punch (Lv 1), Agility, Metal Claw (Lv 21), Iron Defense (Lv 37), Iron Head (Lv 53).
The cutting moves (Fury Cutter, Slash, X-Scissor, Night Slash) are shared with Scyther and match the scythe canon; in Scizor they come from pincers.
Pursuit (Lv 9) and False Swipe (Lv 13) suit a predator that chases down and holds prey rather than killing at once.
Steel Wing and Roost are machine moves: taught, and of little use to an animal that doesn't fly.

ecology.text: A large insect predator of grassland (trophic level about 3-3.5), if Scizor hunts as Scyther does.
In HeartGold's Bug-Catching Contest, Scyther shares the National Park grass with Butterfree, Beedrill, Caterpie and other contest bugs, only on contest days.

humans.text: People make Scizor: it evolves only by trade, holding a Metal Coat.
Scyther's attacks are nearly impossible to parry, and its scythes cut thick logs in one stroke: dangerous at close quarters.

homestead.text: Breaking hard material: its pincers crush any hard object, useful for stone, nuts or scrap metal at the Works.
Timber and brush clearing is Scyther's job rather than Scizor's: Scyther's scythes slice thick logs in one stroke and cut through grass.
A deterrent at the gate: its three-headed pincer display is built to frighten.
Watch it in Blackthorn's cold: it manages its body temperature by flapping its wings, and how well that works in a highland winter is unknown.
Its size is in the rider range, but it cannot fly and no entry says it carries anyone.
Keep people clear when it swings its pincers down; the display can turn into a strike.

niche.foraging: Scyther: ambush from tall grass and high-speed slashing; Scizor: unknown, perhaps crushing hard prey
niche.note: Scizor's own diet is never stated; the machine reading's herbivore comes from the Bug type alone.

relationships.note: Stated for Scyther.
Cover for Scyther's ambush.
National Park Bug-Catching Contest, HeartGold and SoulSilver (Scyther).

ecotypes.name: Tall-grass reaper
ecotypes.reading: A patient ambusher: Razor Wind takes a turn to charge before it cuts, and Night Slash is a high-critical strike from cover. A lineage that waits in grass and lands one decisive blow, the Yellow canon of leaping out of tall grass in heritable form. Fits dense tall-grass meadow.
ecotypes.behavior: Waits motionless in long grass; one strike, rarely two.

ecotypes.name: Last-stand fencer
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that fights through injury: Endure survives a blow that would knock it out, Reversal hits hardest when it is nearly beaten, and Counter returns physical attacks double. It suits Scizor's armour-and-bluff life, where it holds its ground instead of fleeing. Fits contested open ground where it can't hide.
ecotypes.behavior: Never runs; most dangerous when hurt.

ecotypes.name: Wing-singer
ecotypes.reading: Wings used for sound and wind rather than flight: Bug Buzz is a damaging vibration, Silver Wind a gust of wing scales that can boost all its stats. A lineage that turns Scizor's non-flying, fast-flapping wings into a weapon and display. Fits open meadow where sound carries.
ecotypes.behavior: Buzzes loudly when threatened, before any display of the pincers.

open_questions: What does Scizor eat, and does it still hunt as Scyther does?
Does wing-flapping warm it, cool it, or both (212.2, 212.4)?
How does a Scyther become steel? The games require a held Metal Coat and a trade, neither of which has a wild equivalent.
Is there a wild Scizor population anywhere?
Are the pincer eyespots a bluff against particular predators, and which?
How does it cope with Blackthorn's cold, as a steel-bodied insect that relies on its wings for temperature control?

Seaking.summary: The adult of the Goldeen line, a horned river fish whose life centres on its nest. In autumn Seaking gather from all over to spawn, turning the rivers red; the male bores a hole in a riverbed boulder with his drill-like horn, and the pair take turns guarding the eggs for over a month. It defends its eggs with its life. In the highlands it is a rare Super Rod catch in Dark Cave's water, where there are no riverbed boulders to nest in.

anatomy.text: A fish, 1.3 m and 39.0 kg, typed Water.
The horn on its head is sharp like a drill.
In autumn its body becomes fattier and its colours are at their most beautiful, before it courts a mate.

diet.text: No entry says what Seaking eats.
It fattens before the autumn courtship, so it must feed heavily in the months before spawning.
Its level-up moves start with Poison Jab and Peck (Lv 1); like Goldeen's, they are strikes that might double as feeding, but nothing says so.
diet.note: A reading of moves only.

habitat.text: Rivers, creeks and stream beds; it lives in hollowed rocks in streams.

In the highlands in HeartGold and SoulSilver it is only in Dark Cave's water, both ends, by Super Rod 10% (Lv 40). It is widespread elsewhere: Union Cave, Slowpoke Well, Route 42, Mt. Mortar (also surfing 10%), Tohjo Falls, the Kanto routes and the Johto Safari Zone, and it is the main surfing encounter on Mt. Silver (about 90%). The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is waters-edge.
A boulder-nesting river fish recorded in a cave pool: Dark Cave Seaking presumably feed there and spawn somewhere with current and boulders.
habitat.note: Nothing records where Dark Cave's fish breed.

behavior.text: In the autumn spawning season they swim powerfully up rivers and creeks.
Males perform courtship dances in riverbeds to woo females.
Males patrol the area around their nests in autumn to protect their offspring.

social.text: During spawning season Seaking gather from all over, colouring the rivers a brilliant red.
social.analogy: Sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka) turn bright red at spawning, and their mass runs colour whole rivers.

social.text: The male and female take turns patrolling around their nest and eggs.

reproduction.text: The male makes the nest by carving out a boulder in the stream with his horn.
reproduction.analogy: Male three-spined sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus) build the nest, take on red breeding colours and guard the eggs and young.

reproduction.text: The hole stops the eggs from washing away in the current or being attacked.
It is very protective: the guarding of eggs goes on for over a month, and it defends them with its life.
Water 2 egg group, 20 egg cycles, even sex ratio; the line's egg moves sit on Goldeen.

defense.text: To protect its family it will fight with its drill-sharp horn.
Swift Swim and Water Veil, as Goldeen; Agility (Lv 56) and Aqua Ring (Lv 27).

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses.

life_cycle.text: It evolves from Goldeen at Lv 33.
Both stages are described spawning, Goldeen in schools running upstream and Seaking at nests, so the line may breed before it reaches full size.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Horn Drill (Lv 47) is the nest-borer in game form; Horn Attack, Fury Attack and Megahorn (Lv 63) are the horn as a weapon. Waterfall (Lv 40) is a natural move, matching the runs upstream.

ecology.text: An engineer: it bores holes in riverbed boulders, and empty nest holes would shelter other small stream animals.
ecology.note: The boring is canon; later use of the holes by others is not recorded.

ecology.text: A mass autumn gathering of large fish is a seasonal food pulse for predators; none is recorded in the highlands.
ecology.note: Untested.

ecology.text: Its diet, and so its trophic level, is unknown.

humans.text: Its autumn spawning is a spectacle: rivers turn a brilliant red.
Anyone working a stream in autumn should leave nest boulders alone: the guarding parent will fight.

homestead.text: To breed it needs a real stream with boulders; a pond will not do.
Expect it to be aggressive near its nest for over a month each autumn; keep people and stock out of that stretch of stream.
Its horn bores holes in stone; whether it would do so anywhere but at a nest is unknown.
homestead.note: Untested.

homestead.text: A pair of Seaking in the homestead's stream, with the autumn red run as the household's marker of the year turning.

niche.foraging: unknown; nothing records what it eats

relationships.note: Nest sites, bored with the horn.
Empty nest holes as shelter; not recorded.
Dark Cave water.

ecotypes.name: Torrent spawner
ecotypes.reading: Two powerful water attacks in a lineage built for the autumn run up steep, fast streams. Fits highland streams with falls, where the strongest swimmers reach the best nest boulders.
ecotypes.behavior: Nests highest up the stream.

ecotypes.name: Silt nester
ecotypes.reading: Mud moves in a lineage that nests where boulders are scarce, digging into silt and gravel instead of boring rock. Fits slow, muddy reaches and cave pools such as Dark Cave's.
ecotypes.behavior: Digs a hollow rather than drilling one.

ecotypes.name: Heavy guardian
ecotypes.reading: Weight and a tail strike in a nest-guarding lineage that drives intruders off by force. Fits crowded spawning reaches where many pairs nest close together, as when Seaking gather from all over.
ecotypes.behavior: Guards longer and fights harder at the nest.

open_questions: What does Seaking eat, especially to fatten in autumn (119.13)?
Where do Dark Cave's Seaking spawn? A cave pool has no riverbed boulders.
Which season: spring for Goldeen (118.8), autumn for Seaking?
Who guards: the males (119.5) or both parents in turn (119.7)?
What uses the bored nest holes after the young leave?
What eats Seaking or its eggs? Nothing is recorded.

contradictions.text: Crystal says the males patrol the nests in autumn; Sapphire says the male and female take turns patrolling.
contradictions.reading: Male-only versus shared guarding. Possibly both happen; not resolved here.

contradictions.text: Emerald puts Goldeen's spawning runs in spring; the Seaking entries put spawning in autumn.
contradictions.reading: The two stages may spawn in different seasons, or the entries disagree.

Snorlax.summary: A 460 kg animal whose whole life is eating and sleeping. Snorlax is not satisfied until it has eaten roughly 400 kg of food a day, eats anything, moldy or rotten, off the ground if need be, and has a stomach that dissolves any poison; when it has eaten its fill it goes straight to sleep. It is so docile that children play on its belly, and Platinum notes that a full Snorlax is too lethargic to lift a finger. Its young, Munchlax, swallow their own weight in food every day and hide food under their long fur, then forget it is there.

anatomy.text: A huge, upright, round-bellied animal (2.1 m, 460.0 kg); its bulk builds as it eats.
Its stomach is the remarkable organ: its digestive juices dissolve any kind of poison, and moldy or rotten food doesn't upset it.
Its abilities match: Immunity (it can't be poisoned) and Thick Fat (resistant to fire and ice).
Munchlax (0.6 m, 105.0 kg) has long body hair under which it hides food.

diet.text: A generalist that eats anything, including moldy and rotten food and things off the ground.
It needs over 880 pounds (about 400 kg) a day, nearly its own body weight, and doesn't feel full until it has eaten nearly 900 pounds.
diet.analogy: Real large mammals eat a few percent of their body weight a day; an African elephant eats on the order of 150 kg for a body of several tonnes.

diet.text: Munchlax swallows its own weight in food once a day, whole and almost unchewed.
Snorlax stops eating only to sleep.

habitat.text: Its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is mountain; no entry describes where it lives.

In every Gen I-IV game the wild Snorlax are single, sleeping animals blocking a route, woken with the Poké Flute: Route 11 in HeartGold and SoulSilver (with a second on Route 12 under a later story condition), Vermilion City in Gold, Silver and Crystal, and Routes 12 and 16 in Kanto's games.
Munchlax is found only on Honey-slathered trees in Sinnoh, and only in one of the honey-tree encounter groups.

behavior.text: Its typical day is eating and sleeping and nothing else; when it has finished eating it goes promptly to sleep.
It gets steadily lazier as it gets fatter.
What sounds like its cry may be its snoring or its hungry belly rumbling.
Munchlax gulps food so desperately that it forgets the food it has hidden in its fur.
No activity pattern is given; the encounter data show it asleep whenever it is found.

social.text: Docile toward people: children use its belly as a place to play.
Nothing is said about how it treats its own kind; every wild Snorlax in the games is alone.

reproduction.text: Monster egg group, 40 egg cycles (twice the usual), slow growth, and 87.5% male, a ratio most species outside the starters don't have. Munchlax is a baby Pokémon in the Undiscovered group and can't breed.

defense.text: Bulk and indifference: little is described as threatening it, and it is too lethargic to react when full.
Poison doesn't work on it: its stomach dissolves any kind, and Immunity stops poisoning in battle.
Its own moves suit an animal that sits tight: Defense Curl, Amnesia, Rest, and Block (Lv 36), which stops an opponent leaving.

senses.text: Satiety is its one described sense: it doesn't feel full until it has eaten nearly 900 pounds.
Munchlax has Odor Sleuth at Lv 1, which fits an animal that finds food by smell, though no entry says so.

life_cycle.text: Munchlax (0.6 m, 105.0 kg) becomes Snorlax (2.1 m, 460.0 kg) when it levels up with high friendship. The archive lists the line as Snorlax, Munchlax, but Munchlax is the first stage.
The young eat their weight daily and store food in their fur; the adult eats almost its weight daily and stores it as bulk. Hoarding gives way to sleeping it off.
Munchlax's own moves include Stockpile and Swallow (Lv 25 and 28), storing and then swallowing, which matches the hidden food stash; Recycle (Lv 17) re-uses an item already used.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Its level-up list is the canon in move form: Rest (Lv 25), then Snore and Sleep Talk (Lv 28), both used while asleep; Yawn (Lv 20) makes others drowsy.
Belly Drum (Lv 17) sacrifices half its health to raise its attack to the maximum, and Body Slam (Lv 33) and Giga Impact (Lv 49) use its mass.
Lick (Lv 12) is its own, and an egg move too.
Strength and Rock Smash, behind its hauling and clearing records, are machine moves.

ecology.text: An enormous consumer: at roughly 400 kg a day, one Snorlax would strip a local food supply quickly, which may be why each is found alone.
Because it eats moldy and rotten food, it also acts as a scavenger of spoiled material others won't touch.
Munchlax's forgotten food stashes could scatter seeds if food falls out of its fur unchewed.
ecology.note: Nothing says the food falls out or contains seeds.
ecology.analogy: Scatter-hoarders such as Eurasian jays (Garrulus glandarius) plant oaks by failing to recover the acorns they bury.

ecology.text: Trophic level about 2.5: whatever is available, plant or animal, fresh or spoiled.

humans.text: Safe with children: docile enough to be played on, and safe to bounce on when full.
An obstacle: in every Gen I-IV game a sleeping Snorlax blocks a road until someone plays the Poké Flute.

homestead.text: The cost: roughly 400 kg of food a day. No homestead can feed a Snorlax casually; plan the supply before it arrives.
Part of that can be waste: it eats moldy and rotten food without harm, so spoiled stores, kitchen scraps and windfall fruit can go to it.
Hauling: 460 kg of animal with hands; the capability record lists a harness. Strength is taught, and its laziness is the real limit.
A calm, safe animal around children, provided it is fed: the safety note in the Pokédex is about a full belly.
Munchlax will raid stores and carry food off in its fur; lock the kitchen and the berry store. Its Pickup ability also turns up items.
Where it sleeps, it stays: don't let it settle across a path or a gate. The games' Snorlax all block roads.

microhabitat: open routes and paths where it sleeps
niche.foraging: eats anything available in huge quantity, fresh or spoiled, then sleeps; the young hoard food in their fur

relationships.with: any available food, including spoiled food

relationships.note: Children play on its belly; Snorlax is unaffected.

ecotypes.name: Pass sleeper
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that cannot be moved: Curse makes it slower, stronger and tougher, and Counter returns physical blows double. The sleeping-roadblock habit as a whole strategy. Fits narrow mountain passes, its listed habitat, where lying across the way keeps a feeding area to itself.
ecotypes.behavior: Settles in one spot and won't shift; strikes back only when struck.

ecotypes.name: Charming beggar
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that gets fed: Charm sharply lowers an opponent's attack by being endearing, Lick can paralyse at close range. Together they suit an animal that lives off what others provide rather than foraging. Fits village and farm edges, where children already play on Snorlax.
ecotypes.behavior: Approaches people and waits to be fed; hard to stay angry at.

ecotypes.name: Larder guard
ecotypes.reading: A lineage that defends its food: Whirlwind blows rivals away from a feeding patch, and Pursuit hits harder at anything that runs off. For an animal that needs 400 kg a day, keeping competitors off is worth the effort. Fits contested feeding grounds such as berry thickets in a lean season.
ecotypes.behavior: Clears a food patch before eating; chases thieves.

open_questions: How can any animal eat nearly its own weight daily? Where does the mass go?
What do wild Snorlax mostly eat in practice?
Do they ever live together, or does food demand keep them solitary?
Why is Snorlax 87.5% male, like a starter line?
Does Munchlax ever eat its forgotten stash (446.4 says it does; 446.2 and 446.3 say it forgets)?
Is a hungry Snorlax still safe around children, or only a full one (143.11)?

contradictions.text: Munchlax's hidden food: Pearl and Platinum say it forgets the food it hides under its fur; HeartGold and SoulSilver say it carts the stash around and swallows it.
Daily intake: FireRed says over 880 pounds; Pearl says nearly 900. Consistent in scale, but 'over' and 'nearly' bracket the figure from opposite sides.
contradictions.note: Minor.

Swampert.summary: Swampert is a 1.5 m, 82 kg amphibious Pokémon of shores and mud, and enormously strong: it can drag a boulder of more than a ton, swim as fast as a jet ski while towing a large ship, and break rock with a swing of its arms. It nests on beaches, and it hears a storm coming in the sound of the waves and the tidal winds, then piles up boulders to shield its nest. The line grows up in mud: Mudkip breathes through gills on its cheeks and senses water movement with the fin on its head, and Marshtomp must keep its skin wet by playing in mud. No Gen I–IV game has it in the wild; every Swampert comes from a Mudkip given to a trainer.

anatomy.text: An upright, tailed body of 1.5 m and 81.9 kg, Water and Ground type.
Its thick arms are as hard as rock and can break a boulder into pieces with one swing.
It has fins sensitive enough to pick up subtle differences in the sound of waves and tidal winds.
In Mudkip, gills on the cheeks let it breathe in water, a large tail fin drives it through water, and the fin on its head works as a sensitive detector of water and air movement.
anatomy.analogy: The axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) also carries external gills on the sides of its head.

anatomy.text: Marshtomp's body is covered by a thin, sticky film that lets it live on land, but it weakens if its skin dries out.
anatomy.analogy: Amphibians lose water quickly through their thin, mucus-covered skin and must keep it moist.

anatomy.text: Whether the adult keeps gills, or breathes air only, is not stated.

diet.text: No entry for any stage says what the line eats.
Seeing clearly in murky water would help a hunter or a forager of the bottom alike, so it doesn't settle the question.

habitat.text: Gen 3 Pokédex habitat for the whole line: the water's edge.
The adult is coastal: it makes its nest on beautiful beaches and guards a seaside nest against storms and tidal waves.
The juveniles live in mud and fresh water: Mudkip sleeps buried in soil at the water's edge or rests covered in mud at the bottom of a river, and Marshtomp plays in beach mud at low tide.

Not found in the wild in any Gen I–IV game. Mudkip is a starter gift on Route 101 in Ruby, Sapphire and Emerald, and in HeartGold and SoulSilver it is given in Saffron City after beating Red, to a player who received a Kanto starter.

behavior.text: It predicts storms: it senses subtle changes in the sound of waves and tidal winds and, if a storm or tidal wave is coming, piles up boulders to protect itself and its nest.
behavior.analogy: Young blacktip sharks have been recorded leaving shallow nursery waters ahead of a tropical storm, apparently in response to falling air pressure; the cue differs, the early warning is the same.

behavior.text: It swims as fast as a jet ski.
Marshtomp is much faster in mud than in water, burrows into dirt to sleep, and is at its best on muddy ground with poor footing.
Its activity pattern is unknown.

social.text: No entry describes groups, pairs or territory.

reproduction.text: It nests on beaches and defends the nest by building boulder walls before storms.
reproduction.analogy: Sea turtles also nest on sandy beaches above the tide line, where storm surges are the main threat to their nests.

reproduction.text: Monster and Water 1 egg groups, 20 egg cycles, 87.5% male; the sex ratio is shared with the other starter lines and is probably a game convention.
What is in the nest, how long it is tended and by which parent, is not described.

defense.text: It bashes down foes with one swing of its rock-hard arms.
Marshtomp fights on its own ground: it quickly overwhelms foes struggling in mud.
In a tight spot even Mudkip can crush rocks bigger than itself.
Torrent strengthens its Water moves when it is close to defeat, matching the juvenile's burst of strength in a pinch; Protect (Lv 46) is its guard.

senses.text: Powerful vision lets it see even in murky water.
Its fins pick up the sound of waves and tidal winds.
Mudkip relies on its head fin instead of its eyes, sensing water and air movement to tell what is happening around it; the adult adds strong eyesight.
senses.analogy: The lateral line of fishes and aquatic amphibians detects water movement and pressure changes in the same way.

life_cycle.text: Mudkip (0.4 m, 7.6 kg, four-legged) becomes Marshtomp at level 16 (0.7 m, 28 kg, upright, gaining the Ground type) and Swampert at level 36 (1.5 m, 81.9 kg).
Marshtomp's hindquarters are well developed, so it can walk on its hind legs; living on muddy ground with poor footing has made its legs sturdy.

Read as development, the line moves from a gilled, fin-sensing animal of rivers and mud, through an upright mud-dweller that must stay damp, to a powerful swimmer of the coast that sees well in murky water.
life_cycle.analogy: Broadly like amphibian development, from a gilled, water-bound larva to a more land-capable adult, though Swampert returns to open water.

life_cycle.text: Strength is there from the start: Mudkip lifts large boulders by planting its four feet and heaving, and has the strength to crush them.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Mud: Mud-Slap (Lv 6), Mud Shot (Lv 16), Mud Bomb (Lv 25) and Muddy Water (Lv 39), the move form of a life spent in mud.
Arms and ground: Hammer Arm (Lv 69) is the rock-hard swing of its entries, and Earthquake (Lv 52) suits an 82 kg Ground type.
Foresight (Lv 20) sees through evasion, consistent with an animal that perceives its surroundings well in murky conditions.
Surf, Waterfall, Strength, Dig and Rock Climb are machine moves taught by people.

ecology.text: A builder: it piles boulders into storm walls around its nest, changing the shape of the beach.
Those boulder walls would give shelter to other shore animals as well, during and after storms.
ecology.note: Nothing says what else uses them.

ecology.text: Its trophic position is unknown because its diet is never given.

humans.text: It can swim while towing a large ship.
It is strong enough to drag a boulder of more than a ton with ease.
In the games it reaches people only as a starter gift.

homestead.text: Storm warning: it hears a storm coming in the waves and wind. On a mountain lake rather than a coast, how far that sense still works is untested.
Heavy hauling: it drags boulders of more than a ton and tows ships.
Dry-stone walling: it already piles boulders into protective walls of its own accord, which is close to useful building work.
Rock clearing: one swing breaks a boulder into pieces.
Water crossings: it swims as fast as a jet ski, and Surf is a taught move.
Needs: water and a mud wallow, especially for young Marshtomp, which weaken if their skin dries; on cold, dry highland days the mud must not freeze solid.

niche.foraging: not described
niche.note: Diet is never stated for any stage, so no guild or trophic level is given.

relationships.note: Marshtomp keeps its skin wet in mud; the young sleep buried in it.
Nest sites.
Piled into walls before storms.

ecotypes.name: Mudflat brawler
ecotypes.reading: Mud Bomb blinds with a blob of mud, Stomp tramples, and Counter returns a blow twice as hard. A lineage that fights on the soft ground where its rivals flounder, Marshtomp's 'overwhelms foes struggling in mud' kept into adulthood. Fits wide tidal mudflats and estuaries.
ecotypes.behavior: Draws a foe onto the mud and fights it there.

ecotypes.name: Storm-wall mason
ecotypes.reading: Ancient Power lifts and hurls rock, Double-Edge is a full-weight ram, and Curse trades speed for toughness. A lineage given over to building and holding ground, moving stone and bracing against what comes. Fits exposed rocky coasts where storms hit hardest and the nest needs the strongest wall.
ecotypes.behavior: Builds higher walls than its neighbours and sits behind them.

ecotypes.name: Channel ambusher
ecotypes.reading: Whirlpool traps a target in a vortex, and Bite seizes it. A lineage that hunts in moving water, holding prey in the current and then taking it. Fits tidal channels and river mouths with strong flow.
ecotypes.behavior: Lurks where the current narrows and spins up a trap.

ecotypes.name: Cold-river sleeper
ecotypes.reading: Ice Ball rolls a growing ball of ice, and Yawn brings on drowsiness. Read together, a lineage of cold, slow water that spends long spells buried and torpid, as Mudkip already rests covered in mud on the river bottom. Fits icy highland streams such as those around Blackthorn.
ecotypes.behavior: Winters half-asleep in the mud of a cold river bed.

open_questions: What does the line eat?
Does the adult keep Mudkip's gills, and can it stay underwater indefinitely?
Is it a sea animal, a freshwater animal, or both at different ages? (see contradictions)
What does it hear when it predicts a storm, and would that work on a mountain lake?
What is in its beach nest, and who tends it?
Can Marshtomp survive a highland winter if its mud freezes?

contradictions.note: HeartGold, SoulSilver and Emerald put Mudkip in river mud and at the water's edge (258.6, 258.3); Emerald and FireRed put Swampert's nest on beaches facing tidal waves (260.3, 260.4), and Ruby has Marshtomp on beaches at low tide (259.1). It may move from rivers to the coast as it grows, but no entry says so.

Swinub.summary: A small pig of the Ice Path that finds food by smell and digs it up with a nose tough enough for frozen ground. Its favourite food is a mushroom that grows under dead grass, and it also eats berries, which makes it the highlands' clearest link to the fungi that break down dead plants. While rooting it sometimes uncovers hot springs, even under ice. It has the highest encounter rate on every floor of the Ice Path in HeartGold and SoulSilver, which says it is easy to meet, not how many there are.

anatomy.text: A small quadruped, 0.4 m and 6.5 kg, typed Ice and Ground.
The tip of its nose is its digging tool, so tough that even frozen ground poses no problem.
Its nose is also very sensitive.
No Swinub entry mentions a coat. The thick, long hair for enduring cold is described for Piloswine.

diet.text: Its favourite food is a mushroom that grows under the cover of dead or dried grass.
diet.analogy: Wild boar and domestic pigs (Sus scrofa) root for underground fungi, and pigs have long been used to find truffles (Tuber) by smell.

diet.text: It also finds berries, and can locate mushrooms and berries buried under ice.
It forages by rubbing its snout along the ground to find food and dig it up.

Its foods are surface foods: mushrooms under dead grass and berries do not grow in an ice cave. Ice Path Swinub must forage outside on the slopes and meadows, or live on what reaches the cave from outside.
Odor Sleuth at Lv 1 is a scent-tracking move: the wild animal starts life following its nose.

habitat.text: In HeartGold and SoulSilver it is on all four floors of the Ice Path (1F, B1F, B2F, B3F) at 40%, the highest rate there, at any time of day; levels 21-23 on the upper floors and 22-24 on B2F and B3F. Gold and Silver have the same 40% at every time of day; Crystal has it only by day and morning.
The radio's Hoenn and Sinnoh sounds add Makuhita, Absol, Chingling and Bronzor to the same Ice Path tables. Those are radio-only and are not treated as Ice Path residents here.
Everywhere else it is also in cold places: Icefall Cave (FireRed, LeafGreen), Route 217 (a swarm in Diamond and Pearl, resident in Platinum) and Acuity Lakefront. The Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is cave.
Its entries put it on frozen ground and ice, with dead grass nearby: the ground at the edges of snow rather than deep inside rock.

behavior.text: If it smells something enticing, it dashes off headlong to find the source.
It sometimes discovers or roots out hot springs while foraging.
Crystal's tables have it only by day and morning, which hints at a day-active animal; HeartGold and SoulSilver don't split it by time.
behavior.note: Encounter-table time slots are a weak guide to activity, especially inside a cave.

social.text: Nothing is said about groups, pairs or herds. High encounter rates on every floor are not evidence of group size.

reproduction.text: Field egg group, 20 egg cycles, an even sex ratio; nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding or young.

defense.text: Snow Cloak raises its evasion in a hailstorm: in the games it is harder to hit in blowing snow.
Its wild defences are modest: Mud Sport and Mud-Slap, Endure (Lv 16), Mist (Lv 40) and a Take Down charge (Lv 32).
An animal that dashes headlong after smells is not a vigilant one; Piloswine, whose hair covers its eyes, carries this further and simply keeps charging.

senses.text: Smell is its main sense: a very sensitive nose that leads it to food, and to hot springs, even under ice.
Smell stays primary through the line: Piloswine cannot see through its coat and checks its surroundings with its nose, and it is very sensitive to sound.

life_cycle.text: It becomes Piloswine at Lv 33; Piloswine becomes Mamoswine on levelling up while it knows Ancient Power, which Swinub can carry as an egg move or be taught by a tutor, and which Piloswine has at Lv 1.
The digging habit carries through, with the tool changing: Swinub roots with its nose, Piloswine digs up food buried under ice with its tusks, and Mamoswine's tusks are made of ice.
Mamoswine flourished during the ice age and declined as the ice dwindled; a frozen one was dug from 10,000-year-old ice.
life_cycle.analogy: Woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius) declined as the last ice age ended, and frozen carcasses have been recovered from Siberian permafrost.

life_cycle.text: Size through the line: 0.4 m and 6.5 kg, 1.1 m and 55.8 kg, 2.5 m and 291 kg.

moves_in_the_wild.text: The ground moves are its rooting kit: Odor Sleuth (Lv 1), Mud Sport (Lv 4), Mud-Slap (Lv 13), Mud Bomb (Lv 20) and later Earthquake (Lv 37). The ice moves fit its climate: Powder Snow (Lv 8), Icy Wind (Lv 25), Ice Shard (Lv 28), Blizzard (Lv 44).
Dig is a machine move, taught by people; the wild animal digs with its nose, not with the field move.

ecology.text: A fungivore that also eats fruit. Its favourite food is the fruiting body of a fungus living on dead grass, so much of the energy reaching Swinub comes through decomposition rather than straight from living plants.
ecology.analogy: In real grasslands much of the plant growth is never eaten alive and passes to decomposers; animals that eat fungi tap that detrital food chain.

ecology.text: Rooting turns over soil and litter, which would mix the ground and open bare patches.
ecology.note: Follows from the foraging method; the scale is unknown.
ecology.analogy: Rooting by wild boar turns over large areas of soil and changes which plants grow there.

ecology.text: Animals that eat mushrooms often spread the spores in their droppings; Swinub may disperse the fungus it feeds on.
ecology.note: Nothing in the pack says so.
ecology.analogy: Small mammals that eat truffles disperse truffle spores in their droppings.

ecology.text: Exposing hot springs would open warm, snow-free ground and unfrozen water for other animals.
ecology.note: How often it finds springs, and whether others use them, is not recorded.

ecology.text: No predator of Swinub is named. Golbat, which drinks the blood of Pokémon and shares every Ice Path floor with it, is the likeliest.
ecology.note: Co-occurrence plus Golbat's stated diet; no entry links them.

humans.text: No Swinub entry mentions people. An animal that finds hot springs is plainly useful to a mountain community.
It is easy to catch (catch rate 225) and common in the Ice Path, so it is likely one of the first highland species a trainer handles.

homestead.text: A forager for the cold months: it can find mushrooms and berries buried under ice by smell.

Its knack for rooting out hot springs is the most valuable thing it could do for a highland homestead: a found spring means heat and unfrozen water. Whether there is a spring near the homestead to find is unknown.
It can dig frozen ground with its nose.
It needs cold and ground to root in. Keep food stores sealed: it dashes headlong toward any enticing smell.
A Swinub on the vegetable beds in late winter, nosing out what the frost has left.

microhabitat: frozen ground and dead-grass meadows near the cave
niche.foraging: roots by smell, digging up mushrooms (its favourite food) and berries, including from under ice

relationships.with: mushroom that grows under dead grass (non-Pokémon)
mushroom that grows under dead grass (non-Pokémon)
relationships.note: Spore dispersal by fungus-eaters is common; not recorded for Swinub.
It roots them out, exposing warm water; whether that changes the habitat for others is untested.
Golbat drinks the blood of Pokémon and shares every Ice Path floor; no entry names Swinub as its prey.
SoulSilver only.

ecotypes.name: Deep rooter
ecotypes.reading: A move that splits the ground open and one that throws mud: a digging lineage for deep-frozen ground where food is buried deeper, such as the high meadows above the Ice Path.
ecotypes.behavior: Digs deeper pits and leaves broken ground behind it.

ecotypes.name: Ice-tusk line
ecotypes.reading: Ancient Power is what a Piloswine needs to become Mamoswine, and Icicle Spear matches the adult's ice tusks. A lineage on its way to the ice-age giant; fits the coldest, iciest ground.
ecotypes.behavior: More of them reach Mamoswine; armed with ice early.

ecotypes.name: Charging herd
ecotypes.reading: Three full-body charges, the habit Piloswine is known for (it keeps charging, hackles up). A lineage that meets threats head-on; fits open snowfields with nowhere to hide.
ecotypes.behavior: Charges first and roots afterwards.

open_questions: What is the mushroom, and what decomposes the dead grass it grows on? These are the decomposers at the base of Swinub's food chain, and nothing names them.
Where do Ice Path Swinub feed? There is no dead grass in an ice cave.
How does it find hot springs: smell, warmth, the sound of water? 220.8 credits its nose.
Is it day-active? Crystal suggests so; HeartGold and SoulSilver don't split it by time.
Does it eat animal food? Bite is an egg move, but the entries name only mushrooms and berries.
What eats Swinub? No predator is named.

Typhlosion.summary: A large grassland animal with blazing fur that hides behind its own heat. Typhlosion makes the air around it shimmer with intense flame and conceals itself in the haze; when the shimmer rises it is ready to fight, and at the peak of its rage anything that touches it bursts into flame. Its young, Cyndaquil, are timid animals that curl into a ball and flare the fire on their backs only when startled, and whose flames sputter with incomplete combustion when they are tired. The Pokédex never says what the line eats, and no game has it in the wild.

anatomy.text: A heavy quadruped (1.7 m, 79.5 kg) with blazing fur.
Quilava's fur is non-flammable, and it can withstand any fire attack, so the line is insulated against its own fire.
Cyndaquil's fire comes from its back; Quilava attacks with the fire on its back.
What it burns is never said. Incomplete combustion in a tired Cyndaquil implies a fuel and an oxygen supply that can fall out of balance, as in any real flame.

diet.text: No entry for any stage says what the line eats.
An animal that keeps a fire burning must eat a lot for its size, and a tired Cyndaquil's fire fails first, so food and flame are probably linked.

habitat.text: The Gen 3 Pokédex lists the line under grassland; no entry describes where it lives.
It is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game. Cyndaquil is a starter gift in New Bark Town in every Johto game, and a gift in Littleroot Town in Emerald.

behavior.text: It hides behind a shimmering heat haze made with its own intense flames.
behavior.analogy: Heat shimmer is real: light bends as it passes through air layers of different temperature, the same effect as a mirage over a hot road.

behavior.text: The shimmer is also a signal: when heat from its body makes the air shimmer, it is ready to battle.
Cyndaquil is timid: it curls into a ball or stays hunched over, and its back flames burn more strongly when startled or angry.
No activity pattern is given.

social.text: Nothing is said about groups or how it treats its own kind.
Its fire is readable by others: Cyndaquil's flames show anger and tiredness, Quilava's show readiness to fight, and Typhlosion's heat shimmer announces it. A line that signals its state with flame.

reproduction.text: Field egg group, 20 egg cycles, 87.5% male (the usual starter ratio). Nothing in the Pokédex describes breeding or young.

defense.text: At the peak of its rage it gets so hot that anything touching it instantly bursts into flames.
Its 'secret, devastating move' is rubbing its blazing fur together to cause huge explosions; its blasts burn everything to cinders.
Quilava keeps foes back with flame and gusts of superheated air, dodging nimbly while it burns them, and turns its back before a fight to show how fiercely its fire blazes.
Cyndaquil flares its back flames for protection; the flare itself intimidates.
Smokescreen (Lv 6) and Defense Curl (Lv 24) are its own: smoke to blind, and curling up, which matches the young's habit.

senses.text: Nothing is said about its senses.

life_cycle.text: Cyndaquil (0.5 m, 7.9 kg) becomes Quilava at level 14 (0.9 m, 19.0 kg; the archive also lists 17) and Typhlosion at level 36 (1.7 m, 79.5 kg).
Temperament changes with stage: a timid young animal that curls up, a nimble intimidator that shows off its fire, then an adult that hides in heat haze and explodes when pushed.
Its fire moves from a defensive flare on the back to the whole coat: Typhlosion's fur itself blazes.

moves_in_the_wild.text: Level-up moves are its own (it is never wild in the games): Ember, Flame Wheel (Lv 20), Lava Plume (Lv 35), Flamethrower (Lv 42) and Eruption (Lv 57), which is strongest at full health, for the explosive blasts of the canon.
Lava Plume hits everything around it and can burn, the closest move to 'anything that touches it goes up in flames'.
Defense Curl followed by Rollout (Lv 46) is a curl-and-roll pairing that suits a line whose young curl into a ball.
Blast Burn, Fire Punch and Thunder Punch are tutor moves: taught, not wild.

ecology.text: Its role in a food web is unknown because its diet is.
An animal that bursts into flame when enraged and blasts things to cinders is a fire risk in dry grassland, its listed habitat.

humans.text: Its line reaches people as a Johto starter, given in New Bark Town.
No entry describes it working with people; the record is about its fire and its temper.

homestead.text: A heat source for a cold highland: a Fire type that can make the air shimmer around it. It needs a calm life; heat rises with its anger.
Not for wooden buildings or hay: anything that touches an enraged Typhlosion ignites, and its fur-rubbing explosions are its signature attack.
Indoors, watch a tired Cyndaquil: its flames sputter with incomplete combustion, and incomplete combustion produces smoke and carbon monoxide. Good ventilation wherever the young sleep.
A flame that tells you how it is doing: sputtering means tired, vigorous means angry or startled.
Fire-safe handling gear could borrow from Quilava's non-flammable fur, if shed fur can be collected.
Could it gently warm the hatchery's egg racks? Possibly, but the Glasshouse already has a Magcargo hearth, and a startled Cyndaquil flares.
homestead.note: No entry says it warms anything gently; its heat is tied to fear and anger.

homestead.text: Needs: quiet. Cyndaquil is timid, and every stage's fire rises with fear or anger.

niche.foraging: unknown; no entry says what any stage eats
niche.note: Guild left empty: the machine reading's thermotroph comes from the Fire type alone.

ecotypes.name: Wildfire charger
ecotypes.reading: The rage canon made into a lineage: Howl raises its attack, Flare Blitz is a burning full-body charge that hurts the user too, and Thrash is an uncontrolled rampage. An animal that answers threats with all-out attack, matching the Typhlosion that ignites anything touching it at the peak of its rage. Fits dry, open grassland where there is nowhere to hide.
ecotypes.behavior: Builds to a howl, then charges in flames; dangerous to everything nearby, including grass.

ecotypes.name: Grass-root forager
ecotypes.reading: A clawed, searching lineage: Foresight finds hidden or evasive targets, and Fury Swipes and Crush Claw rake and tear. A digger and seeker of things hidden in turf and soil rather than a fire-fighter. Fits short grassland and field edges with soft soil.
ecotypes.behavior: Noses through the turf and claws out what it finds; uses fire less.

ecotypes.name: Ember pilferer
ecotypes.reading: A timid opportunist: Covet snatches what the target is holding, Quick Attack gets in and out first, and Extrasensory is an odd psychic sense that would help it judge when to move. The shy Cyndaquil temperament carried into adulthood, taking food rather than fighting for it. Fits farm edges and settlements where food is lying about.
ecotypes.behavior: Steals and runs; flares only when cornered.

open_questions: What does it eat, and what fuels its fire?
Where does a wild population live? The games give it only as a starter; 'grassland' is the only habitat on record.
How does rubbing its fur cause explosions (157.2)?
Does Typhlosion keep Quilava's non-flammable fur?
Does it live alone or in groups, and who reads its flame signals?
No relationships are recorded: no entry names prey, predators or other species, and it has no wild range to share.

contradictions.text: Cyndaquil's posture: Gold and HeartGold say it always curls itself up in a ball; Silver and SoulSilver say it usually stays hunched over.
contradictions.note: Minor: a ball versus a hunch.

Tyranitar.summary: An armoured mountain giant with a life cycle like an insect's: larva, pupa, adult. Larvitar is born deep underground and eats soil until it has eaten its way to the surface and, as two Hoenn entries put it, can finally see its parents' faces; once it has eaten 'a large mountain' it sleeps and becomes Pupitar, a rock-hard pupa that still moves and can launch itself by venting gas. The adult brings down mountainsides to make its nest and roams the peaks looking for a fight; in a rampage it buries rivers, and maps must be redrawn. In Johto the young live on Mt. Silver.

anatomy.text: A huge upright animal (2.0 m, 202.0 kg) whose body, by its own entries, can't be harmed by any sort of attack.
anatomy.note: An overstatement in game terms: as a Rock/Dark type it has several weaknesses.

anatomy.text: Its hands are its main tool: one is enough to make the ground shake and mountains crumble.
Larvitar is extraordinarily dense: 72.0 kg at 0.6 m tall, which fits an animal that eats soil and rock.
Pupitar's shell is as hard as sheet rock or bedrock and survives collision with solid steel; arms and legs are already formed beneath it.
Pupitar makes gas inside its body, compresses it and vents it to propel itself like a jet or rocket.

diet.text: Larvitar eats soil, and keeps eating until it has eaten 'a large mountain'.
diet.analogy: Earthworms also eat soil and digest the organic matter in it; Larvitar does the same at an impossible scale.

diet.text: No entry says what Pupitar or Tyranitar eat. A pupa probably doesn't feed; the adult's diet is simply missing.
Whether Larvitar digests the minerals or the organic matter in soil is not said.

habitat.text: Mountains: the adult wanders and nests in them; its Gen 3 Pokédex habitat is mountain.
Larvitar starts life deep underground and has to eat its way up to the surface.

Tyranitar is not found in the wild in any Gen I-IV game. In HeartGold and SoulSilver, Larvitar is uncommon (5%) on every level of Mt. Silver and a little commoner at the top (10%); Pupitar is on Mt. Silver 3F (5%). Larvitar also appears in the Johto Safari Zone.

Elsewhere it is a special find: a Poké Radar encounter on Sinnoh's Route 207 in Diamond, a swarm on Route 206 in Platinum, rare in Sevault Canyon in FireRed and LeafGreen, and a Game Corner prize in Crystal.

behavior.text: It seeks fights: it roams the mountains looking for new opponents, and, unable to be harmed, is eager to challenge them.
Insolent: it doesn't care about others.
Larvitar alternates feeding and sleep: once it has eaten enough, it falls asleep so it can grow.
Pupitar will not stay still, even as a pupa.
Crystal has Larvitar and Pupitar only by day and morning; Gold, Silver, HeartGold and SoulSilver have Larvitar at all hours.

social.text: Larvitar cannot see its parents until it reaches the surface, so at least one parent is somewhere above it while it digs.
The adult is indifferent to others and roams alone looking for opponents.

reproduction.text: Monster egg group, an even sex ratio, slow growth, and 40 egg cycles, twice the usual.
Read together, the entries suggest a nesting system: the adult brings down a mountainside to make its nest, the young are born deep underground, and they eat their way up to reach their parents.
reproduction.note: No single entry connects the nest to the buried young; this is a reading of four entries together.

reproduction.text: If so, the parents bury their offspring under rubble and the young dig out alone, which is unusual parental care: protection by burial, not by tending.

defense.text: Armour at every stage: a near-invulnerable adult body, a pupal shell that withstands steel, and a dense, rock-skinned larva.
